She should not be discharged. The on-call obstetrics and gynaecology service should be phoned now, intravenous access secured, blood taken for group and hold, and same-night transfer or imaging arranged.

learning_point: A woman with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding and a positive pregnancy test has an ectopic pregnancy until ultrasound proves otherwise; stable observations and a quantitative hCG cannot exclude it.
setting_note: Where ultrasound is unavailable overnight, discuss immediately with the on-call obstetrics and gynaecology service, secure intravenous access and a group and hold, and arrange transfer or same-night imaging rather than discharging her to return for a scan; involve the retrieval service early if she deteriorates.

references.title: South Australian Perinatal Practice Guideline - Ectopic Pregnancy
references.locator: Diagnosis - pregnancy of unknown location, role of serum hCG and transvaginal ultrasound

references.title: RANZCOG - Early pregnancy complications (ectopic pregnancy) clinical guidance
references.locator: Assessment of pain and bleeding in early pregnancy

plan: Tests interpretation of early pregnancy pain and bleeding when ultrasound is unavailable (outcomes 1.4, 1.5, 1.9). A woman at 7 weeks with unilateral pain, spotting and hCG 2,100 IU/L asks to go home. The distractors each misuse one reassuring feature (stable observations, hCG above the discriminatory level, laterality) to reach a false diagnosis. Supported by the SA Perinatal Practice Guideline on ectopic pregnancy.
tutor_context: Key facts: pregnancy of unknown location is a positive hCG with no intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy seen on ultrasound; the discriminatory hCG level helps interpret an ultrasound, not replace it; ectopic pregnancy remains a leading cause of maternal death in the first trimester; risk factors include previous ectopic, tubal surgery, pelvic infection and assisted reproduction but most women have none. Common misconceptions: that normal observations exclude ectopic; that bleeding means miscarriage; that a 'high' hCG proves an intrauterine pregnancy. Out of scope: methotrexate versus surgical management.

critic.blind_reasoning: A positive pregnancy test with pain and bleeding and no ultrasound is a pregnancy of unknown location; ectopic must be assumed until an intrauterine pregnancy is demonstrated. A serum hCG above the discriminatory zone without a visible intrauterine pregnancy, if anything, raises suspicion of ectopic rather than confirming an intrauterine gestation.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Strong item. The explanation should address the disposition question raised in the stem (phone O&G, likely not safe to discharge without a plan, consider transfer) since the lead-in only asks interpretation. Target difficulty 4 is generous; this is closer to 2-3.

stem: You are the junior doctor in the emergency department of a regional hospital with a small medical ward, no intensive care unit, CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 19-year-old woman with known asthma arrives at 02:00 with 6 hours of worsening wheeze after a viral illness. In the past hour she has had salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer three times, ipratropium and oral prednisolone 50 mg. She can speak only in single words, sits forward using her accessory muscles, and has a respiratory rate of 32, heart rate 128, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min oxygen by mask and a quiet chest with faint wheeze. A venous blood gas shows pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L and lactate 2.8 mmol/L. The nurse comments that the gas 'looks normal'.
lead_in: How should the blood gas result be interpreted?

options.text: The normal pH and pCO2 confirm a moderate attack that can continue on the current treatment
A normal or rising pCO2 in a patient this breathless indicates exhaustion and impending respiratory failure
The raised lactate indicates sepsis as the cause of her deterioration
A venous gas cannot be interpreted in acute asthma and an arterial sample is required before any decision

explanations.A: A patient breathing at 32 per minute should be blowing off carbon dioxide and have a low pCO2. A 'normal' pCO2 here is abnormal, and her clinical features (single words, accessory muscles, quiet chest) already place her in the severe to life-threatening category regardless of the gas.
explanations.B: In severe asthma, a pCO2 that is normal or rising means ventilation is no longer keeping up with the work of breathing: she is tiring and is at risk of respiratory arrest. This requires immediate senior involvement, continuous nebulised salbutamol, intravenous magnesium and, in a hospital without intensive care, an urgent call to the retrieval service and the physician on call.
explanations.C: A mildly raised lactate in acute asthma is common and is largely due to high-dose salbutamol and the work of breathing; nothing here suggests sepsis, and chasing that explanation would distract from the airway threat.
explanations.D: A venous gas is adequate to screen pCO2 and pH in acute asthma, and arterial sampling should not delay escalation. The clinical picture alone demands action.

learning_point: In acute asthma a hyperventilating patient should have a low pCO2; a normal or rising pCO2 with severe clinical features signals exhaustion and impending respiratory failure and requires immediate senior and retrieval involvement.
setting_note: With no intensive care unit on site, this patient needs an urgent call to the retrieval service and the physician on call now, continuous nebulised salbutamol and intravenous magnesium while awaiting transfer; do not wait for further deterioration before calling.

references.title: National Asthma Council Australia - Australian Asthma Handbook
references.locator: Acute asthma in adults and adolescents - assessing severity and indications for intensive care

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory
references.locator: Acute asthma in adults - severe and life-threatening asthma

plan: Tests interpretation of a deceptively normal blood gas in severe asthma at a hospital without intensive care (outcomes 1.5, 1.9). A young woman with severe clinical features has a normal pCO2 and a mildly raised lactate. Distractors are false reassurance from the gas, misattribution of lactate to sepsis, and insistence on an arterial sample. Supported by the Australian Asthma Handbook and Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory.
tutor_context: Key facts: severity is judged clinically (ability to speak, work of breathing, oxygen saturation, conscious state, chest sounds); a normal or raised pCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic is a sign of fatigue; salbutamol causes lactate rise; life-threatening asthma warrants continuous nebulised salbutamol, intravenous magnesium 10 mmol, and early intensive care or retrieval. Common misconceptions: that a normal gas is reassuring; that arterial sampling is needed before acting; that a quiet chest means improvement. Out of scope: ventilation strategies.

critic.blind_reasoning: In acute severe asthma the pCO2 should be low from hyperventilation; a normal pCO2 of 44 in a patient speaking single words with a quiet chest indicates fatigue and impending respiratory failure, a life-threatening feature. The lactate is most likely from salbutamol and work of breathing.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good item. Explanation should mention this patient needs retrieval activation and that a venous gas is acceptable for pCO2 screening.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital at 23:00; the medical registrar is on site and the orthopaedic registrar is on call from home. A 23-year-old man presents with 4 days of severe low back pain after lifting a heavy box at work. Today he has developed numbness around his buttocks and perineum, has had difficulty starting his urine stream, and did not notice passing a small amount of urine in his underwear. Examination shows power 4/5 in ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally, reduced sensation in the S3 to S4 dermatomes and reduced anal tone. His observations are normal and he is afebrile. A bladder scan shows a post-void residual of 650 mL. He asks for strong pain relief so he can go home and see his GP.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Inform the registrar now and request urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine
Request plain X-rays of the lumbar spine and review the result before escalating
Insert an indwelling catheter, give analgesia and admit for physiotherapy review in the morning
Discharge with analgesia and a referral for an outpatient MRI within one week

explanations.A: Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention with overflow, bilateral leg weakness and reduced anal tone are cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise. The intern's job is immediate escalation to the registrar and an emergency MRI (or CT if MRI is unavailable), with referral to the spinal or neurosurgical service, because outcome depends on time to decompression. An indwelling catheter and analgesia are given alongside, not instead.
explanations.B: Plain X-rays do not show disc herniation or cord compression and will not change the need for MRI; waiting for them delays the diagnosis.
explanations.C: Catheterising a retaining bladder is appropriate supportive care, but admitting him for physiotherapy in the morning treats this as mechanical back pain and misses the surgical emergency.
explanations.D: Discharge is unsafe. Red flags for cauda equina syndrome require same-day imaging, not an outpatient scan.

learning_point: Back pain with saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence and reduced anal tone is cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise and needs immediate escalation and emergency MRI, because outcome depends on time to decompression.
setting_note: In a rural hospital without MRI the same findings mandate an immediate phone call to the on-call surgical or spinal service and arrangement of urgent transfer for imaging; do not wait for morning.

references.title: Low Back Pain Clinical Care Standard (2022)
references.locator: Quality statement 1 - Initial clinical assessment: features suggesting serious pathology including cauda equina syndrome

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology
references.locator: Low back pain - red flags and urgent referral

plan: Tests recognition and immediate escalation of cauda equina syndrome by an intern (outcomes 1.4, 1.9, 1.7). A young man with mechanical-sounding back pain develops saddle anaesthesia, retention and reduced anal tone. Distractors are X-ray first, supportive care with morning physiotherapy, and discharge with outpatient MRI. Supported by the ACSQHC Low Back Pain Clinical Care Standard.
tutor_context: Key facts: cauda equina red flags are bilateral sciatica or leg weakness, saddle sensory change, bladder or bowel dysfunction (retention, overflow, loss of sensation of voiding) and reduced anal tone; a post-void residual above about 200 mL supports retention; MRI is the investigation of choice and the time window for decompression is hours. Common misconceptions: that unilateral or young patients cannot have cauda equina syndrome; that X-rays are a useful first step. Out of scope: surgical technique and outcomes data.

critic.blind_reasoning: Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention with overflow, reduced anal tone and bilateral weakness is cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency requiring immediate senior involvement and urgent MRI. Plain films, admission for physiotherapy or outpatient MRI would all delay decompression.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Clinical picture is quite florid for a difficulty 2 item; fine for PGY1. B and D are weak distractors.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with 24-hour imaging. A 56-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of constant mid-thoracic back pain that wakes her at night and is not relieved by rest or paracetamol. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.1%) and finished oral antibiotics for a urinary tract infection 3 weeks ago. She has had sweats and feels generally unwell. Temperature is 38.1 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg. There is midline tenderness over T7 to T8 without deformity. Lower limb power, sensation and reflexes are normal and she has no sphincter symptoms. Blood tests show a white cell count of 13.8 x 10^9/L and CRP 164 mg/L. A thoracic spine X-ray is reported as normal for age.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?

options.text: Mechanical back pain with a residual urinary infection, suitable for analgesia and GP follow-up
An osteoporotic vertebral fracture not yet visible on X-ray, needing a repeat film in 2 weeks
Probable vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess, needing urgent MRI and blood cultures
Thoracic pain of cardiac origin, to be investigated with troponin and ECG before spinal imaging

explanations.A: Night pain unrelieved by rest, fever, sweats and a CRP of 164 mg/L are red flags that are incompatible with simple mechanical back pain. A recent urinary infection is a plausible source of bacteraemia seeding the spine, not a reason for reassurance.
explanations.B: An insufficiency fracture can be radiographically occult, but it does not cause fever, sweats and a markedly raised CRP. Waiting 2 weeks for a repeat film risks progression to cord compression if infection is present.
explanations.C: Fever, raised inflammatory markers, diabetes and recent infection with localised spinal tenderness make spinal infection the diagnosis to exclude. Plain X-rays are often normal for weeks, and neurological signs appear late. The correct actions are blood cultures before antibiotics (if she remains stable), urgent MRI of the whole spine and early discussion with the infectious diseases and spinal or neurosurgical teams; antibiotics start empirically if she becomes septic or develops neurological deficit.
explanations.D: Constant pain over 2 weeks with midline tenderness and fever is not an acute coronary syndrome pattern. A screening ECG is reasonable in a diabetic woman, but it must not delay spinal imaging.

learning_point: Back pain with fever, raised inflammatory markers and risk factors such as diabetes or recent infection suggests spinal infection; a normal X-ray and normal neurological examination do not exclude it, and MRI with blood cultures is the next step.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without MRI, take blood cultures, discuss with the physician or infectious diseases service on call and arrange transfer for MRI; start empirical antibiotics after cultures only if she is septic or develops neurological signs.

references.title: Low Back Pain Clinical Care Standard (2022)
references.locator: Quality statement 1 - features suggesting serious pathology (infection, fracture, malignancy)

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Vertebral osteomyelitis and spinal epidural abscess - diagnosis and empirical therapy

plan: Tests interpretation of red-flag back pain pointing to spinal infection with a normal X-ray and intact neurology (outcomes 1.4, 1.5). A diabetic woman with night pain, fever, recent urinary infection and CRP 164 mg/L is the vignette. Distractors anchor on the normal X-ray, the recent urinary infection or her cardiac risk. Supported by the ACSQHC Low Back Pain Clinical Care Standard and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic.
tutor_context: Key facts: red flags for spinal infection are fever, immunosuppression or diabetes, intravenous drug use, recent bacteraemia or instrumentation, and raised CRP or ESR; MRI with contrast is the investigation of choice and plain films are insensitive early; take at least two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics unless the patient is septic; neurological deficit is a late sign and a surgical emergency. Common misconceptions: that a normal X-ray or normal neurology excludes serious spinal pathology; that antibiotics should be started before cultures in a stable patient. Out of scope: choice and duration of antibiotics.

critic.blind_reasoning: Subacute thoracic back pain with night pain, fever, sweats, poorly controlled diabetes, recent infection, midline tenderness and markedly raised CRP is spinal infection until proven otherwise; a normal X-ray does not exclude it and neurology can be normal early. Urgent MRI and blood cultures before antibiotics are required.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Trim C to match the length of the others (e.g. 'Probable vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess requiring urgent MRI and blood cultures') and move the 'despite normal X-ray' point into the explanation.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): C is noticeably longer than the other options and pre-empts the obvious objections ('despite the normal X-ray and neurology'), which reads as the examiner's explanation and cues the key.

stem: You are the intern at a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with specialist advice available by phone. A 21-year-old man presents at 20:00 with 2 days of fever, productive cough and increasing shortness of breath. He has no chronic lung disease and does not smoke. Observations: respiratory rate 28, heart rate 112, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, temperature 38.9 C, SpO2 89% on room air. There are coarse crackles at the right base. The nurse has applied oxygen by nasal prongs at 2 L/min and asks you to prescribe the oxygen on the medication chart with a target saturation range so that she knows when to titrate it up or down overnight.
lead_in: Which target oxygen saturation range should be prescribed for this patient?

options.text: At least 98%

explanations.A: A target of 88 to 92% is reserved for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as those with COPD, severe obesity or neuromuscular disease. A healthy 21-year-old with pneumonia is not in that group and would be under-oxygenated.
explanations.B: Australian and New Zealand guidance for acute oxygen use in adults sets a target of 92 to 96% for acutely unwell patients without risk of hypercapnia. Prescribing the target lets nursing staff titrate flow safely and recognise rising oxygen requirements as deterioration.
explanations.C: A range of 94 to 98% is used in some overseas guidelines but is not the Australian recommendation, and the upper end encourages unnecessary oxygen that can mask deterioration.
explanations.D: Aiming for 98% or above means running high-flow oxygen regardless of need; hyperoxia is not beneficial and a saturation of 100% hides a rising oxygen requirement.

learning_point: For acutely unwell adults without a risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, oxygen is prescribed to a target saturation of 92 to 96%; 88 to 92% is reserved for patients at risk of hypercapnia such as those with COPD.
setting_note: In a regional hospital with no intensive care unit and a finite oxygen supply, titrating to a target rather than running high-flow oxygen by default conserves supply and reveals deterioration early; a young patient needing more than a few litres per minute to hold 92% should prompt an early call to the physician on call and the retrieval service.

references.title: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand - Acute oxygen use in adults: 'Swimming between the flags' (Beasley et al., Respirology 2015)
references.locator: Recommendations - target oxygen saturation 92 to 96% for most acutely unwell patients; 88 to 92% if at risk of hypercapnia

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory
references.locator: Acute oxygen therapy - target saturations

plan: Tests recall of the Australian target oxygen saturation range for an acutely unwell adult without hypercapnia risk (outcomes 1.8, 1.9). A young man with pneumonia and SpO2 89% needs oxygen prescribed overnight at a regional hospital. Distractors are the COPD target, an overseas range and a maximal target. Supported by the TSANZ acute oxygen guideline and Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory.
tutor_context: Key facts: oxygen is a drug and must be prescribed with a target range; 92 to 96% for most acutely unwell adults, 88 to 92% for those at risk of hypercapnia; a rising oxygen requirement is an escalation criterion; this patient also needs sepsis assessment, blood cultures and antibiotics per community-acquired pneumonia guidance. Common misconceptions: that more oxygen is always safer; that a saturation of 100% is the goal. Out of scope: antibiotic choice for pneumonia and the SMART-COP score.

critic.blind_reasoning: For an acutely unwell adult without risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, the Australian TSANZ guideline and eTG recommend a target SpO2 of 92-96%; 88-92% is reserved for those at risk of hypercapnia, and higher targets risk hyperoxia.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Explanation must cite TSANZ (Beasley et al.) and eTG and explicitly contrast with the BTS 94-98% target, or candidates trained on BTS will dispute the key. Consider also noting this patient is hypoxic enough that nasal prongs at 2 L may be insufficient and senior review is needed.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with on-site intensive care. A 29-year-old man is brought in by ambulance 25 minutes after a petrol fire in a shed. He has partial-thickness burns to his face, neck, anterior chest and both forearms, estimated by paramedics at 18% of total body surface area. The burns have not been cooled. He has singed nasal hairs and eyebrows, soot around his mouth, a hoarse voice and is coughing up carbonaceous sputum. He speaks in full sentences but his voice has changed since the paramedics first assessed him. Observations: respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% on 15 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather mask, heart rate 118, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg. He has one intravenous cannula and is in severe pain. The ED consultant is with another patient.
lead_in: Which of the following should be done first?

options.text: Call the ED consultant and anaesthetist to secure the airway early
Start cooling the burns with cool running water for 20 minutes
Calculate the fluid requirements and start the resuscitation infusion
Give intravenous morphine and cover the burns with cling film

explanations.A: Facial burns with singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth, carbonaceous sputum and a voice that is changing are signs of inhalation injury. Airway oedema progresses over hours and intubation becomes much harder once it develops, so the airway must be assessed by the most senior available doctor now and secured early. Everything else follows once help is on its way.
explanations.B: Cooling with running water for 20 minutes is effective for up to 3 hours after a burn and should be done, but it is not the first priority when the airway is threatened; it can be started by nursing staff while senior help is called.
explanations.C: Fluid resuscitation is needed for an 18% burn and is calculated from the time of injury, but it is a circulation step that comes after the airway is addressed.
explanations.D: Analgesia and simple covering of the burns are important, but opioids before the airway is assessed may hasten obstruction in a patient with inhalation injury.

learning_point: Facial burns with singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth, carbonaceous sputum and a changing voice indicate inhalation injury with impending airway obstruction; securing the airway early with senior help takes precedence over cooling, fluids and dressings.
setting_note: In a rural hospital the same signs mean calling the GP anaesthetist or the retrieval service immediately, because the airway may need to be secured before transfer and the window closes as oedema develops.

references.title: Australian and New Zealand Burn Association - Emergency Management of Severe Burns (EMSB) course manual
references.locator: Primary survey - airway and inhalation injury; first aid for burns

references.title: Australian and New Zealand Burn Association - Burn first aid and referral criteria
references.locator: Cooling for 20 minutes within 3 hours; referral criteria including inhalation injury

plan: Tests prioritisation of the airway in a burns patient with inhalation injury (outcomes 1.9, 1.4). A man with 18% facial and chest burns has singed nasal hairs, carbonaceous sputum and a changing voice; the consultant is busy. Distractors are the other correct but lower-priority steps: cooling, fluids, analgesia and dressings. Supported by the ANZBA EMSB manual.
tutor_context: Key facts: inhalation injury signs are facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in sputum, hoarseness, stridor and burns sustained in an enclosed space; airway oedema peaks over hours, so early intubation by an experienced operator is the rule; first aid is 20 minutes of cool running water within 3 hours; fluid resuscitation for burns over 15 to 20% is calculated from the time of injury; burns to the face, hands and airway meet burn unit referral criteria. Common misconceptions: that normal saturations exclude airway compromise; that cooling must be done before anything else. Out of scope: formulae for fluid volume and escharotomy.

critic.blind_reasoning: Facial burns in an enclosed-space fire with singed nasal hair, soot, carbonaceous sputum and a progressively hoarse voice indicate inhalation injury with evolving airway oedema; airway comes first and early intubation before obstruction is the priority. Cooling, fluids and analgesia follow.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good prioritisation item with a tempting distractor in B. Explanation should note cooling can proceed in parallel once help is called and should not be delayed beyond 3 hours.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with specialist advice by phone. A 28-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents with 2 days of vomiting after running out of insulin. He is alert, with heart rate 118, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 and dry mucous membranes. Point-of-care results: glucose 29 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L. The nurse has started 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour and has drawn up an insulin infusion (50 units in 50 mL) according to the hospital DKA protocol. She asks you to prescribe the insulin now. The physician on call has not yet returned your call.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start the insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour and add potassium to the next litre of fluid
Give insulin 10 units as an intravenous bolus, then start the protocol insulin infusion
Withhold insulin, replace potassium intravenously and recheck before starting the infusion
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis before starting insulin

explanations.A: Starting insulin with a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L drives potassium into cells and can cause life-threatening hypokalaemia and arrhythmia within the first hour. Potassium must be replaced first.
explanations.B: An intravenous insulin bolus is not recommended in adult DKA and does not change the need to correct potassium before any insulin is given.
explanations.C: Australian guidance is that insulin is withheld if the potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L, potassium is replaced intravenously (for example 10 mmol/hour via a peripheral line with cardiac monitoring, or faster under senior direction), and insulin is started once the potassium is 3.5 mmol/L or above. Fluid resuscitation continues meanwhile, and the physician on call and the retrieval service should be contacted early for a patient with pH 7.14.
explanations.D: Bicarbonate is not routinely used in DKA and is considered only for severe acidosis (pH below about 7.0) on senior advice; it also lowers potassium further.

learning_point: In DKA, insulin must be withheld if the potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L; replace potassium first and recheck, because insulin drives potassium into cells and can precipitate fatal arrhythmia.
setting_note: The potassium rule does not change with setting, but in a regional hospital the physician on call and the retrieval service should be contacted early for a patient this acidotic, and continuous cardiac monitoring is essential during potassium replacement.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetes
references.locator: Diabetic ketoacidosis in adults - potassium replacement and timing of insulin infusion

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Potassium chloride - intravenous replacement, monitoring

plan: Tests the potassium-before-insulin rule in DKA at a level a PGY1 must know when the nurse is pushing to start insulin and the physician has not called back (outcomes 1.8, 1.9). The vignette gives pH 7.14 and potassium 3.1 mmol/L. Distractors are starting insulin with potassium in the next bag, an insulin bolus and bicarbonate. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Diabetes and the AMH.
tutor_context: Key facts: total body potassium is depleted in DKA even when the serum level is normal or high; insulin and correction of acidosis both lower serum potassium; thresholds are withhold insulin below 3.5 mmol/L, replace with insulin between 3.5 and 5.0, and withhold potassium above 5.0 or if anuric; insulin infusion rate is 0.1 units/kg/hour without a bolus; monitor potassium hourly initially with ECG monitoring. Common misconceptions: that high glucose makes insulin the first priority; that bicarbonate is needed for pH 7.1. Out of scope: management of cerebral oedema and sodium correction.

critic.blind_reasoning: In DKA, insulin must not be started while potassium is below about 3.3-3.5 mmol/L because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and can precipitate arrhythmia; the correct step is to withhold insulin, replace potassium intravenously and recheck before starting the infusion. Bolus insulin and bicarbonate are not recommended.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Well-constructed safety item. Explanation should give the threshold used by SA Health/eTG (hold insulin if K < 3.5, replace at 10-20 mmol/h with monitoring) and note the need for cardiac monitoring and retrieval discussion.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with on-site intensive care. You are managing a 31-year-old man with type 1 diabetes in diabetic ketoacidosis, admitted 2 hours ago with pH 7.08, glucose 32 mmol/L and potassium 5.1 mmol/L. He has received 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride, an insulin infusion is running at 6 units/hour and potassium 10 mmol/hour was started with the second litre. He is alert. The nurse hands you the 2-hour results and a list: the venous gas shows pH 7.18, glucose 14.2 mmol/L and potassium 3.1 mmol/L; the glucose is now below the level at which the protocol requires a 10% glucose infusion to be added; the ED consultant has asked you to phone the medical registrar to refer him for admission; and the patient is asking for a drink of water. The ED consultant is now intubating a trauma patient.
lead_in: Which of these should you attend to first?

options.text: Add 10% glucose so that the insulin infusion can continue at its current rate
Phone the medical registrar to refer him for admission, as the consultant asked
Chart oral fluids so that he can have the drink of water he is asking for
Increase potassium replacement; ask a senior about reducing or pausing insulin

explanations.A: Adding glucose when the blood glucose falls below about 15 mmol/L is a protocol step that is due within the hour, but a glucose of 14 mmol/L is not dangerous right now, whereas the potassium is.
explanations.B: The referral can wait a few minutes; the registrar will want to know what you have done about the potassium in any case.
explanations.C: Sips of water are reasonable in an alert patient who is no longer vomiting, but this is the least urgent item on the list.
explanations.D: The potassium has fallen from 5.1 to 3.1 mmol/L in 2 hours while insulin and fluids continue to drive it lower, and a level below 3.5 mmol/L carries a risk of fatal arrhythmia. The most time-critical action is to increase potassium replacement with cardiac monitoring and, because the consultant is unavailable, to speak to the medical or intensive care registrar about reducing or pausing insulin until the potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L. Protocol steps and the referral follow.

learning_point: During DKA treatment a potassium that has fallen below 3.5 mmol/L is the most time-critical abnormality, because insulin and fluids drive it lower and the risk is fatal arrhythmia; escalate and replace it before the routine protocol steps.
setting_note: In a rural hospital a falling potassium during DKA treatment and limited capacity for cardiac monitoring or higher-rate potassium replacement are reasons to involve the retrieval service early; the order of priorities does not change.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetes
references.locator: Diabetic ketoacidosis in adults - monitoring, potassium replacement and adding glucose

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Potassium chloride - intravenous administration rates and monitoring

plan: Tests prioritisation during ongoing DKA treatment when several protocol steps compete with a dangerous potassium (outcomes 1.9, 1.8, 2.8). Two hours in, potassium has fallen to 3.1 mmol/L while the glucose threshold for adding dextrose, a referral and a patient request all call for attention. Distractors are each a legitimate task but none is time-critical. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Diabetes and the AMH.
tutor_context: Key facts: potassium typically falls steeply in the first hours of DKA treatment; check it at least hourly initially; below 3.5 mmol/L insulin is paused or reduced and potassium replacement increased with ECG monitoring; peripheral replacement is usually limited to 10 mmol/hour, with higher rates needing a central line or senior approval; glucose 10% is added when blood glucose falls below about 15 mmol/L so that insulin can continue to clear ketones. Common misconceptions: that falling glucose is the main marker of progress; that insulin should never be interrupted in DKA. Out of scope: resolution criteria and transition to subcutaneous insulin.

critic.blind_reasoning: Potassium has fallen from 5.1 to 3.1 in two hours on 10 mmol/h with insulin at 6 units/h; this is the most dangerous abnormality and takes priority. Protocols require increasing potassium replacement and reducing or pausing insulin when K falls below 3.3-3.5. The glucose infusion is also needed but hypoglycaemia at 14.2 mmol/L is not imminent; the referral and oral fluids can wait.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: B and C are throwaway distractors; the item is really a two-way choice between A and D. Acceptable for difficulty 4, but the explanation must argue explicitly why hypokalaemia outranks adding glucose and should say both must be done promptly. Specify which senior (medical registrar or ICU) given the ED consultant is intubating.

stem: You are working in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with 24-hour CT. A 68-year-old woman is brought in by her husband. Two hours ago, while lifting a pot plant in the garden, she developed a sudden severe occipital headache that reached its maximum within seconds; she describes it as the worst headache of her life. She vomited once and has felt nauseated since. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and no history of migraine. On arrival the headache has eased to 6 out of 10 after paracetamol. She is alert and orientated with a GCS of 15, no neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit and normal fundi. Blood pressure is 168/96 mmHg, heart rate 84 and temperature 36.7 C.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this presentation?

options.text: A thunderclap headache in which subarachnoid haemorrhage must be excluded by urgent CT brain
A first episode of migraine without aura that can be treated with analgesia and reviewed if it recurs
A hypertensive headache that will settle once her blood pressure is controlled
A tension-type headache precipitated by exertion that does not require imaging

explanations.A: A headache that reaches maximum intensity within a minute is a thunderclap headache, and subarachnoid haemorrhage is the diagnosis to exclude regardless of how she looks now. Onset with exertion, vomiting and age over 50 add to the risk. She needs an urgent non-contrast CT brain and senior review; if the CT is normal and performed more than 6 hours after onset, lumbar puncture or CT angiography follows.
explanations.B: A new migraine at 68 with no prior history and an abrupt onset is a red-flag presentation, not a first migraine; migraine builds over minutes to hours.
explanations.C: A blood pressure of 168/96 mmHg is a response to pain and anxiety and does not cause a thunderclap headache; treating the pressure and discharging her could miss a haemorrhage.
explanations.D: Tension-type headache is gradual, bilateral and mild to moderate; exertional sudden headache in an older woman is never labelled tension-type without imaging.

learning_point: A headache that reaches maximum intensity within a minute (thunderclap headache) is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise, even when the pain has eased and the examination is normal; it needs urgent CT.
setting_note: In a rural hospital without CT overnight, a thunderclap headache is an indication for urgent discussion with the physician on call and the retrieval service for transfer to a site with CT, rather than observation until morning.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology
references.locator: Headache - red flags and thunderclap headache; subarachnoid haemorrhage

references.title: Ottawa Subarachnoid Haemorrhage Rule (Perry et al., JAMA 2013)
references.locator: High-risk features: age 40 or over, onset during exertion, thunderclap onset, neck pain or stiffness, loss of consciousness

plan: Tests recognition of thunderclap headache as a red flag requiring urgent CT (outcomes 1.4, 1.9). An older woman has a sudden maximal exertional headache that has eased, with a normal examination. Distractors are the benign labels a junior doctor might reach for: first migraine, hypertensive headache and tension-type headache. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology.
tutor_context: Key facts: thunderclap headache is maximal within one minute; CT within 6 hours of onset on a modern scanner read by an experienced radiologist is highly sensitive for subarachnoid haemorrhage, after which lumbar puncture for xanthochromia or CT angiography is needed; other causes of thunderclap headache include reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and cervical artery dissection. Common misconceptions: that improvement with analgesia or a normal examination excludes haemorrhage; that the first ever headache in an older person can be migraine. Out of scope: aneurysm management.

critic.blind_reasoning: Sudden maximal-onset occipital headache with exertion, vomiting and 'worst ever' in a hypertensive 68-year-old is a thunderclap headache; subarachnoid haemorrhage must be excluded by urgent CT regardless of improvement with analgesia and a normal examination.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Appropriate for difficulty 1. Explanation can note CT sensitivity within 6 hours and the role of LP or CTA if CT is negative beyond that window.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital. A 52-year-old woman sustained a closed mid-shaft tibial fracture when a horse kicked her 5 hours ago. The fracture has been reduced and placed in a plaster backslab by the orthopaedic registrar, who has since gone to theatre. She is awaiting a ward bed. The nurse calls you because the patient's leg pain is 9 out of 10 and increasing despite morphine 10 mg intravenously over the past hour, and she says the pain feels 'different' from when she arrived. The foot is warm and pink, capillary refill is 2 seconds and the dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable. You are considering acute compartment syndrome and want to examine for its earliest reliable sign before you phone the registrar in theatre.
lead_in: Which clinical finding is the earliest reliable sign of acute compartment syndrome?

options.text: Absence of the dorsalis pedis pulse
Pallor and coolness of the injured foot
Paralysis of toe and ankle movement
Pain on passive stretch of the muscles

explanations.A: Compartment pressures that cause muscle ischaemia are well below arterial pressure, so distal pulses are usually preserved until very late. A palpable pulse must never be used to exclude compartment syndrome.
explanations.B: Pallor and coolness are late findings that indicate arterial compromise; by then irreversible muscle and nerve damage may already have occurred.
explanations.C: Paralysis is a late sign reflecting established nerve and muscle ischaemia; waiting for it means missing the window for fasciotomy.
explanations.D: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment are the earliest and most reliable clinical signs, followed by paraesthesia. The immediate actions are to split the cast and padding down to skin, keep the limb at heart level, phone the orthopaedic registrar in theatre and not to simply increase the opioid dose.

learning_point: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs of compartment syndrome; pulses, colour and capillary refill are usually preserved until late, so their presence must never be used to exclude it.
setting_note: In a rural hospital suspected compartment syndrome means splitting the cast and padding to skin, keeping the limb at heart level and urgent phone contact with the on-call orthopaedic service and the retrieval service, because fasciotomy within hours determines the outcome for the limb.

references.title: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons - Emergency Management of Severe Trauma (EMST) course manual
references.locator: Musculoskeletal trauma - compartment syndrome: clinical signs and initial management

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pain and Analgesia
references.locator: Acute pain after trauma - escalating analgesic requirement as a warning sign

plan: Tests recall of the earliest reliable sign of compartment syndrome in a casted tibial fracture (outcomes 1.4, 1.9). A woman has escalating pain despite opioids with preserved pulses and perfusion. Distractors are the late 'P' signs that interns commonly and dangerously wait for. Supported by the EMST manual.
tutor_context: Key facts: the tibia is the commonest site; the classic early features are pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and paraesthesia; the 'P' signs of pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late; compartment pressure measurement can help but should not delay surgical review; treatment is fasciotomy. Common misconceptions: that a palpable pulse or normal capillary refill excludes the diagnosis; that increasing opioids is the right response to escalating pain in a casted limb. Out of scope: pressure thresholds for fasciotomy.

critic.blind_reasoning: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles are the earliest reliable findings in acute compartment syndrome; pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late signs indicating established ischaemia.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Easy for a difficulty 3 target. The more valuable junior-doctor action is to split the backslab and dressings to skin immediately and call the registrar; consider a management lead-in instead, or add that to the explanation.

stem: You are working in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital at 19:00; a registrar is on site overnight. A 55-year-old man fell from his bicycle at low speed 90 minutes ago, striking his helmeted head on the road. Bystanders report he was unresponsive for less than a minute. He cannot remember the 5 minutes before the fall. He has vomited once in the department, has a mild frontal headache and has a small scalp haematoma over the right parietal region with no palpable step and no laceration. There are no signs of a basal skull fracture, his pupils are equal and reactive and there is no focal neurological deficit. His GCS has been 15 since the ambulance arrived. He takes no antiplatelet or anticoagulant medication and has not been drinking alcohol. The registrar asks you to apply the head injury guideline's CT criteria.
lead_in: Which single finding, if present, would make a CT brain mandatory for this patient?

options.text: A single episode of vomiting
Amnesia for the 5 minutes before impact
Two or more episodes of vomiting
A scalp haematoma without a palpable skull defect

explanations.A: A single vomit after a head injury is common and is not by itself a CT criterion in the Canadian CT Head Rule used in Australian guidelines; it does warrant a period of observation.
explanations.B: Retrograde amnesia becomes a criterion only when it exceeds 30 minutes before impact; 5 minutes does not meet the threshold.
explanations.C: Two or more episodes of vomiting is a high-risk criterion, alongside a GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture and age 65 or over. Any one of these mandates CT. He currently has none, so structured neurological observations and reassessment of his GCS at 2 hours are the plan, with a CT if he vomits again or his GCS drops.
explanations.D: A scalp haematoma on its own is not a criterion; it becomes relevant only if there is a palpable depression, a large boggy haematoma suggesting fracture, or signs of basal skull fracture.

learning_point: In a GCS 15 adult with minor head injury, two or more episodes of vomiting is one of the high-risk features (with GCS below 15 at 2 hours, suspected skull fracture, age 65 or over and anticoagulation) that mandates CT; a single vomit, a small scalp haematoma or brief amnesia alone do not.
setting_note: In a rural hospital without CT, a patient who meets a CT criterion needs transfer for imaging, while one who does not can be observed locally with structured neurological observations and discharged with written head injury advice to a responsible adult.

references.title: NSW Institute of Trauma and Injury Management - Initial Management of Closed Head Injury in Adults (2nd edition), incorporating the Canadian CT Head Rule
references.locator: Risk assessment and indications for CT in mild head injury

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology
references.locator: Head injury - assessment and indications for imaging

plan: Tests recall of the CT criteria for minor head injury in an adult with GCS 15 (outcomes 1.4, 1.5). A middle-aged cyclist has brief loss of consciousness, one vomit, short amnesia and a scalp haematoma, none of which mandates CT. Distractors are the near-miss versions of real criteria. Supported by the NSW ITIM adult head injury guideline and the Canadian CT Head Rule.
tutor_context: Key facts: Canadian CT Head Rule high-risk criteria are GCS below 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture, two or more vomits, and age 65 or over; medium-risk criteria are retrograde amnesia over 30 minutes and a dangerous mechanism; anticoagulant use is a separate indication in Australian practice; discharge requires a responsible adult and written advice. Common misconceptions: that any loss of consciousness mandates CT; that a scalp haematoma means a skull fracture. Out of scope: paediatric head injury rules.
uncertainty_note: The item uses the Canadian CT Head Rule criteria as adopted in Australian adult head injury guidelines; local SA Health pathways may add criteria such as anticoagulant use or lower the threshold for imaging.

critic.blind_reasoning: In the Canadian CT Head Rule and the Australian (NSW ITIM) adult head injury guideline, two or more episodes of vomiting is a high-risk criterion mandating CT; a single vomit is not, retrograde amnesia must exceed 30 minutes, and a scalp haematoma without a sign of skull fracture is not itself a criterion.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Name the guideline (e.g. NSW ITIM Adult Closed Head Injury or Canadian CT Head Rule) in the stem. Explanation should also acknowledge that the overall picture may justify CT on clinical grounds even if no single mandatory criterion is met.

soft_flags: clarity: The stem refers to 'the head injury guideline' without naming it; thresholds differ slightly between CCHR, NICE and NSW ITIM, so the explanation (and ideally the stem) should name the guideline used.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident covering the emergency department and ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre overnight. A 79-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter at 23:00. Three hours earlier, after an argument, she swallowed 20 tablets of immediate-release paracetamol 500 mg (10 g) from a packet of 24. She weighs 62 kg, took nothing else and does not drink alcohol. She is alert and orientated with normal observations and feels mildly nauseated. Her only regular medicine is perindopril. The hospital laboratory can run a paracetamol concentration with a turnaround of about one hour, and the Poisons Information Centre is available on 13 11 26. She says she regrets what she did and asks to go home.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing the paracetamol ingestion?

options.text: Measure a 4-hour paracetamol level and treat by the nomogram
Give a single 50 g dose of activated charcoal by mouth now
Start intravenous acetylcysteine now without waiting for a level
Observe her overnight and check liver function tests at 24 hours

explanations.A: For a single acute immediate-release ingestion presenting within 8 hours, the decision to treat rests on a paracetamol concentration taken 4 hours or more after ingestion and plotted on the Australian and New Zealand nomogram, with acetylcysteine started if the level is on or above the treatment line. Her level can be drawn in an hour and reported before 8 hours have elapsed, so this is the correct pathway. The Poisons Information Centre should be called, and she must not be discharged before the result and a mental health risk assessment.
explanations.B: Activated charcoal is recommended within 2 hours of an immediate-release overdose of 10 g or more, and up to 4 hours only for massive or modified-release ingestions. At 3 hours after 10 g it is not indicated.
explanations.C: Empirical acetylcysteine is started when the concentration cannot be obtained and acted on within 8 hours of ingestion, or for massive, staggered or late presentations. Here the level will be available well inside 8 hours, so treatment is guided by the nomogram; starting acetylcysteine would not be dangerous, but it is not the best next step.
explanations.D: Liver function tests are normal in the first 24 hours even after serious overdose; waiting for them misses the window in which acetylcysteine is most effective.

learning_point: For a single acute immediate-release paracetamol overdose presenting within 8 hours, the decision to start acetylcysteine is based on a paracetamol concentration taken at least 4 hours after ingestion plotted on the nomogram; acetylcysteine is started empirically only if the level cannot be obtained before 8 hours.
setting_note: In a country hospital whose laboratory cannot return a paracetamol concentration within 8 hours of ingestion, start acetylcysteine empirically and stop it if the level is later below the line; discuss every overdose with the Poisons Information Centre and arrange a mental health assessment, which may be by telehealth.

references.title: Guidelines for the management of paracetamol poisoning in Australia and New Zealand (Chiew AL et al., Medical Journal of Australia, 2020 update)
references.locator: Acute immediate-release ingestion presenting within 8 hours - timing of paracetamol concentration, nomogram and activated charcoal

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology
references.locator: Paracetamol poisoning - assessment and acetylcysteine

plan: Tests the standard assessment pathway for an acute paracetamol overdose presenting at 3 hours (outcomes 1.7, 1.9, 1.4). An older woman at a country hospital with an on-site laboratory asks to go home. Distractors are charcoal outside its window, empirical acetylcysteine when a timely level is available, and watchful waiting. Supported by the Australian and New Zealand paracetamol poisoning guideline.
tutor_context: Key facts: toxic dose threshold is 10 g or 200 mg/kg; the nomogram line starts at 150 mg/L at 4 hours; charcoal is for presentation within 2 hours (4 hours for massive or modified-release); empirical acetylcysteine if the level will not be available within 8 hours; older patients and those on enzyme-inducing drugs are not treated differently under the current guideline; every deliberate overdose requires a mental health risk assessment and safe-keeping of medicines. Common misconceptions: that normal early liver function tests are reassuring; that a remorseful patient can go home. Out of scope: the two-bag acetylcysteine regimen and massive ingestion thresholds.

critic.blind_reasoning: A 10 g (161 mg/kg) immediate-release paracetamol ingestion presenting at 3 hours should have a serum concentration taken at 4 hours post-ingestion and be treated with acetylcysteine if above the nomogram line; with a 1-hour turnaround the result will be available well within 8 hours, so empirical acetylcysteine is not required. Activated charcoal is only recommended within 2 hours for this dose.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good item. The explanation should note that the patient cannot simply go home: she needs the 4-hour level, a mental health risk assessment and, under the SA Mental Health Act if required, appropriate safeguards. Consider adding 'and call the Poisons Information Centre' to the key to model good practice.

stem: You are the only doctor on site overnight in the 4-bed emergency department of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula; the GP is on call from home. At 02:10 a 58-year-old man is brought in by his wife. They were watching television together when, at 01:30, he suddenly stopped speaking properly and his right arm went weak. On examination he has expressive dysphasia, right facial droop and right arm power 2 out of 5; he is alert. Blood pressure is 172/94 mmHg, heart rate 88 and regular, SpO2 97% on room air and bedside glucose 6.2 mmol/L. He has hypertension and takes no anticoagulant, has had no recent surgery or bleeding, and his wife asks whether you can give him an aspirin.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give aspirin 300 mg orally now and reassess his deficit in one hour
Activate the acute stroke pathway now and call for time-critical imaging and reperfusion assessment
Phone the GP on call and ask them to come in and assess him before any further decisions are made
Admit him for observation and arrange a CT brain and physician review in the morning

explanations.A: Aspirin is withheld until intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded on imaging, and it is not given before thrombolysis. Reassessing in an hour wastes time within the treatment window.
explanations.B: A sudden focal deficit with a witnessed onset 40 minutes ago is a time-critical emergency: he may be eligible for thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and thrombectomy beyond that. The junior doctor's job is to activate the stroke pathway immediately, which in this setting means phoning the state stroke or telestroke service and the retrieval service for urgent transfer to a CT-capable, thrombolysis-capable hospital, while recording the onset time, checking glucose and keeping him nil by mouth. In a hospital with CT it means calling the stroke code and going straight to the scanner.
explanations.C: The GP on call should be informed, but waiting for them to arrive before activating the pathway delays reperfusion; both calls can be made in parallel and the stroke call comes first.
explanations.D: Overnight observation treats a hyperacute stroke as a routine admission and removes any chance of reperfusion therapy.

learning_point: A sudden focal neurological deficit with a known onset time is a time-critical emergency: activate the stroke pathway immediately and arrange urgent imaging and reperfusion assessment, and do not give aspirin until haemorrhage has been excluded on CT.
setting_note: In a tertiary hospital this means calling the stroke code and going straight to CT; in a rural hospital without CT it means an immediate call to the retrieval service and the state telestroke or on-call stroke service, with the GP on call informed in parallel rather than waited for.

references.title: Stroke Foundation - Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
references.locator: Pre-hospital and emergency assessment; reperfusion therapy eligibility and time windows; antiplatelet therapy after imaging

references.title: SA Health Statewide Stroke Clinical Network - acute stroke and telestroke pathways for rural sites
references.locator: Rural acute stroke pathway - early notification and retrieval

plan: Tests immediate activation of the stroke pathway by a junior doctor (outcomes 1.9, 1.7) in a way that applies to any setting. A man with a witnessed onset of dysphasia and hemiparesis 40 minutes earlier presents overnight and his wife asks for aspirin. Distractors are early aspirin, waiting for the GP on call, and overnight observation. Supported by the Stroke Foundation guidelines.
tutor_context: Key facts: thrombolysis is considered up to 4.5 hours from onset and thrombectomy up to 24 hours in selected patients, so every minute counts; glucose must be checked to exclude hypoglycaemia as a mimic; aspirin is given only after haemorrhage is excluded and not within 24 hours of thrombolysis; record the time last known well, medications and contraindications for the receiving team. Common misconceptions: that aspirin is harmless to give early; that the stroke call should wait for a senior doctor to confirm the diagnosis. Out of scope: thrombolysis dosing and blood pressure thresholds.

critic.blind_reasoning: Sudden dysphasia, facial droop and arm weakness with onset 40 minutes ago is an acute stroke within the reperfusion window; the sole doctor should activate the stroke pathway immediately (telestroke, retrieval, time-critical imaging). Aspirin before imaging is contraindicated, and GP review or morning CT would lose the window.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound. Explanation should name the SA telestroke / rural stroke pathway and state that the GP on call should be notified in parallel, not instead.

stem: You are the intern covering the emergency department and ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre overnight; the GP is on call from home. A 78-year-old man presents at 03:00 with 45 minutes of central chest heaviness radiating to the left arm, with nausea and sweating. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Observations: heart rate 54 and regular, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96% on room air. The nurse hands you the 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm at 54 per minute, 2 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF, 1 to 2 mm ST depression in leads I and aVL, and no ST change in the anterior leads. An ECG from an admission 2 years ago was normal.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this ECG?

options.text: Acute pericarditis, because of ST elevation in several leads
Early repolarisation, a normal variant that explains the ST elevation
Posterior myocardial infarction, indicated by the ST depression
Inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction requiring immediate reperfusion

explanations.A: Pericarditis produces widespread concave ST elevation, often with PR depression, and does not cause reciprocal ST depression in the lateral leads. Reciprocal change points firmly to infarction.
explanations.B: Early repolarisation is seen in young, healthy people, mainly in the anterior leads, with notched J points and no symptoms. New ST elevation compared with a previously normal ECG in a 78-year-old with typical pain is not a normal variant.
explanations.C: Posterior infarction shows ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves. Here the depression in I and aVL is the reciprocal mirror of the inferior elevation, not a separate territory.
explanations.D: ST elevation of 1 mm or more in two contiguous inferior leads with reciprocal depression in I and aVL is an inferior STEMI. The bradycardia and low-normal blood pressure suggest right ventricular involvement or vagal tone, so nitrates should be used with caution. The intern should give aspirin 300 mg, phone the GP on call and the cardiology or retrieval service immediately, and work through the fibrinolysis checklist, because primary PCI cannot be reached within the recommended time from this hospital.

learning_point: ST elevation in two contiguous leads with reciprocal ST depression in the opposite leads is a STEMI; in a rural hospital far from a catheterisation laboratory this triggers the chest pain pathway for an immediate fibrinolysis decision and transfer.
setting_note: In a tertiary hospital the patient goes straight to the catheterisation laboratory; 90 minutes from a PCI centre, fibrinolysis in the emergency department is usually indicated, so the intern should phone the cardiology on-call or retrieval service and the GP on call at once while giving aspirin and preparing the fibrinolysis checklist.

references.title: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand - Australian Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes
references.locator: Diagnosis of ST-elevation myocardial infarction; reperfusion strategy where primary PCI is not available within the recommended time

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Acute coronary syndromes - STEMI recognition and reperfusion

plan: Tests ECG interpretation of an inferior STEMI with reciprocal changes by a solo rural intern (outcomes 1.5, 1.9). An older diabetic man with typical pain has inferior ST elevation, lateral ST depression and bradycardia. Distractors are pericarditis, early repolarisation and posterior infarction, each anchored on one feature. Supported by the NHF/CSANZ acute coronary syndrome guidelines.
tutor_context: Key facts: STEMI criteria are new ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads (1 mm in most leads, higher thresholds in V2 to V3 depending on age and sex); reciprocal depression increases specificity; inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension suggests right ventricular involvement, in which nitrates can cause profound hypotension and right-sided leads (V4R) help; fibrinolysis is indicated when primary PCI cannot be achieved within about 90 to 120 minutes of first medical contact. Common misconceptions: that ST elevation in more than one lead group means pericarditis; that a slow heart rate is reassuring. Out of scope: fibrinolytic drug selection and contraindication lists.

critic.blind_reasoning: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL, ischaemic chest pain and a previously normal ECG is an inferior STEMI; the reciprocal change excludes pericarditis and early repolarisation, and posterior MI would show anterior ST depression.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Easier than difficulty 3. Explanation should cover right-sided leads for RV infarction, caution with nitrates, and the rural reperfusion pathway (pre-hospital/in-hospital thrombolysis then transfer).

stem: You are the PGY2 on an evening cover shift at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre, covering the ward and emergency department overnight. A 34-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis, maintained on oral mesalazine for 8 months, presents with 3 weeks of malaise, low-grade fever, arthralgia and a faint maculopapular rash. Her colitis is quiescent with one formed stool daily. She denies NSAID use and has no vomiting or diarrhoea. Observations: temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 84/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, mucous membranes moist. Creatinine is 310 micromol/L (baseline 68 micromol/L 6 months ago), urea 14 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, eosinophils 1.1 x 10^9/L. Urinalysis: leucocytes 2+, protein 1+, no blood. Urine microscopy reports white cell casts, no red cell casts, no bacteria. Bedside bladder scan shows 40 mL post-void. The physician is available by phone.
lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains her acute kidney injury?

options.text: Prerenal acute kidney injury from volume depletion
Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis
Post-infectious glomerulonephritis
Acute pyelonephritis with early urosepsis

explanations.A: Prerenal injury is the commonest cause of acute kidney injury on a ward, but this woman is euvolaemic with no fluid losses, and a prerenal state does not produce white cell casts, eosinophilia, fever, rash or arthralgia.
explanations.B: Subacute kidney injury with fever, rash, arthralgia, peripheral eosinophilia, sterile pyuria and white cell casts in a patient established on mesalazine is the classic picture of drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, a recognised and under-recognised adverse effect of mesalazine. The next steps are to withhold mesalazine, avoid nephrotoxins, and discuss urgently with the physician and renal team in Adelaide, since biopsy and corticosteroids may be considered.
explanations.C: Glomerulonephritis typically produces haematuria with red cell casts and heavier proteinuria, often with hypertension and oedema; the urine here has no blood and shows white cell casts instead.
explanations.D: Pyelonephritis would be expected to cause flank pain, dysuria and bacteriuria with a positive culture; sterile pyuria over three weeks with rash and eosinophilia points away from infection.

learning_point: Fever, rash, eosinophilia and sterile pyuria with white cell casts in a patient on a culprit drug such as mesalazine, a proton pump inhibitor, an NSAID or an antibiotic suggests acute interstitial nephritis, and the first action is to stop the drug.
setting_note: In a country hospital without on-site nephrology, the junior doctor's role is to recognise the pattern, stop the likely culprit, hold nephrotoxins and seek same-night phone advice from the physician and the tertiary renal unit, who will decide on transfer for biopsy and treatment.

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Mesalazine: adverse effects (interstitial nephritis) and monitoring of renal function

references.title: Kidney Health Australia, Acute Kidney Injury clinical guidance for health professionals
references.locator: Causes of AKI: intrinsic renal causes including acute interstitial nephritis

plan: Tests recognition of the urine and blood pattern of drug-induced interstitial nephritis in a patient on mesalazine, evidencing 1.5 and 1.8. The after-hours rural setting makes the resident the one who has to read the result and decide what to stop before phoning for help. Distractors are the commonest ward cause (prerenal), the alternative intrinsic cause (glomerulonephritis) and the trap of calling sterile pyuria infection. Supported by AMH mesalazine monograph and KHA AKI guidance.
tutor_context: Key facts: acute interstitial nephritis presents with a subacute rise in creatinine, often with fever, rash, arthralgia, eosinophilia and eosinophiluria, sterile pyuria and white cell casts; common culprits are NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, beta-lactams, sulfonamides and mesalazine. Misconceptions: assuming ward AKI is always prerenal; treating sterile pyuria as a urinary tract infection with antibiotics. Out of scope: decisions on renal biopsy and corticosteroid therapy, which belong to the renal team.

critic.blind_reasoning: Subacute fever, arthralgia, maculopapular rash, eosinophilia, sterile pyuria with white cell casts and a large creatinine rise in a euvolaemic patient on mesalazine is classic drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis. No red cell casts or haematuria argues against glomerulonephritis; no bacteria, no hypotension and a 3-week indolent course argue against pyelonephritis.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound diagnostic item. The rural/after-hours framing adds nothing to a diagnosis question and could be trimmed.

stem: You are the PGY2 on the medical ward of a regional hospital with no ICU, on-site CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 79-year-old woman admitted with symptomatic iron deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 66 g/L, heart rate 104/min, breathless walking to the bathroom) has been prescribed one unit of packed red cells, with iron studies and a gastroenterology referral arranged. The unit was signed out of the blood fridge and the transfusion commenced at 14:10. At 15:30 the nurse tells you the pump has been alarming intermittently for a positional cannula and only half the unit has infused. She asks by what time this unit must be finished.
lead_in: What is the maximum time from removal from controlled storage within which the unit must be completely infused?

options.text: 1 hour
2 hours
4 hours
6 hours

explanations.A: One hour is too restrictive; a unit of red cells is routinely infused over 1 to 3 hours, and a rate this fast would not be appropriate for an elderly woman at risk of circulatory overload.
explanations.B: Two hours is a reasonable usual duration for a unit in a patient at risk of overload, but it is not the limit; the regulatory maximum is longer.
explanations.C: Red cells must be completely infused within 4 hours of leaving controlled temperature storage because of the risk of bacterial proliferation and loss of cell viability. This unit left the fridge at about 14:10, so it must finish by 14:10 plus 4 hours; the cannula should be resited or the rate adjusted now, and if that is not achievable the remainder is discarded and a new unit requested.
explanations.D: Six hours exceeds the accepted maximum; a unit still running at that point should have been discontinued and discarded.

learning_point: A unit of red cells must be fully infused within 4 hours of leaving controlled storage; if it cannot be, the remainder is discarded, not run faster.
setting_note: In a regional hospital with a small blood fridge and limited stock, a wasted unit may mean a delay while a replacement is sent from Adelaide, so the junior doctor should address cannula problems early rather than letting the clock run out.

references.title: ANZSBT Guidelines for the Administration of Blood Products
references.locator: Section on duration of transfusion: red cells completed within 4 hours of removal from controlled storage

references.title: National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards, Blood Management Standard
references.locator: Safe administration of blood and blood products

plan: Tests a single safety fact every resident prescribing blood must know, the 4-hour completion limit for red cells, evidencing 1.8 and 1.1. The regional setting adds the real consequence of a wasted unit. Distractors are the usual transfusion durations and an over-long period. Supported by the ANZSBT administration guideline and the NSQHS Blood Management Standard.
tutor_context: Key facts: red cells are transfused over 1 to 3 hours, slower (up to the 4-hour limit) for patients at risk of transfusion-associated circulatory overload; the 4-hour limit is counted from removal from the blood fridge, not from the start of infusion. Misconceptions: speeding up the infusion to beat the clock; counting from when the drip started. Out of scope: platelet and plasma infusion times and massive transfusion.

critic.blind_reasoning: ANZSBT/Lifeblood and hospital transfusion policy require a red cell unit to be completely infused within 4 hours of removal from controlled storage, so this unit must finish by 18:10.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Straightforward recall; the long rural scene-setting is unnecessary for a recall item but harmless.

stem: You are the PGY2 on the general ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with specialist advice by phone. A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and a recent variceal bleed, now stable, is receiving his second unit of packed red cells for a haemoglobin of 64 g/L. Fifteen minutes into the unit the nurse calls you urgently: he has developed rigors and loin pain, his temperature has risen from 37.0 C to 39.1 C, heart rate is 118/min and blood pressure has fallen from 128/76 to 92/58 mmHg. He is anxious but talking. The first unit, completed 2 hours earlier, was uneventful. The nurse has already pressed the pause button on the pump and is waiting for your instruction.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and give paracetamol 1 g orally for a febrile non-haemolytic reaction
Phone the transfusion laboratory to confirm the unit's compatibility before deciding
Collect blood cultures from the patient and the unit and send them to the laboratory
Stop the transfusion, disconnect the unit and keep the cannula patent with sodium chloride 0.9%

explanations.A: Slowing the rate and giving paracetamol is acceptable only for a mild isolated fever (rise of less than 1.5 C with no other features); rigors, loin pain, a rise above 1.5 C and hypotension mark a severe reaction in which continuing to infuse the unit could be fatal.
explanations.B: Checking compatibility with the laboratory is part of the subsequent work-up, but phoning first delays the one action that limits harm: no further product should enter the patient while the call is made.
explanations.C: Cultures of the patient and the unit are needed to investigate bacterial contamination and haemolysis, but they are collected after the transfusion has been stopped and the patient stabilised, not before.
explanations.D: Loin pain, rigors, a temperature rise above 1.5 C and hypotension early in a unit suggest acute haemolytic transfusion reaction or bacterial contamination. The first priority is to stop the transfusion, disconnect the unit and giving set, maintain IV access with sodium chloride 0.9%, check the patient's identity against the unit, start resuscitation and escalate under the hospital's Rapid Detection and Response criteria. The physician is then phoned and the unit and samples returned to the laboratory.

learning_point: Any transfusion reaction with hypotension, rigors, loin or back pain or a temperature rise of 1.5 C or more means stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with sodium chloride 0.9%, and only then investigate.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without ICU, a severe reaction triggers early phone escalation to the physician and the retrieval service in Adelaide, and the single junior doctor must manage the airway, breathing and circulation steps and recheck patient and unit identity while waiting.

references.title: ANZSBT Guidelines for the Administration of Blood Products
references.locator: Management of adverse transfusion reactions: stop the transfusion and maintain IV access

references.title: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood, Transfusion reactions (Transfusion.com.au)
references.locator: Acute transfusion reactions: initial management

references.title: SA Health Recognising and Responding to Clinical Deterioration (Rapid Detection and Response) policy
references.locator: Escalation criteria for hypotension and tachycardia

plan: Tests prioritisation in a severe acute transfusion reaction: stop first, investigate second, evidencing 1.8, 1.9 and 1.1. The Mid North setting means the resident acts alone before phone advice. Distractors are the mild-reaction response misapplied, a laboratory call that delays action, and investigations done out of order. Supported by ANZSBT administration guidelines, Lifeblood guidance and the SA Health RDR policy.
tutor_context: Key facts: a mild reaction (temperature rise under 1.5 C, no other symptoms) can be managed by slowing the infusion and observing; anything more, particularly hypotension, rigors, loin pain, dyspnoea or haemoglobinuria, requires stopping the unit, resuscitation, identity check and laboratory investigation. Misconceptions: that pausing the pump is the same as disconnecting the unit; that cultures or paperwork come first. Out of scope: management of transfusion-related acute lung injury and the SHOT-style reporting process.

critic.blind_reasoning: Rigors, loin pain, fever rise of 2 degrees and hypotension within 15 minutes of a unit is a suspected acute haemolytic (or septic) reaction; the first action is to stop the transfusion, disconnect the unit and maintain IV access with 0.9% sodium chloride before investigations and laboratory contact.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good prioritisation item. Metadata lists context as ward but the item is correctly a ward scenario.

stem: You are the intern on the medical ward of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with on-site intensive care. A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes was admitted from the emergency department 90 minutes ago with vomiting and diabetic ketoacidosis after missing insulin doses during a gastroenteritis. In the emergency department he received 1 L of sodium chloride 0.9% over the first hour. Observations now: heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, alert. Repeat venous gas: pH 7.16, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, glucose 27 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Blood ketones 5.4 mmol/L. The emergency department has not yet started insulin. The medical registrar is in a resuscitation and asks you to write up the next hour of fluids and insulin according to the hospital DKA protocol.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add potassium chloride 40 mmol to the next litre of sodium chloride 0.9% and defer the insulin infusion until potassium exceeds 3.5 mmol/L
Start an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately, with potassium-free sodium chloride 0.9% running alongside at 250 mL/hour
Give a further 1 L bolus of sodium chloride 0.9% and repeat the gas in one hour before deciding on potassium
Give sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 100 mL intravenously to correct the acidosis before starting insulin

explanations.A: In diabetic ketoacidosis, total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level is normal, and insulin drives potassium into cells. With serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L, Australian DKA protocols direct replacing potassium in the intravenous fluid (commonly 40 mmol per litre, via an infusion pump, with cardiac monitoring) and withholding the insulin infusion until potassium is at least 3.5 mmol/L, then rechecking potassium every one to two hours. Fluid resuscitation continues meanwhile.
explanations.B: Starting insulin with a serum potassium of 3.2 mmol/L and no replacement risks a rapid fall to life-threatening hypokalaemia with arrhythmia; insulin should wait until potassium is corrected.
