plan: Tests whether a PGY2 recognises delirium from sepsis when a nurse frames the presentation as psychosis, in a regional ward with the physician by phone. Distractors: mental health triage, antipsychotic and wait, Mental Health Act detention. Supported by the ACSQHC Delirium and Sepsis Clinical Care Standards and SA Health RDR criteria.
tutor_context: Key facts: delirium is distinguished from primary psychosis by acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, disorientation and a medical precipitant; visual hallucinations favour delirium. First psychotic episodes rarely present with fever and hypotension. Sepsis management includes cultures, lactate, 20 mL/kg fluid bolus for hypotension, antibiotic review and reassessment within the hour. Misconceptions: calling psychiatry first because of hallucinations; sedating and waiting; using the Mental Health Act for delirium. Culturally safe practice means family presence and the ALO, without delaying treatment.

critic.blind_reasoning: Acute-onset disorientation, inattention and hallucinations in a woman with pyelonephritis who is now febrile, tachycardic and hypotensive is delirium from worsening sepsis; she meets Rapid Detection and Response criteria and needs bedside assessment, escalation and the physician phoned, not a psychiatric pathway.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Key is correct and important. Suggest balancing option length and swapping D for a medically-flavoured but wrong option (e.g. give IV haloperidol and continue current antibiotics) to raise discrimination.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): C is the longest option and the only one naming physiological deterioration; the psychiatric options are internally consistent with the nurse's red herring but read as a set of three wrong answers.

stem: You are the intern on an evening cover shift at a regional hospital with a small medical ward, no intensive care, and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 19-year-old man was admitted 4 days ago with a tibial fracture after a motorbike crash and is waiting for transfer for surgery, which has been postponed twice. At 20:00 the nurse tells you he has eaten little for 2 days, has been tearful, and tonight said he does not see the point of the operation and would not mind if he did not wake up. He is on oxycodone 10 mg four times daily for pain and slept poorly. He is alert, orientated, with normal observations. When you sit with him he says he feels like a burden to his parents, who drive 2 hours each way to visit, and that things will not get better.
lead_in: How should these statements be interpreted?

options.text: A normal adjustment reaction to injury and delay that needs no action tonight beyond reassurance
Possible suicidal ideation that requires a direct risk assessment this evening and escalation to the on-call doctor
Opioid-related mood change that should be managed by reducing the oxycodone dose and reviewing tomorrow
A request for help with sleep that should be met with a short course of temazepam

explanations.A: Hopelessness, feeling a burden and a wish not to wake up go beyond expected adjustment; these are recognised warning signs for suicide and must be asked about directly, not reassured away.
explanations.B: Correct. Passive death wishes, hopelessness and perceived burdensomeness in a young man with poor sleep, pain and social isolation are indicators of possible suicidal ideation. The intern should ask directly about thoughts of suicide, plans, means and intent, document the assessment, ensure he is safe on the ward (including access to medications and the environment), and escalate the same evening to the on-call doctor and the mental health triage service rather than leaving it for the day team.
explanations.C: Opioids can lower mood, but attributing suicidal statements to medication and deferring assessment would miss a risk that needs action now; medication review can follow the risk assessment.
explanations.D: Insomnia is part of the picture but prescribing a hypnotic without a risk assessment ignores the content of what he has said and adds a potential means of harm.

learning_point: Statements of hopelessness, feeling a burden or wishing not to wake up are warning signs for suicide; ask directly about suicidal thoughts, ensure safety and escalate the same shift.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without on-site psychiatry the intern phones the on-call doctor and the state mental health triage line for same-night advice, and ensures nursing observations and environmental safety on the medical ward; a tertiary hospital would have a consultation-liaison or emergency mental health team available overnight.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Suicide and deliberate self-harm - assessment of suicide risk

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm (2016)
references.locator: Risk assessment and asking directly about suicidal ideation

plan: Tests interpretation of passive suicidal statements by a young inpatient on an evening shift, with opioids and insomnia as distractor explanations. Rural scene with escalation by phone. Distractors: normal adjustment, opioid effect, hypnotic request. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic and the RANZCP self-harm guideline.
tutor_context: Key facts: asking directly about suicide does not increase risk; warning signs include hopelessness, perceived burdensomeness, social withdrawal, insomnia and reduced intake; risk factors in young men include impulsivity, substance use and access to means. A structured assessment covers ideation, plan, intent, means, protective factors and previous attempts. Misconceptions: that such statements are normal after injury; that medication explains everything; that assessment can wait for the day team. Out of scope: antidepressant choice.

critic.blind_reasoning: Passive death wish, hopelessness, feeling a burden, poor intake and sleep in a 19-year-old with a prolonged admission is possible suicidal ideation and warrants a direct, structured risk enquiry tonight and escalation; it should not be reframed as adjustment, opioid effect or insomnia.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good item. Explanation should include what a direct enquiry covers (plan, means, intent, protective factors) and ward safety measures.

presentation: involuntary treatment under the Mental Health Act
stem: You are the intern covering the wards overnight at a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with the on-call doctor at home and specialist advice by phone. At 02:00 the nurse calls about a 34-year-old woman admitted 2 days ago for intravenous antibiotics for cellulitis, which is improving. Over the evening she has become increasingly suspicious, believes the antibiotics are poison sent by a neighbour, and is now dressed and trying to leave through the locked fire door, saying voices have told her to walk to the highway. She has a history of schizophrenia and stopped her medication a month ago. She is physically well with normal observations, has no weapon and has not been aggressive. The nurse asks whether she can leave, since she was admitted voluntarily.
lead_in: What should you do first?

options.text: Let her leave after documenting that she declined to stay, because she is a voluntary patient
Give olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly now so that she is unable to leave the ward
Phone the local police and ask them to come to the ward and take her into custody
Keep her on the ward under close watch and phone the on-call doctor and mental health triage

explanations.A: A patient who is acutely psychotic and intends to walk to a highway at night is at serious risk; allowing her to leave would breach the duty of care. Voluntary status can be changed by making an inpatient treatment order where the criteria for involuntary treatment are met.
explanations.B: Forced intramuscular medication to prevent a patient leaving is not justified here: she is not violent, de-escalation has not been attempted, and treatment without consent requires a lawful basis such as an inpatient treatment order.
explanations.C: Police have powers to apprehend people with apparent mental illness in the community, but she is an inpatient in a hospital where a medical practitioner can assess her; calling police first bypasses the appropriate medical process and is likely to escalate her distress.
explanations.D: Correct. The first priority is safety: use the least restrictive means (staff presence, a quiet space, de-escalation) to keep her on the ward while the lawful process is set in motion. Under the SA Mental Health Act 2009 a medical practitioner may make a Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order when a person appears to have a mental illness that requires immediate treatment, there is a risk to their safety, and no less restrictive option is available. An intern should not make this decision alone: the on-call doctor must be contacted now, and the mental health triage service can advise on the order and arrange assessment.

learning_point: When a voluntary inpatient becomes acutely psychotic and unsafe to leave, keep them safe using the least restrictive means while urgently contacting the senior doctor and mental health service about an inpatient treatment order under the Mental Health Act 2009.
setting_note: Regional hospitals have no on-site psychiatry overnight; the on-call doctor can make a Level 1 order and the mental health triage service arranges psychiatrist review, often by video, within the required timeframe; a tertiary centre would have an emergency mental health team to attend in person.

references.title: SA Health, Office of the Chief Psychiatrist: Mental Health Act 2009 - Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Orders guideline
references.locator: Criteria and who may make a Level 1 order

references.title: Mental Health Act 2009 (SA)
references.locator: Part 5: Inpatient treatment orders - Level 1

plan: Tests prioritisation overnight when a voluntary inpatient becomes psychotic and unsafe: safety first with least restrictive means, then urgent escalation about an inpatient treatment order. Distractors: let her leave, sedate to prevent leaving, call police. Supported by the SA Chief Psychiatrist guideline on Level 1 orders and the Mental Health Act 2009.
tutor_context: Key facts: Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order criteria in SA are that the person has or appears to have a mental illness, the illness requires immediate treatment, there is a risk to the person's or others' health or safety, and no less restrictive means are reasonably available. The order is made on the prescribed form, lasts up to 7 days, requires the patient to be given a copy and a statement of rights, notification to the Chief Psychiatrist, and examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours (video assessment is permitted). Misconceptions: that voluntary patients can never be stopped from leaving; that IM sedation is a substitute for lawful detention; that police are the first call for an inpatient. Out of scope: Level 2 and 3 orders and community treatment orders.
uncertainty_note: Interns hold provisional registration and may legally be able to make a Level 1 order, but local policy and safe practice expect senior involvement; the item is written around escalation rather than the intern completing the order alone.

critic.blind_reasoning: A psychotic woman intending to walk to a highway at 02:00 cannot safely be allowed to leave despite voluntary status; the lawful path is to keep her safe under observation while the on-call doctor assesses for a Level 1 inpatient treatment order under the SA Mental Health Act 2009 and mental health triage is contacted.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Key correct. Shorten D and strengthen one distractor (e.g. 'persuade her to stay and offer her regular antipsychotic, documenting she remains voluntary') so the item discriminates at difficulty 2.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): D is far longer than the other options and the only one that names a lawful process; the other three are clearly inappropriate.

presentation: involuntary treatment under the Mental Health Act
stem: You are the intern at a regional hospital with a small medical ward, no intensive care, on-site CT during business hours only, and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 55-year-old man was brought in by police at 14:00 after his wife found him in the shed with a rope. The general practitioner on duty assessed him, found severe depression with a fixed plan to end his life, and made a Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order under the Mental Health Act 2009 at 15:00 before leaving for the day. He is now settled on the medical ward with one-to-one nursing, has been given a copy of the order and the statement of rights, and the Chief Psychiatrist notification has been sent. At 22:00 the nurse asks you which of the outstanding tasks must be done tonight. The on-call doctor is available by phone, and the Rural and Remote Mental Health Service psychiatrist can assess by video.
lead_in: Which task is most time-critical for you to arrange tonight?

options.text: Video examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner before 15:00 tomorrow
A full admission clerking with bloods, ECG and chest X-ray before the morning ward round
Booking a non-urgent ambulance for transfer to an Adelaide mental health unit tomorrow afternoon
Writing a letter to his general practitioner to arrange follow-up after his discharge

explanations.A: Correct. Under the SA Mental Health Act 2009 a Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order made by a medical practitioner who is not a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner must be followed by examination of the patient by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours, who confirms or revokes it. In a regional hospital this is arranged through the Rural and Remote Mental Health Service, usually by video, and the Act expressly allows audiovisual examination. Missing the deadline leaves the detention without a lawful basis, so the referral must be made tonight.
explanations.B: A medical clerking is good practice and should happen, but it has no statutory deadline and he is physically well with one-to-one nursing; it can be completed in the morning.
explanations.C: Transfer to an approved treatment centre depends on bed availability and the psychiatrist's decision; booking it is not time-critical tonight and does not replace the statutory examination.
explanations.D: Discharge planning is important but is days away and has no bearing on the lawfulness of his current detention.

learning_point: A Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order made by a non-psychiatrist must be followed by examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours; in regional South Australia this is arranged urgently through the rural mental health service, usually by video.
setting_note: In Adelaide the examination is done in person by the on-site psychiatry team; in a regional hospital the junior doctor must actively arrange the video assessment with the Rural and Remote Mental Health Service and should confirm the time of the order so the 24-hour window is not missed.

references.title: SA Health, Office of the Chief Psychiatrist: Mental Health Act 2009 - Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Orders guideline
references.locator: Examination within 24 hours by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner; use of audiovisual conferencing

references.title: Mental Health Act 2009 (SA)
references.locator: Part 5 Division 2: Level 1 inpatient treatment orders - examination and confirmation

plan: Tests a PGY1 at difficulty 4 on which statutory step is time-critical after a GP makes a Level 1 order in a regional hospital: the 24-hour examination, arranged by video. Distractors are reasonable tasks without a deadline (clerking, transfer booking, GP letter). Supported by the Chief Psychiatrist Level 1 ITO guideline and the Mental Health Act 2009 (SA).
tutor_context: Key facts: a Level 1 order lasts up to 7 days; the patient must receive a copy and a statement of rights; the Chief Psychiatrist must be notified; if the order was made by someone other than a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner, examination within 24 hours by one of those is required and the order can be confirmed or revoked; examination by audiovisual link is permitted. Patients should be transferred to an approved treatment centre as soon as practicable. Misconceptions: that medical clerking is the overnight priority; that the order stands for 7 days without review. Out of scope: Level 2 orders and SACAT review.
uncertainty_note: The 24-hour examination requirement for Level 1 orders made by non-psychiatrists is as understood from the Mental Health Act 2009 (SA) as amended; reviewers should confirm against the current Chief Psychiatrist guideline.

critic.blind_reasoning: Under the SA Mental Health Act 2009 a Level 1 inpatient treatment order requires examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours of the order (video examination permitted in rural areas) to confirm, vary or revoke it; the order was made at 15:00 so that examination is the time-critical task.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good SA-specific item. Distractors C and D are weak; consider replacing one with 'formal notification to the Public Advocate' or 'completing the Level 2 order yourself' as a more tempting legal distractor.

presentation: refeeding risk in an eating disorder
stem: You are the intern in the outpatient clinic of a regional hospital with a small medical ward, no intensive care, and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air; the physician is reviewing another patient and the on-call physician is reachable by phone. A 47-year-old woman is referred by her general practitioner with weight loss. She has a long history of anorexia nervosa and has restricted her intake to a few hundred calories a day for the past 3 weeks, losing 8 kg in 2 months. Her weight is 39 kg (body mass index 14.3). She is orthostatic (lying blood pressure 92/58, standing 76/50), heart rate 42, temperature 35.4. Bloods taken this morning show potassium 2.9 mmol/L, phosphate 0.6 mmol/L, magnesium 0.6 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L. She says she feels fine and would prefer to manage at home with the dietitian.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide a high-energy meal plan to follow at home and review her in clinic in one week
Prescribe oral potassium and phosphate supplements and review her in 48 hours
Admit her today for monitored refeeding, electrolyte replacement and thiamine
Refer her to the community eating disorder service for outpatient dietitian review

explanations.A: Starting unsupervised full feeding at home in a severely malnourished patient with low phosphate is the classic setting for refeeding syndrome, with risk of arrhythmia, heart failure and death.
explanations.B: Her bradycardia, hypothermia, postural hypotension and electrolyte derangement are markers of medical instability that need inpatient monitoring; oral replacement and review in 2 days is unsafe.
explanations.C: Correct. A body mass index below 15, rapid weight loss, minimal intake for more than a week, bradycardia below 50, hypothermia and low potassium, phosphate and magnesium place her at high risk of refeeding syndrome and of cardiac complications. National and RANZCP guidance is admission for medical stabilisation: cardiac monitoring, correction of electrolytes, thiamine before and during refeeding, cautious nutrition started at a low rate with daily electrolytes. The intern should discuss with the physician today and not let her go home.
explanations.D: Community eating disorder services are essential for ongoing care but cannot provide the monitoring she needs now; outpatient referral is the next step after medical stabilisation.

learning_point: Severe malnutrition with bradycardia, hypothermia, postural hypotension or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium means high refeeding risk and medical instability: admit for monitored refeeding with electrolyte replacement and thiamine.
setting_note: A regional hospital without intensive care can begin stabilisation but should discuss early with the on-call physician and the statewide eating disorder service about transfer to Adelaide for cardiac monitoring if bradycardia or electrolytes worsen; a tertiary hospital would admit directly to a medical ward with telemetry.

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of eating disorders (2014)
references.locator: Indications for medical admission and management of refeeding risk

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Eating disorders - medical complications and refeeding syndrome

references.title: National Eating Disorders Collaboration (NEDC): Eating disorders - a professional resource for general practitioners
references.locator: Medical indicators for hospital admission

plan: Tests the basic decision to admit a medically unstable patient with anorexia nervosa for monitored refeeding, from an outpatient clinic in a regional hospital. Distractors: home meal plan, oral supplements with early review, community referral. Supported by the RANZCP eating disorder guidelines, Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic and the NEDC resource.
tutor_context: Key facts: refeeding syndrome is driven by insulin-induced intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium when carbohydrate is reintroduced; high-risk features include BMI under 16, weight loss over 15 percent in 3-6 months, minimal intake for over 10 days, and low baseline electrolytes. Admission indicators also include heart rate under 50 awake, systolic under 90 or postural drop over 20 mmHg, temperature under 35.5, and ECG abnormalities. Give thiamine before feeding, replace electrolytes, start nutrition cautiously with daily bloods for the first week. Misconceptions: that the patient feeling fine is reassuring; that oral supplements suffice; that a low BMI alone defines risk.

critic.blind_reasoning: BMI 14.3, heart rate 42, temperature 35.4, postural hypotension and hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and hypomagnesaemia are medical admission criteria for anorexia nervosa with high refeeding risk; she needs monitored admission, electrolyte replacement and thiamine, discussed with the physician, not outpatient management.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound. Explanation should address her preference to go home (capacity, involving the physician and if needed the MHA/guardianship pathway) and the possibility of transfer to a monitored bed.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital with a registrar on site overnight. A 70-year-old man is brought in by ambulance at 23:30 after his neighbour found him in the bathroom with cuts to his left forearm. The lacerations are superficial and have stopped bleeding under a dressing. He is tearful and says he wanted to die after his wife went into residential care. On further questioning he says that about 90 minutes before cutting himself he swallowed a handful of his wife's amitriptyline tablets, perhaps 20 of 50 mg. He is drowsy but rousable, heart rate 112, blood pressure 108/70, pupils dilated, mucous membranes dry. The nurse has placed him in a cubicle and asks whether you want to suture the arm first or call the mental health team, as both are waiting.
lead_in: What should you do first?

options.text: Suture the forearm lacerations and then take a detailed mental health history
Move him to a monitored bed, obtain a 12-lead ECG and inform the ED registrar of the amitriptyline ingestion now
Refer him to the mental health team for an urgent risk assessment before any medical investigations
Give activated charcoal and wait for the paracetamol level before deciding further

explanations.A: Superficial lacerations with haemostasis are not urgent; spending 30 minutes suturing while a tricyclic overdose evolves could mean missing the window to treat a widening QRS, seizures or arrhythmia.
explanations.B: Correct. A 1 g amitriptyline ingestion is potentially lethal: anticholinergic signs and tachycardia are already present and sodium channel blockade can cause broad-complex arrhythmia, seizures and hypotension within hours. The first priority is a monitored area, 12-lead ECG looking at QRS duration and the terminal R wave in aVR, intravenous access, and immediate escalation to the registrar so that sodium bicarbonate, airway planning and Poisons Information Centre advice can be arranged. The lacerations and psychiatric assessment follow once he is medically safe.
explanations.C: Mental health assessment is essential but cannot be done meaningfully in a drowsy patient and would delay life-saving monitoring; every self-harm presentation needs medical stabilisation before psychiatric review.
explanations.D: Charcoal is reasonable within an hour in an alert patient with a protected airway, but he is drowsy 90 minutes post-ingestion, and waiting on a paracetamol level is not the time-critical issue; the ECG and monitoring are.

learning_point: In any self-harm presentation, medical risk comes first: a tricyclic antidepressant overdose needs immediate cardiac monitoring, a 12-lead ECG and escalation before wound care or psychiatric assessment.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the same priorities apply with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 and early retrieval discussion, because tricyclic toxicity can require intubation and intensive care that the hospital cannot provide.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology
references.locator: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning - risk assessment, ECG monitoring and sodium bicarbonate

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm (2016)
references.locator: Medical assessment and stabilisation before psychosocial assessment

plan: Tests prioritisation in a self-harm presentation where a hidden tricyclic overdose outranks the visible wounds and the psychiatric referral. Metro ED with a registrar on site, so escalation is in person. Distractors: suture first, mental health first, charcoal and wait. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and the RANZCP self-harm guideline.
tutor_context: Key facts: tricyclic ingestion over 10 mg/kg is potentially life-threatening; warning ECG features are QRS over 100 ms (seizure risk) and over 160 ms (arrhythmia risk), and an R wave over 3 mm in aVR; treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg for QRS widening or hypotension, benzodiazepines for seizures, early intubation and hyperventilation if severe. Always ask about co-ingestants and take a paracetamol level, but do not let it dictate the sequence. Misconceptions: wounds first because they are visible; psychiatry first because of the stated intent; assuming an elderly man's overdose is minor. Out of scope: detailed ventilation strategy.

critic.blind_reasoning: A 1 g amitriptyline ingestion with drowsiness, tachycardia, mydriasis and dry mucosa is a potentially lethal tricyclic overdose; cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG for QRS widening and immediate senior notification come before suturing or psychiatric assessment.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good. Explanation should mention sodium bicarbonate for QRS over 100 ms, PIC call, and that psychiatric assessment follows medical stabilisation.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital on a busy night with a registrar on site. A 69-year-old man presents at 23:00 asking for something to help him sleep. His wife died 4 months ago and he lives alone; his daughter is interstate. He has been drinking a bottle of wine most nights, has lost 6 kg, and says he has not slept properly in weeks. When you ask directly, he says he often thinks he would be better off dead and has thought about taking his late wife's leftover morphine tablets, which are still in the house; he has not set a date and says he came in instead because he was frightened by the thought. He has no prior psychiatric history. The registrar, who is managing a resuscitation, suggests over the phone that you give him some temazepam and ask his GP to follow up.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Prescribe a small supply of temazepam and arrange general practitioner review within 48 hours as suggested
Ask him to agree to a no-harm contract and discharge him with the crisis line number
Phone his daughter to arrange for the morphine to be removed from the house and then discharge him
Tell the registrar you assess him as high risk and arrange an urgent mental health assessment before any discharge

explanations.A: A hypnotic would add a means of overdose and does not address the risk. The registrar's suggestion was made without the information you now have; an intern must escalate the new finding rather than follow the original plan.
explanations.B: No-harm contracts have no evidence of reducing suicide and can give false reassurance; discharging a high-risk patient with a phone number alone is unsafe.
explanations.C: Restricting access to means is a valuable part of a safety plan, but it is not sufficient on its own for a man with active suicidal thoughts, a potential method, recent bereavement, alcohol use and social isolation.
explanations.D: Correct. Older men, recently bereaved, living alone, drinking heavily, with weight loss, insomnia and suicidal thoughts that include an identified method, are at high risk of suicide. The right step is graded assertiveness: tell the registrar clearly what you have found and that you believe he needs an urgent mental health assessment in the department tonight, and ensure he is kept safe in the department until that assessment is done. Means restriction and family involvement form part of the subsequent safety plan.

learning_point: Suicidal thoughts with an identified method in an older bereaved man who drinks and lives alone indicate high risk; escalate assertively to the senior doctor and arrange urgent mental health assessment before any discharge.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without an on-site mental health team the same assessment is arranged through the state mental health triage line and the on-call doctor, with the patient kept safe in the department or admitted overnight rather than sent home.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Suicide and deliberate self-harm - risk assessment and immediate management

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm (2016)
references.locator: Assessment of suicide risk and decisions about discharge

references.title: AMC National Framework for Prevocational Medical Training: Outcome statements
references.locator: 1.1 graded assertiveness and escalation; 2.4 working within limits of expertise

plan: Tests prioritisation and graded assertiveness: the intern uncovers high suicide risk after the registrar has suggested a quick discharge. Metro ED at night. Distractors: follow the hypnotic plan, no-harm contract, means restriction alone. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic, the RANZCP self-harm guideline and the AMC outcome statements.
tutor_context: Key facts: older men have the highest suicide rate in Australia; bereavement, living alone, alcohol use, insomnia, weight loss and access to means are risk factors; coming in because he was frightened is a protective sign but does not lower the acute risk. Risk assessment covers ideation, plan, intent, means, previous attempts, protective factors and a mental state examination. Misconceptions: no-harm contracts work; a phone number is a safety plan; a senior's plan made with incomplete information must be followed. Out of scope: antidepressant initiation.

critic.blind_reasoning: A recently bereaved, isolated older man with heavy alcohol use, weight loss, insomnia and suicidal thoughts with an identified means at home is high risk; the intern must not discharge on a hypnotic and should communicate the risk to the registrar and arrange urgent mental health assessment. No-harm contracts are not evidence-based.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good. B and C are weak; consider making C 'means restriction plus GP review tomorrow' more tempting by adding a safety plan, so the discriminator is the need for assessment tonight.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the medical ward of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, where a 4-bed emergency department is staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. A 36-year-old woman was admitted last night after taking 20 tablets of paracetamol following an argument with her partner; she is receiving acetylcysteine and is medically stable. The mental health triage service will assess her by video this afternoon. The nurse looking after her asks you, while you are reviewing her history together, which part of the history matters most for her future risk of dying by suicide. The history includes a previous overdose 3 years ago requiring admission, full-time work as a teacher, two children aged 8 and 10, and no current alcohol or drug use.
lead_in: Which feature of her history is the strongest predictor of future suicide?

options.text: Her past suicide attempt
Her age under 40 years
Being a female patient
Her full-time employment

explanations.A: Correct. A previous suicide attempt is consistently the strongest single predictor of future suicide and of repeated self-harm; the year after an attempt carries the highest risk. This history should be prominent in the handover to the mental health team and in discharge planning.
explanations.B: Suicide rates in Australia are highest in middle-aged and older adults, particularly men; age under 40 is not a strong risk marker in itself.
explanations.C: Women attempt self-harm more often, but men die by suicide at about three times the rate; female sex is not a predictor of completed suicide.
explanations.D: Employment and responsibility for children are generally protective factors; unemployment and social isolation increase risk.

learning_point: A previous suicide attempt is the strongest predictor of future suicide; always ask about and document prior attempts and pass them on at handover.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Suicide and deliberate self-harm - risk factors

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm (2016)
references.locator: Risk factors for repetition and suicide after self-harm

plan: Tests recall of the strongest predictor of future suicide, with a stable inpatient after paracetamol overdose in a rural Yorke Peninsula ward. Distractors are demographic features juniors confuse with risk (young age, female sex) and a protective factor (employment). Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic and the RANZCP self-harm guideline.
tutor_context: Key facts: risk factors for suicide include previous attempt, male sex, older age, psychiatric illness (especially depression and substance use), chronic pain or illness, recent loss, social isolation, unemployment, access to lethal means, and family history. Protective factors include dependent children, social connection, employment and help-seeking. Risk stratification tools have poor predictive value; the point of identifying factors is to inform a safety plan and follow-up. Misconceptions: that women are at higher risk of suicide because they self-harm more; that a previous attempt that was 'not serious' can be discounted.

critic.blind_reasoning: A previous suicide attempt is the single strongest predictor of future suicide; female sex, younger age and employment are either protective or associated with lower risk.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Accurate but all three distractors are rated 1, so the item will not discriminate even at difficulty 1. Consider distractors that are genuine risk factors but weaker than a prior attempt (e.g. recent relationship conflict, access to means) to make the 'strongest' judgement real.

stem: You are the PGY2 on a term in a general practice linked to a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with specialist advice by phone. A 22-year-old woman presents with 2 days of light vaginal spotting and intermittent mild left-sided lower abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive a week ago. She has had no previous pregnancies, no history of pelvic infection and does not use an intrauterine device. Heart rate 78, blood pressure 118/74, abdomen soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no peritonism. Serum beta-hCG this morning is 1,800 IU/L. A transvaginal ultrasound at the hospital today shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 12 mm, no adnexal mass, and a trace of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. The supervising GP asks for your interpretation before you discuss her with the obstetric registrar in Adelaide.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?

options.text: A complete miscarriage, since the uterus is empty and bleeding is light, requiring no further follow-up
A normal early intrauterine pregnancy that is simply too early to see, requiring routine antenatal booking
A pregnancy of unknown location in which ectopic pregnancy has not been excluded
A confirmed ectopic pregnancy requiring immediate transfer to Adelaide for laparoscopy

explanations.A: Complete miscarriage cannot be diagnosed from an empty uterus unless an intrauterine pregnancy was previously confirmed; an empty uterus with a positive hCG may be an ectopic pregnancy.
explanations.B: At an hCG of 1,800 IU/L an intrauterine pregnancy is often, though not always, visible on transvaginal scan; with unilateral pain and free fluid it is unsafe to assume a normal pregnancy and book routine care.
explanations.C: Correct. A positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy seen on transvaginal ultrasound is a pregnancy of unknown location. With an hCG near the discriminatory zone, unilateral pain and free fluid, ectopic pregnancy must be actively excluded: she is haemodynamically stable, so the plan is a repeat hCG in 48 hours with repeat ultrasound, discussion with the obstetric service, and explicit safety-netting to present immediately with worsening pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or heavy bleeding, bearing in mind the 2-hour distance to definitive surgery.
explanations.D: Ectopic pregnancy has not been confirmed: there is no adnexal mass and she is stable. Immediate transfer for surgery is not justified on these findings, although the threshold for transfer is lower given the distance.

learning_point: A positive hCG with no pregnancy seen on transvaginal ultrasound is a pregnancy of unknown location; ectopic pregnancy must be excluded with serial hCG, repeat ultrasound and clear safety-netting, especially when the patient lives far from surgical care.
setting_note: In a regional practice 2 hours from Adelaide the follow-up plan must be explicit: a named person to review the 48-hour hCG, early discussion with the obstetric registrar, a low threshold for transfer, and advice that any deterioration means calling an ambulance rather than driving; in a metropolitan setting the early pregnancy assessment service would manage the same plan in person.

plan: Tests interpretation of a pregnancy of unknown location with features suggestive but not diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy, in a regional general practice where distance makes the follow-up plan critical. Distractors: complete miscarriage, too early to see, confirmed ectopic needing immediate surgery. Supported by the Queensland early pregnancy loss guideline, RANZCOG guidance and Therapeutic Guidelines.
tutor_context: Key facts: the discriminatory zone for transvaginal ultrasound is commonly quoted as hCG 1,500-2,000 IU/L but is not absolute; in a viable intrauterine pregnancy hCG typically rises by at least 50-60 percent over 48 hours, a plateau or slow rise suggests ectopic, and a fall suggests miscarriage or resolving pregnancy of unknown location. Free fluid raises concern. Anti-D is needed for Rh-negative women with bleeding. Misconceptions: empty uterus equals miscarriage; hCG below the discriminatory zone excludes ectopic; a stable patient does not need safety-netting. Out of scope: methotrexate criteria.

critic.blind_reasoning: A positive pregnancy test with bleeding and pain, hCG 1,800 IU/L and a transvaginal scan showing no intrauterine or adnexal pregnancy is a pregnancy of unknown location; ectopic pregnancy is neither confirmed nor excluded and she needs serial hCG and specialist follow-up.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good item. Explanation should note that PUL with hCG near the discriminatory level in a symptomatic patient warrants same-day obstetric discussion, safety-netting and repeat hCG at 48 hours.

stem: You are the PGY2 in the emergency department of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 31-year-old woman presents at 10:00 on a Sunday asking for emergency contraception after a condom broke during intercourse at about 02:00 on Thursday, around 80 hours ago. She weighs 86 kg (body mass index 31). She is not on any regular contraception, has regular cycles with her last period 12 days ago, takes no other medications, is not breastfeeding and has no history of liver disease or venous thromboembolism. She does not want an intrauterine device. The nearest open pharmacy is some distance away and she asks you to prescribe whatever is most likely to work. You have access to the hospital pharmacy stock.
lead_in: Which emergency contraceptive is most appropriate?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single dose
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally as a single dose
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally, repeated after 12 hours
Combined ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel tablets, two now and two in 12 hours

explanations.A: Levonorgestrel is licensed up to 72 hours and its efficacy falls with time and with higher body weight; at 80 hours in a woman weighing over 70 kg it is clearly inferior to ulipristal.
explanations.B: Correct. Ulipristal acetate 30 mg is effective up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse and is more effective than levonorgestrel at every time point, particularly between 72 and 120 hours and probably in women with higher body weight. Since she declines a copper intrauterine device, which is the most effective option, ulipristal is the best oral choice. She should be advised that it may delay ovulation and her period, that any hormonal contraception started afterwards should be delayed by 5 days, to use condoms meanwhile, and to do a pregnancy test if her period is more than 7 days late.
explanations.C: Doubling the levonorgestrel dose (3 mg) is a strategy some guidelines suggest for women over 70 kg or body mass index over 26 when ulipristal is unavailable, but it is still not recommended beyond 72 hours and ulipristal is available here.
explanations.D: The Yuzpe regimen is less effective than either levonorgestrel or ulipristal and causes more nausea; it has no place when dedicated products are available.

learning_point: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg is the most effective oral emergency contraceptive, works up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse, and is preferred over levonorgestrel after 72 hours or in women of higher body weight; a copper intrauterine device remains the most effective option overall.
setting_note: Ulipristal and levonorgestrel are both available from community pharmacies in Australia without prescription, and SHINE SA and regional pharmacies can provide them; a regional hospital may not stock ulipristal, in which case double-dose levonorgestrel within 72 hours or referral for a copper intrauterine device are the alternatives.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
references.locator: Emergency contraception - choice of method and timing

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Ulipristal - emergency contraception; Levonorgestrel - emergency contraception

references.title: Family Planning Alliance Australia / SHINE SA: Emergency contraception clinical guidance
references.locator: Ulipristal versus levonorgestrel and body weight considerations

plan: Tests recall at difficulty 4 of the preferred oral emergency contraceptive beyond 72 hours in a woman of higher body weight who declines an IUD. Metro ED with pharmacy stock available. Distractors: standard levonorgestrel, doubled levonorgestrel, Yuzpe regimen. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Sexual and Reproductive Health, the AMH and family planning guidance.
tutor_context: Key facts: copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception (failure under 0.1 percent) and can be inserted up to 5 days after intercourse or ovulation; ulipristal 30 mg works to 120 hours; levonorgestrel 1.5 mg to 72 hours (some use to 96 hours with reduced efficacy), with a doubled dose considered for weight over 70 kg or BMI over 26. Ulipristal is reduced in efficacy by progestogens taken in the following 5 days, and breastfeeding should be paused for a week. Neither oral method is abortifacient. Misconceptions: that 72 hours is the limit for all oral methods; that the Yuzpe regimen is still standard; that emergency contraception is contraindicated in obesity. Both oral agents are pharmacist-only medicines in Australia.
uncertainty_note: Evidence on body weight and ulipristal efficacy is less certain than for levonorgestrel; Australian guidance still favours ulipristal at 72-120 hours regardless of weight.

critic.blind_reasoning: At 80 hours ulipristal acetate 30 mg is the only oral emergency contraceptive licensed and effective up to 120 hours and it remains more effective than levonorgestrel, including in women over 70 kg or BMI over 26; copper IUD would be most effective but is declined. Levonorgestrel single or doubled is for use within 72 hours and the Yuzpe regimen is obsolete.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound. Explanation should add that the copper IUD was the most effective option and should be re-offered, that UPA is OTC in Australia, and to advise no progestogen for 5 days and a pregnancy test in 3 weeks.

stem: A 46-year-old woman attends the gynaecology outpatient clinic of a regional hospital, where the visiting gynaecologist reviews patients by phone between monthly visits. She has had irregular periods for a year and assumed she was perimenopausal, but now has seven weeks of amenorrhoea, light spotting and three days of mild left iliac fossa discomfort. She is haemodynamically stable (heart rate 78/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg) with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no peritonism. Serum beta-hCG is 1,800 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound this morning shows an empty uterus, a 2.5 cm left adnexal mass without a yolk sac or fetal cardiac activity, and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Liver and renal function and full blood count are normal. She lives on a station 250 km away, has no car this week and says she cannot return for blood tests until the next clinic in a month. The gynaecologist is considering methotrexate.
lead_in: Which feature makes medical management with methotrexate unsuitable for her?

options.text: A serum beta-hCG of 1,800 IU/L
A small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
Her inability to return for serial beta-hCG monitoring
An adnexal mass of 2.5 cm without fetal cardiac activity

explanations.A: A beta-hCG of 1,800 IU/L is well below the level (around 5,000 IU/L) above which methotrexate failure becomes likely; a low hCG favours medical management.
explanations.B: A small volume of free pelvic fluid is common in unruptured ectopic pregnancy and, in a stable woman without peritonism, does not by itself indicate rupture or exclude methotrexate; a large haemoperitoneum or haemodynamic instability would.
explanations.C: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy requires serum beta-hCG on days 4 and 7 and then weekly until undetectable, plus ready access to emergency care if rupture occurs. A woman who cannot attend this follow-up or reach hospital quickly is not a candidate, and surgical management should be discussed with her instead.
explanations.D: A mass under 3.5 cm with no fetal cardiac activity is within the usual criteria for methotrexate; a larger mass or cardiac activity would be reasons to prefer surgery.

learning_point: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy is only safe when the woman is stable, has a low beta-hCG and a small mass without cardiac activity, and can reliably return for serial beta-hCG monitoring and urgent care.
setting_note: In a regional hospital, distance and transport often decide between medical and surgical management: a woman who cannot return for day 4 and 7 bloods or reach an operating theatre quickly if she ruptures should be discussed with the gynaecologist for laparoscopy, either locally when the visiting surgeon is available or in Adelaide.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health
references.locator: Ectopic pregnancy: medical management with methotrexate, patient selection and follow-up

references.title: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Early pregnancy loss
references.locator: Ectopic pregnancy: criteria for methotrexate and follow-up

plan: Tests recall of patient-selection criteria for methotrexate in ectopic pregnancy, evidencing 4.1 and 1.7. A perimenopausal woman in a regional clinic with an unruptured ectopic makes the follow-up constraint real. Distractors are features interns misread as contraindications (small free fluid, hCG level, mass size). Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines and the Queensland early pregnancy loss guideline.
tutor_context: Key facts: methotrexate is for stable women with unruptured ectopic, hCG usually under 5,000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, normal FBC/LFT/UEC and reliable follow-up (hCG day 4 and 7, then weekly). Misconceptions: any free fluid means rupture; age alone is a contraindication. Out of scope: methotrexate dosing and the decision itself, which belong to the gynaecologist.
uncertainty_note: Exact hCG and mass-size cut-offs for methotrexate vary between guidelines (3,500 to 5,000 IU/L; 3.5 to 4 cm); the item avoids hinging on a specific numeric cut-off.

critic.blind_reasoning: Beta-hCG 1,800 IU/L, a 2.5 cm adnexal mass without cardiac activity and a small volume of free fluid in a stable woman are all within accepted criteria for methotrexate. Inability to attend for serial beta-hCG monitoring (days 4, 7 and weekly to negative) is a recognised contraindication because treatment failure and rupture cannot be detected.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound recall item. Editor may consider toning down the final stem sentence to reduce the juxtaposition of 'cannot return for blood tests' with 'considering methotrexate'.

stem: A 22-year-old woman sees you in a general practice attached to a metropolitan general hospital. Her last period was six weeks ago and a home pregnancy test yesterday was positive. For 24 hours she has had intermittent right iliac fossa pain, worse this morning, and a small amount of brown vaginal spotting. She had chlamydia treated two years ago. She looks well: heart rate 86/min, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, afebrile. Abdominal examination shows mild right iliac fossa tenderness without guarding or rebound. A urine pregnancy test in the practice is positive. She asks whether she can wait and see, because the pain has eased with paracetamol and she has work tomorrow. The practice has no ultrasound; the hospital runs an early pregnancy assessment service and has an emergency department.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a pelvic ultrasound through a community radiology practice for later in the week and review the report when it arrives
Refer her today to the hospital early pregnancy assessment service for serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound
Request serum beta-hCG and progesterone through community pathology and review her tomorrow with the results
Prescribe regular paracetamol and repeat the urine pregnancy test in one week if the pain persists

explanations.A: An ultrasound in several days leaves a possible ectopic pregnancy undiagnosed during the period when it may rupture; the scan should be transvaginal and performed the same day, which community practices often cannot provide.
explanations.B: Any woman with a positive pregnancy test, abdominal pain and bleeding has a possible ectopic pregnancy until an intrauterine pregnancy is seen. Previous chlamydia increases her risk. Same-day serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound through an early pregnancy assessment service, with clear instructions to attend the emergency department if pain worsens or she feels faint, is the standard of care even when she looks well.
explanations.C: A serum beta-hCG alone cannot locate the pregnancy, and a single progesterone does not exclude ectopic pregnancy; waiting a day for results delays definitive imaging.
explanations.D: Analgesia and watchful waiting for a week risks rupture and haemorrhage; pain easing with paracetamol does not exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

learning_point: Pain or bleeding in early pregnancy requires same-day serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound to locate the pregnancy, regardless of how well the woman looks.
setting_note: In a regional centre without same-day ultrasound, phone the on-call obstetric or gynaecology team and arrange an urgent scan or transfer the same day; give clear instructions to present to the nearest emergency department immediately if pain increases, she feels faint or bleeding becomes heavy.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health
references.locator: Ectopic pregnancy: presentation and diagnosis

references.title: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Early pregnancy loss
references.locator: Assessment of pain and bleeding in early pregnancy; pregnancy of unknown location

plan: Tests the management decision that early pregnancy pain and bleeding need same-day hospital-based assessment (4.1, 1.7). A general practice setting with a stable young woman who wants to wait creates the temptation to defer. Distractors are the delays an intern might accept: outpatient scan, community bloods, watchful waiting. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines and the Queensland early pregnancy loss guideline.
tutor_context: Key facts: positive pregnancy test plus pain or bleeding equals possible ectopic until an intrauterine pregnancy is seen; same-day beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound; risk factors include previous pelvic infection, tubal surgery, IUD, IVF. Misconceptions: a stable, well-looking woman can wait; a single hCG or progesterone is diagnostic. Out of scope: interpretation of serial hCG trends and choice of treatment.

critic.blind_reasoning: A symptomatic early pregnancy with unilateral pain, spotting and a prior chlamydia infection is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise; she needs same-day serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound through the early pregnancy assessment service, with clear advice to attend ED if pain worsens.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Straightforward and safe. Consider whether a general practice setting fits a PGY1 tag; setting 'any' is fine.

stem: A 45-year-old woman at 35 weeks of gestation attends her general practitioner for a routine shared-care antenatal visit; the practice is linked to a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. This is an IVF pregnancy using a donor egg. Her booking blood pressure was 112/70 mmHg and her antenatal course has been uncomplicated. Today her blood pressure is 142/92 mmHg and, after ten minutes of rest, 144/90 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows no protein. She mentions two days of epigastric discomfort and nausea that she has attributed to reflux, with no headache or visual symptoms. Fetal movements are normal and the fundal height is appropriate. She has no oedema. Her next hospital clinic appointment is in two weeks.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe an antacid for reflux and recheck her blood pressure at a nurse visit in one week
Start labetalol 100 mg twice daily and review her blood pressure and a urine protein-creatinine ratio in one week
Request full blood count, liver and renal function and urine protein-creatinine ratio through community pathology and review the results tomorrow
Refer her the same day to the hospital maternity assessment unit for pre-eclampsia investigations and fetal assessment

explanations.A: Treating her as reflux ignores new hypertension after 20 weeks combined with epigastric pain, a recognised warning symptom of pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome; waiting a week is unsafe.
explanations.B: Antihypertensive treatment may be needed, but starting it in general practice without investigating for pre-eclampsia delays diagnosis; the blood pressure is only mildly raised, and the concerning feature is the epigastric pain.
explanations.C: These are the right investigations but the wrong timeframe: community pathology results take hours to a day, there is no fetal assessment, and a woman with possible pre-eclampsia and epigastric pain should be assessed in hospital today.
explanations.D: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks must be assessed for pre-eclampsia, which can occur without proteinuria. Epigastric pain with new hypertension is a red flag for hepatic involvement, so same-day hospital assessment with blood tests, urine protein-creatinine ratio and fetal monitoring is required, with the obstetric team deciding on antihypertensives and timing of birth.

learning_point: Epigastric pain with new hypertension in the second half of pregnancy is a pre-eclampsia red flag that needs same-day hospital assessment even when proteinuria is absent and the blood pressure rise is mild.
setting_note: From a regional practice, phone the on-call obstetric team at the nearest birthing hospital and arrange same-day assessment there or transfer; if blood pressure reaches 160/110 mmHg or she develops severe symptoms, she should travel by ambulance.

references.title: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023
references.locator: Definition and diagnosis of pre-eclampsia; assessment of new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks; warning symptoms

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Hypertension in pregnancy: assessment and when to refer

plan: Tests recognition that mild new hypertension with epigastric pain is a pre-eclampsia red flag needing same-day hospital assessment (4.1, 1.7). An older IVF pregnancy in shared care sets up the temptation to manage in general practice. Distractors are plausible slower pathways: treat reflux, start an antihypertensive, order the right bloods through community pathology. Supported by the SOMANZ 2023 guideline and Therapeutic Guidelines.
tutor_context: Key facts: hypertension in pregnancy is 140/90 mmHg or above on repeated measurement after 20 weeks; pre-eclampsia is hypertension plus any maternal organ involvement (renal, hepatic, haematological, neurological) or fetal growth restriction, and proteinuria is no longer required; epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, headache, visual disturbance and reduced fetal movements are warning symptoms. Misconceptions: no proteinuria means no pre-eclampsia; mild blood pressure means low urgency. Out of scope: choice and dose of antihypertensive, magnesium sulfate and timing of birth.

critic.blind_reasoning: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks (confirmed on repeat) with epigastric pain and nausea at 35 weeks in a 45-year-old IVF donor-egg pregnancy is pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise; epigastric pain is a severe feature and SOMANZ practice is same-day maternity assessment, not community pathology.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good item; the absent proteinuria is a nice trap for candidates who equate pre-eclampsia with protein.

stem: A 23-year-old woman attends the outpatient clinic of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, five days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth at the regional maternity unit. She has felt feverish and shivery for 24 hours, with lower abdominal cramping and offensive-smelling lochia. She is breastfeeding and her breasts are soft and non-tender. Her perineum is intact. Observations: temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 98%. The uterus is tender and slightly bulky on abdominal palpation; there is no loin tenderness. Urine dipstick shows a trace of leucocytes. She has no drug allergies. The GP obstetrician is on call by phone and the hospital has a small inpatient ward.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit her for blood cultures and intravenous amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole
Prescribe oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid and arrange review in the clinic in 48 hours
Prescribe oral cefalexin for a urinary tract infection and send a midstream urine for culture
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to look for retained products before deciding on antibiotics

explanations.A: Fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia five days postpartum indicate endometritis. With a temperature of 38.6 °C and tachycardia she has systemic features and should be admitted for blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics covering aerobes and anaerobes, as Therapeutic Guidelines recommends for postpartum endometritis; the GP obstetrician should be informed. Gentamicin and metronidazole are compatible with breastfeeding.
explanations.B: Oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid is reasonable for mild endometritis in a well woman with low-grade fever who can be reviewed, but her tachycardia and high fever place her outside that group and a 48-hour gap risks progression to sepsis.
explanations.C: A trace of leucocytes on dipstick is common postpartum and does not explain uterine tenderness and offensive lochia; treating for a urinary infection misses the diagnosis and under-treats her.
explanations.D: Ultrasound may be considered later if she fails to improve, but imaging should not delay antibiotics in a febrile, tachycardic postpartum woman.

learning_point: Postpartum fever with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia is endometritis; systemic features such as fever above 38 °C with tachycardia mean admission, blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics rather than oral treatment and outpatient review.
setting_note: In a rural hospital with one junior doctor overnight, admit her early rather than relying on review in 48 hours, phone the GP obstetrician on call, and apply the local deteriorating-patient criteria; if she meets sepsis criteria or does not improve within 24 to 48 hours, discuss transfer to the regional maternity unit or Adelaide.
