references.locator: Postpartum endometritis: intravenous regimen for moderate to severe infection; oral regimen for mild infection

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Gentamicin and metronidazole: use in breastfeeding

plan: Tests the decision between oral outpatient and inpatient intravenous treatment of postpartum endometritis (4.1, 1.7, 1.8). A young breastfeeding woman in a rural outpatient clinic with systemic features makes the choice consequential. Distractors are the oral option that suits milder cases, misattribution to urinary infection, and imaging before antibiotics. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the AMH.
tutor_context: Key facts: endometritis is the commonest cause of postpartum fever after day 2; diagnosis is clinical (fever, uterine tenderness, offensive lochia); intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole for systemic illness, oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for mild cases; also consider mastitis, urinary infection, wound infection, venous thromboembolism. Misconceptions: breastfeeding precludes gentamicin or metronidazole; imaging is needed before treating. Out of scope: management of retained products and surgical evacuation.

critic.blind_reasoning: Day 5 postpartum fever, rigors, tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia is endometritis with systemic features; Therapeutic Guidelines recommend IV amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole (after cultures) for moderate to severe infection, and a tachycardic febrile postpartum woman should be admitted rather than sent home on oral antibiotics.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: B is a strong distractor by design. If the intended key is A, consider making systemic features slightly more unequivocal (e.g. HR 112, rigors on the ward) so B is not arguable.

presentation: pregnant patient in the emergency department
stem: A 45-year-old woman at 30 weeks of gestation presents at 2200 to the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital with two days of swelling and aching in her left calf, which is now painful to walk on. She has no chest pain or breathlessness. She has a singleton pregnancy conceived by IVF and a body mass index of 34. Observations: heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, afebrile. The left calf is 4 cm larger in circumference than the right, warm and tender along the medial calf. The ultrasound department does not open until 0800 and the obstetric registrar is on site.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a D-dimer and, if it is below the laboratory threshold, discharge her with antenatal clinic review
Start therapeutic enoxaparin now and arrange compression ultrasound of the leg when imaging opens
Start warfarin tonight and arrange compression ultrasound of the leg as an outpatient
Advise compression stockings, elevation and analgesia, with review in the antenatal clinic in one week

explanations.A: D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy, so a positive result is uninterpretable, and a negative result is not validated to exclude deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy; it should not guide discharge.
explanations.B: Pregnancy, IVF and obesity are risk factors, and unilateral calf swelling with a 4 cm difference makes deep vein thrombosis likely. Because imaging is delayed, therapeutic weight-based low-molecular-weight heparin should be started now and compression ultrasound performed when available; enoxaparin does not cross the placenta and is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy. The obstetric registrar should be informed.
explanations.C: Warfarin crosses the placenta, is teratogenic and is associated with fetal haemorrhage; it is not used for venous thromboembolism in pregnancy, and outpatient imaging delays confirmation.
explanations.D: Conservative measures alone leave a probable deep vein thrombosis untreated for a week, risking extension and pulmonary embolism.

learning_point: Suspected deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy is treated with weight-based therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin while awaiting compression ultrasound, and D-dimer should not be used to exclude it.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without overnight ultrasound, the same approach applies: start enoxaparin after discussing with the obstetric team on call and arrange imaging the next morning locally or in Adelaide; if she develops chest pain or breathlessness, treat as possible pulmonary embolism and arrange urgent transfer.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy: diagnosis and treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin

references.title: SOMANZ and ASTH consensus: Recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in pregnancy and the postpartum period
references.locator: Diagnostic approach; role of D-dimer; empirical anticoagulation when imaging delayed

plan: Tests the management of suspected deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy when imaging is delayed (4.1, 1.7, 1.8). An older, obese IVF pregnancy at night in a general hospital makes the choice between empirical heparin and waiting realistic. Distractors are the D-dimer trap, warfarin, and conservative measures. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines and the SOMANZ/ASTH consensus.
tutor_context: Key facts: pregnancy increases venous thromboembolism risk four- to five-fold; left leg is more often affected; compression ultrasound is the first-line test; therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily (or 1.5 mg/kg daily) based on current weight; warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in pregnancy. Misconceptions: a negative D-dimer excludes clot in pregnancy; anticoagulation must wait for imaging. Out of scope: management of pulmonary embolism, imaging choice for suspected PE, peripartum anticoagulation planning.

critic.blind_reasoning: Clinically likely DVT in pregnancy: anticoagulate with therapeutic LMWH now and confirm with compression ultrasound when available. D-dimer is unhelpful in pregnancy and warfarin is contraindicated.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Easy, safe item at the stated difficulty.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is seen in the outpatient clinic of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, referred by the practice nurse after a positive pregnancy test. By dates she is six weeks pregnant; the pregnancy is unplanned but wanted. Her medications are perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension started two years ago, sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for generalised epilepsy (seizure-free for three years), sertraline 50 mg daily for anxiety, and folic acid 0.5 mg daily that she started last week. Her blood pressure today is 128/80 mmHg. Her neurologist is in Adelaide and sees her annually; the GP obstetrician is available by phone. You are the PGY2 resident running the clinic.
lead_in: Which action should you take before she leaves the clinic today?

options.text: Cease perindopril today and ask the GP obstetrician whether an alternative antihypertensive is needed
Cease sodium valproate today and request an urgent appointment with her neurologist in Adelaide
Change sertraline to a different antidepressant with more pregnancy safety data and review in two weeks
Replace sodium valproate with lamotrigine today and arrange an urgent neurology review

explanations.A: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, fetal death), and should be stopped as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Her blood pressure today is 128/80 mmHg so she may need nothing for now; the GP obstetrician should decide whether labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa is required. This is within a resident's scope and must happen today.
explanations.B: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the antiepileptic drugs and her neurologist should be contacted urgently this week, but abrupt cessation risks breakthrough seizures that endanger her and the pregnancy. Antiepileptic changes in pregnancy are specialist decisions.
explanations.C: Sertraline is one of the better-studied antidepressants in pregnancy and is usually continued; switching risks relapse and offers no safety benefit.
explanations.D: Lamotrigine is a safer antiepileptic in pregnancy, but a switch requires slow cross-titration under neurologist supervision with monitoring of levels; a resident substituting it in clinic is unsafe and outside scope.

learning_point: When pregnancy is confirmed in a woman on an ACE inhibitor, stop it the same day and arrange a safe alternative if needed; antiepileptic drugs are never stopped or swapped abruptly and need urgent specialist input, with folic acid increased to 5 mg daily.
setting_note: In a rural clinic the urgent specialist phone calls are part of the same day's work: the GP obstetrician for antihypertensive choice and shared-care antenatal planning, and the neurologist's rooms in Adelaide or the on-call neurology registrar for an expedited valproate review. Increase folic acid to 5 mg daily today because she is on valproate.

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Perindopril and ACE inhibitors: pregnancy (contraindicated); Antiepileptics: pregnancy and valproate

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology
references.locator: Epilepsy: management in pregnancy; do not stop antiepileptic therapy abruptly

plan: Tests prioritisation of medication changes at pregnancy confirmation: which action is urgent and within a resident's scope versus which needs a specialist (4.1, 1.7, 1.8). A rural clinic with specialists by phone makes scope and sequencing matter. Distractors are the tempting but unsafe immediate valproate changes and an unnecessary sertraline switch. Supported by the AMH and Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology.
tutor_context: Key facts: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are stopped at confirmation of pregnancy and replaced with labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa if needed; valproate is the most teratogenic antiepileptic but must not be stopped or swapped abruptly; women on valproate need folic acid 5 mg daily; sertraline is generally continued. Misconceptions: stopping valproate immediately protects the fetus; sertraline must be changed. Out of scope: antiepileptic cross-titration regimens and pregnancy category labelling details.
uncertainty_note: AMH and the TGA advise ceasing ACE inhibitors at confirmation of pregnancy; data on first-trimester malformation risk are mixed, but cessation itself is uncontroversial. High-dose folic acid is also a same-day action and is addressed in the learning point and setting note rather than as an option.

critic.blind_reasoning: ACE inhibitors should be stopped as soon as pregnancy is confirmed; her BP of 128/80 means no replacement is urgently needed, so cease today and discuss alternatives. Valproate must not be stopped or switched abruptly (seizure risk; neural tube closure has already occurred) but needs urgent neurology input; sertraline is acceptable in pregnancy.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good prioritisation item. Ensure the explanation covers why valproate is not stopped today and the 5 mg folate dose.

secondary_areas: Palliative care and goals of care
stem: You are the evening cover resident at a large metropolitan teaching hospital. At 2130 a nurse asks you to review a 79-year-old woman with severe COPD on home oxygen, admitted two days ago with pneumonia. Her respiratory rate is 32/min, oxygen saturation 86% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, heart rate 118/min and blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, and she is drowsy but rousable, meeting rapid response criteria. The nurse shows you a certified Advance Care Directive in the notes: she refuses intubation and CPR in any circumstances, but wants treatments that may get her home, including a trial of mask ventilation. No Resuscitation Plan (7-Step Pathway) has been completed by the day team. Her husband, her substitute decision-maker, is not contactable yet. The medical registrar is in the emergency department.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Activate a rapid response call and proceed with full escalation, including intubation if required, because no Resuscitation Plan has been completed
Withhold further active treatment and start end-of-life comfort care, in keeping with the limits in her directive
Activate a rapid response call and treat within her directive's limits, including non-invasive ventilation
Defer treatment decisions until her husband can be reached to give consent as her substitute decision-maker

explanations.A: Under the Advance Care Directives Act 2013 (SA), a binding refusal of CPR or intubation in a certified directive must be followed when it applies to the current circumstances; a missing Resuscitation Plan does not override it. Intubating her against her refusal would be unlawful.
explanations.B: Her directive refuses only intubation and CPR; it explicitly asks for treatment that might get her home. Withholding controlled oxygen, antibiotics, bronchodilators and non-invasive ventilation misreads a limitation of treatment as a request for palliation.
explanations.C: She is deteriorating and meets escalation criteria, so the rapid response team should be called now. Her directive sets the ceiling of care (no intubation or CPR) and permits a trial of non-invasive ventilation, so treatment proceeds within those limits. The registrar should document a Resuscitation Plan reflecting the directive, and the husband should be updated when reached.
explanations.D: A substitute decision-maker cannot override a binding refusal, and his consent is not needed for treatment she has asked for; delaying escalation while he is contacted risks avoidable harm.

learning_point: A certified Advance Care Directive sets the ceiling of treatment, not the floor: a refusal of intubation and CPR is binding and does not prevent active escalation of everything else the patient wants.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without on-site intensive care, the same ceiling applies; non-invasive ventilation may be available in the emergency department or ward, and the directive informs whether retrieval to Adelaide for higher-level care is appropriate, which should be discussed with the on-call physician.

references.title: Advance Care Directives Act 2013 (SA): information for health practitioners
references.locator: Binding and non-binding provisions; when a refusal of health care must be followed; role of substitute decision-makers

references.title: SA Health Resuscitation Planning: 7 Step Pathway policy directive
references.locator: Documenting a Resuscitation Plan consistent with an Advance Care Directive; care within agreed limits

plan: Tests applying an Advance Care Directive to an acute deterioration after hours (1.4, 3.2, 1.9). A woman with severe COPD and a directive that refuses intubation but requests a trial of mask ventilation makes the ceiling-of-care distinction necessary. Distractors are the two misreadings of the directive and deferring to the absent husband. Supported by SA Health guidance on the ACD Act and the 7 Step Pathway.
tutor_context: Key facts: in SA a certified Advance Care Directive's refusal of specific treatment is binding when the person lacks capacity and the refusal applies to the circumstances; other provisions are wishes that guide care; a substitute decision-maker cannot consent to treatment the person has refused; a Resuscitation Plan is the clinical order that translates the directive into bedside instructions. Misconceptions: no Resuscitation Plan means full resuscitation regardless; a directive means do nothing. Out of scope: resolving disputes between family and directive, and the technical delivery of non-invasive ventilation.

critic.blind_reasoning: A certified SA Advance Care Directive containing a binding refusal of intubation and CPR must be respected when she lacks capacity, but she wants active treatment short of that; so activate the rapid response call and treat within those limits, including a trial of NIV. The absence of a Resuscitation Plan does not override the directive, and her husband's consent is not required because her own directive governs.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Well constructed. Explanation should note that the rapid response team/ICU then determines NIV suitability given drowsiness.

stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the surgical ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North the afternoon before an elective inguinal hernia repair by the visiting surgeon. He is independent, has well-controlled type 2 diabetes and is otherwise well. While you are clerking him he hands you a copy of his Advance Care Directive, completed last year after his wife's death. It states that he refuses CPR and life support 'if I am dying from an illness that cannot be cured and will not recover a meaningful quality of life'. He has not discussed it with the surgeon. The nurse asks whether she should write 'not for CPR' on his chart and whether the anaesthetist needs to know.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Record 'not for resuscitation' on his observation chart tonight because his directive refuses CPR
Return the directive to him and explain that it does not apply while he has decision-making capacity
Ask the visiting surgeon to override the directive before he goes to theatre tomorrow morning
Clarify his theatre wishes, tell the surgeon and anaesthetist, and document a Resuscitation Plan

explanations.A: His refusal is conditional on dying from an incurable illness without prospect of recovery; a reversible anaesthetic or surgical complication in a well man does not meet that condition, so a blanket not-for-CPR order misapplies the directive and could cost him his life.
explanations.B: The directive only takes effect if he loses capacity, but it is still relevant information that must be filed, flagged and considered; dismissing it discourages him from raising his wishes and leaves the team unprepared.
explanations.C: A directive is the patient's own expression of wishes and cannot be overridden by a surgeon; the right step is to clarify it with the patient, not to seek to set it aside.
explanations.D: The binding provisions of a directive apply only in the circumstances the person described and only once they have lost capacity. The intern should clarify with him, while he has capacity, what he would want if a potentially reversible complication occurred in theatre, place the directive in the notes, alert the surgeon and anaesthetist, and ensure a Resuscitation Plan (7 Step Pathway) is completed that reflects his wishes.

learning_point: An Advance Care Directive's refusals apply only in the circumstances it describes and once capacity is lost, so a well patient before elective surgery should be asked directly what he wants perioperatively and the team informed.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the visiting surgeon and anaesthetist may arrive the morning of the list, so the conversation and documentation should be done the afternoon before and handed over explicitly; if the patient's wishes are unclear, the on-call physician can help before theatre.

references.title: Advance Care Directives Act 2013 (SA): information for health practitioners
references.locator: When binding refusals apply; relevance of capacity; health practitioner obligations

references.title: SA Health Resuscitation Planning: 7 Step Pathway policy directive
references.locator: Completing a Resuscitation Plan with the patient before a procedure

plan: Tests how an intern handles a directive presented by a capable patient before elective surgery (1.4, 3.2, 1.2). A regional surgical ward with a visiting surgeon makes timely handover of the conversation important. Distractors are the blanket not-for-CPR order, dismissing the directive, and asking the surgeon to override it. Supported by SA Health ACD Act guidance and the 7 Step Pathway.
tutor_context: Key facts: a directive speaks for the person only when they cannot; binding refusals apply only in the circumstances described; perioperative resuscitation wishes should be discussed explicitly with a patient who has capacity and documented in a Resuscitation Plan that the anaesthetist and surgeon see. Misconceptions: any mention of CPR refusal means not-for-resuscitation; directives are irrelevant while the patient can speak. Out of scope: anaesthetic-specific consent for suspension of limitations during surgery.

critic.blind_reasoning: His refusal is conditional on a dying, incurable illness and does not apply to a reversible perioperative event in a fit man, so 'not for CPR' must not be charted. The directive should be acknowledged, his perioperative wishes clarified, the surgeon and anaesthetist informed and the discussion documented.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Key is sound, but D is cued by length and the 'document a Resuscitation Plan' wording should be softened to documentation of the discussion/plan with senior involvement.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): D is the longest, most comprehensive, three-part option and is the only one phrased as a balanced process; test-wise candidates will select it on form alone.

stem: An 88-year-old woman on the surgical ward of a metropolitan teaching hospital is three days post repair of a fractured neck of femur. She is taking oxycodone immediate-release 2.5 mg four times a day for pain, regular paracetamol, and her usual amlodipine and pantoprazole. She has not opened her bowels since admission five days ago and reports bloating and discomfort. Her abdomen is soft and mildly distended with normal bowel sounds; rectal examination shows soft stool in the rectum. She is eating small meals, drinking about 800 mL a day, and mobilises only short distances with physiotherapy. She has no history of bowel obstruction, is not vomiting, and has normal renal function. No laxative was charted on admission.
lead_in: Which laxative is most appropriate to prescribe?

options.text: Psyllium husk 3.5 g twice daily in water
Docusate with senna 2 tablets nocte
Liquid paraffin 15 mL at night
Methylnaltrexone 8 mg subcutaneously daily

explanations.A: Bulk-forming laxatives need a good fluid intake and mobility to work; in an immobile older patient drinking under a litre a day and taking opioids they can worsen distension and cause impaction.
explanations.B: Opioid-induced constipation responds to a stimulant laxative, usually combined with a softener, taken regularly rather than as needed. Docusate with senna is the standard first-line choice in Therapeutic Guidelines and should be charted whenever an opioid is prescribed for more than a day or two in an older person.
explanations.C: Liquid paraffin carries a risk of aspiration lipoid pneumonia in older or frail patients and interferes with absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; it is not recommended.
explanations.D: Methylnaltrexone, a peripherally acting opioid antagonist, is reserved for opioid-induced constipation that has failed conventional laxatives, usually in palliative care; it is not first line.

learning_point: A regular stimulant laxative such as senna with docusate should be charted alongside any opioid for an older inpatient; bulk-forming agents are unsuitable when fluid intake and mobility are poor.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal
references.locator: Constipation in adults: opioid-induced constipation; choice of laxative

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Laxatives: comparative information; bulk-forming laxatives and fluid intake; liquid paraffin precautions

plan: Tests recall of first-line laxative choice for opioid-induced constipation in an older inpatient (1.4, 3.2, 1.8). A post-hip-fracture woman on oxycodone with no laxative charted is the everyday scenario. Distractors are the bulk-forming agent interns reach for, liquid paraffin, and a second-line agent. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal and the AMH.
tutor_context: Key facts: prescribe a regular stimulant laxative (senna) with or without a softener (docusate) whenever starting an opioid; osmotic laxatives (macrogol, lactulose) are acceptable alternatives or add-ons; bulk-forming agents need fluid and mobility; liquid paraffin is avoided in older people; methylnaltrexone is for refractory opioid-induced constipation. Misconceptions: fibre supplements are the gentlest first choice for everyone; laxatives should be as-needed only. Out of scope: management of faecal impaction and bowel obstruction.

critic.blind_reasoning: Opioid-induced constipation in an immobile older patient with low fluid intake needs a stimulant with or without softener; docusate-senna is the standard first-line ward choice. Bulk-forming agents are inappropriate with low fluid intake and opioids, liquid paraffin carries aspiration risk in the elderly, and methylnaltrexone is reserved for refractory cases.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Easy, appropriate for difficulty 1. Explanation could mention that a laxative should have been co-prescribed with the opioid.

stem: You are the evening cover intern at a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. At 2000 a nurse phones about an 81-year-old woman admitted yesterday with a urinary tract infection. She lives independently, drives, and had no confusion on admission. She is now pulling at her intravenous cannula, trying to climb over the bed rails and insisting she needs to get to the bus stop, and she does not know where she is. She has refused her evening medications. Her last observations two hours ago were heart rate 96/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, temperature 37.6 °C and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Her chart includes intravenous ceftriaxone, oxycodone 5 mg as needed (given twice today for back pain) and temazepam 10 mg at night, started on admission. The nurse asks you to chart something to settle her.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Chart olanzapine 5 mg wafer as needed over the phone so the nurse can give a dose now and reassess later
Chart an additional dose of temazepam 10 mg tonight to help her settle and sleep through
Attend now to assess for pain, retention, hypoxia and medication causes, and start non-pharmacological measures
Request an urgent CT brain tonight to exclude a stroke as the cause of her new confusion and agitation

explanations.A: Antipsychotics for delirium are reserved for severe distress or imminent danger when non-drug measures have failed, and only after the patient has been assessed; prescribing by phone without examination risks oversedation, falls and masking a deteriorating cause.
explanations.B: Benzodiazepines worsen and prolong delirium in older people and increase falls; the temazepam started on admission is itself a likely contributor and should be ceased, not increased.
explanations.C: This is new acute confusion with inattention in a previously independent woman: delirium. The intern should attend, repeat observations, check a blood glucose and bladder scan, assess pain and bowels, review the medication chart (oxycodone and temazepam are likely contributors) and ask the nurses to implement reorientation, lighting, hearing aids and glasses, and family presence, as set out in the Delirium Clinical Care Standard.
explanations.D: Imaging is indicated if there are focal neurological signs, a head injury, or anticoagulation and a fall; with an obvious precipitant (infection, opioid, benzodiazepine) and no focal signs, a CT is not the first step.

learning_point: Acute confusion in an older inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise: assess in person for precipitants and treat them, use non-pharmacological measures first, and never prescribe sedatives over the phone.

references.title: Delirium Clinical Care Standard (2021)
references.locator: Quality statements 3 to 6: assessment, identifying and treating causes, non-pharmacological interventions, minimising antipsychotic use

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Delirium: management; avoidance of benzodiazepines; limited role of antipsychotics

plan: Tests the intern's first response to a phone call about a newly confused older patient after hours (1.4, 3.2, 1.8). A previously independent woman with infection, an opioid and a new benzodiazepine makes the reversible precipitants obvious once sought. Distractors are the two sedatives the nurse is implicitly requesting and a reflex CT. Supported by the ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard and Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic.
tutor_context: Key facts: delirium is an acute change in attention and cognition with a fluctuating course; common precipitants are infection, drugs (opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics), pain, retention, constipation, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance; first-line management is treating causes and non-pharmacological care; antipsychotics only for severe distress or danger after assessment. Misconceptions: sedation is treatment; benzodiazepines help agitation in older people. Out of scope: antipsychotic dosing and management in Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia.

critic.blind_reasoning: New hyperactive delirium in an 81-year-old with infection, opioids and newly started temazepam requires bedside assessment for precipitants (pain, retention, hypoxia, drugs) and non-pharmacological management first; charting sedation over the phone or adding a benzodiazepine is unsafe, and CT is not first-line without focal signs.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound. The temazepam started on admission is a good teaching point for the explanation.

stem: You are the PGY2 covering the medical ward of a metropolitan general hospital at 2100; the medical registrar is resuscitating a patient in the emergency department. An 87-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's dementia, admitted yesterday with community-acquired pneumonia, has been increasingly restless since dinner. When a nurse tried to redirect him back to bed he pushed her and shouted; she is unhurt. He is now standing at the ward exit, agitated, demanding to go home to his wife, who died two years ago. He has had no analgesia today, has not passed urine since 1400, and his oxygen saturation is 93% on room air with a respiratory rate of 22/min. His daughter, who usually settles him, lives 15 minutes away. The nurse in charge asks you to 'give him something' and is considering calling security.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first action?

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 0.5 mg orally now so that he can be returned to bed and the ward kept safe overnight
Ask the nurse in charge to call security to escort him back to bed and apply a physical restraint
Page the registrar from the emergency department to review him before any treatment or redirection
De-escalate calmly with familiar staff, assess for reversible causes, and ask his daughter to come in

explanations.A: Antipsychotics in dementia increase stroke and death risk and are reserved for severe distress or imminent harm when non-drug approaches have failed; he has not been assessed, has likely reversible triggers, and is not currently striking anyone.
explanations.B: Physical restraint escalates agitation, causes injury and is a restrictive practice requiring justification and authorisation; security may be needed if imminent danger develops but is not the first step.
explanations.C: The registrar is managing a critical patient. Assessing and de-escalating an agitated patient on the ward is within a PGY2's scope; the registrar should be informed, but waiting for them delays safe care.
explanations.D: Behavioural symptoms in dementia are usually a response to unmet needs or a medical trigger: here untreated pain, possible urinary retention, borderline hypoxia, an unfamiliar environment and grief for his wife. The priority is safety through calm de-escalation by familiar staff, a focused check for reversible causes, and bringing in the person who settles him. Medication is considered only if he remains at imminent risk of harm.

learning_point: For behavioural symptoms in dementia, the first priority is de-escalation and a search for pain, retention, hypoxia and other triggers, with family involvement; antipsychotics and restraint come only when there is imminent danger after these fail.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia: assessment of triggers, non-pharmacological management, limited role of antipsychotics

references.title: Delirium Clinical Care Standard (2021) and Psychotropic medicines in cognitive disability or impairment Clinical Care Standard (2022)
references.locator: Non-pharmacological strategies first; psychotropics only for severe distress or risk of harm

plan: Tests prioritisation when an agitated patient with dementia threatens ward safety and the registrar is unavailable (1.4, 3.2, 2.8). Untreated pain, possible retention and bereavement are embedded as the real drivers. Distractors are the nurse's implicit request for sedation, security and restraint, and deferring to the registrar. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic and ACSQHC clinical care standards.
tutor_context: Key facts: behavioural symptoms in dementia often signal pain, retention, constipation, infection, hypoxia or delirium superimposed on dementia; de-escalation, familiar faces and family are first line; antipsychotics have modest benefit and real harms (stroke, death, falls) and need a specific indication of severe distress or danger; restraint is a last resort governed by policy. Misconceptions: a nurse being pushed means immediate sedation; waiting for the registrar is always safer. Out of scope: choice and dosing of antipsychotic if required, and Mental Health Act considerations.

critic.blind_reasoning: Agitation in a man with dementia and pneumonia who has had no analgesia, has not voided for seven hours and is mildly hypoxic calls for calm de-escalation, treatment of reversible drivers and involvement of a familiar person before any antipsychotic, restraint or security involvement.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Key is correct and safe; cueing is mild for a difficulty-3 item but the editor may wish to shorten D or lengthen A/C.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): D is the longest option and the only one listing three positive, guideline-flavoured actions; the stem also enumerates exactly the items D addresses (no analgesia, no urine, hypoxia, daughter), so the pattern-match is strong.

presentation: discharge planning for an older person
stem: You are the evening cover resident at a regional hospital with a small medical ward. An 88-year-old woman admitted four days ago with a urinary tract infection and a fall at home is due for discharge tomorrow morning. The nurse asks you to check that the discharge is still appropriate. The physiotherapist's note from this afternoon reads: 'Timed Up and Go 24 seconds with four-wheeled frame. Requires standby assistance for sit-to-stand and turning. Reports two falls in the past three months. Lives alone on a farm 40 km from town; no community services; daughter in Adelaide.' Her observations are normal, she is oriented and she says she is keen to go home to feed her dogs. The day team's plan says 'home when physio happy'.
lead_in: How should the physiotherapy assessment be interpreted?

options.text: She is at high falls risk and needs standby assistance, so discharge home alone tomorrow is unsafe without supports
A Timed Up and Go of 24 seconds is acceptable at her age, so discharge home tomorrow morning can proceed as planned
She needs transfer to Adelaide for inpatient geriatric rehabilitation before any discharge home can be considered
She can no longer manage at home and the plan should change to placement in permanent residential aged care

explanations.A: A Timed Up and Go above about 12 to 14 seconds indicates increased falls risk, and she also needs standby assistance for transfers and has had recurrent falls. Discharged alone to an isolated farm without services she is likely to fall again. The resident should document this and flag it clearly at handover so the day team, physiotherapist and social worker arrange supports (daughter, home care services, transitional care or a short extension of stay) before she leaves, rather than cancelling the discharge unilaterally overnight.
explanations.B: A Timed Up and Go of 24 seconds is well above the threshold associated with falls risk, and the need for standby assistance shows she cannot safely transfer alone; age does not normalise the result.
explanations.C: Rehabilitation may help, but regional hospitals often provide this locally or through transitional care, and a single assessment does not mandate transfer to Adelaide; this over-reads the note.
explanations.D: Needing assistance after an acute illness does not mean permanent care is required; function often improves with rehabilitation, and placement decisions involve the patient, family, geriatric assessment and her own wishes.

learning_point: A Timed Up and Go above 12 to 14 seconds and a need for standby assistance indicate high falls risk; discharge home alone should not proceed until supports are arranged, and the evening resident's job is to flag this clearly for the day team.
setting_note: Distance magnifies the risk: 40 km from town with no services means a fall may go unnoticed for hours. Regional hospitals often have access to transitional care, Commonwealth Home Support services and district nursing that the social worker can arrange, and a short extension of stay is reasonable while this happens.

references.title: Preventing Falls and Harm From Falls in Older People: Best Practice Guidelines for Australian Hospitals (2009)
references.locator: Falls risk screening and assessment; Timed Up and Go; discharge planning

references.title: Australian and New Zealand Falls Prevention Society: Timed Up and Go test
references.locator: Interpretation thresholds (12 to 14 seconds) for increased falls risk in older adults

plan: Tests interpretation of a functional assessment in the context of an isolated home (1.4, 3.2, 1.1). An evening resident asked to confirm a discharge makes the handover action concrete. Distractors are normalising the result and over-reading it as needing Adelaide rehabilitation or permanent care. Supported by the ACSQHC falls guidelines and ANZFPS guidance on the Timed Up and Go.
tutor_context: Key facts: the Timed Up and Go measures rising from a chair, walking 3 metres, turning and sitting; under 10 seconds is normal, over about 12 to 14 seconds indicates increased falls risk in community-dwelling older people; two or more falls in a year and the need for standby assistance are independent risk markers; safe discharge needs a match between function and the home environment. Misconceptions: a stated wish to go home and normal observations equal a safe discharge; the overnight resident must either cancel or rubber-stamp the plan. Out of scope: detailed aged care assessment processes.

critic.blind_reasoning: A Timed Up and Go of 24 seconds (well above the 12-14 second falls-risk threshold), standby assistance for transfers, recurrent falls and living alone on a farm with no services together mean discharge home alone tomorrow is unsafe without supports; the physio note does not say 'happy'.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good interpretation item; explanation should state the evening resident's action is to document and hand over, not to re-plan discharge alone.

stem: A 70-year-old woman on the general ward of a metropolitan teaching hospital, admitted with cellulitis and taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, is found on the floor beside her bed at 0300 by the night nurse. The fall was unwitnessed. You are the PGY2 covering. She is alert with a GCS of 15, normal pupils, no focal neurological deficit, no neck pain, and no visible scalp wound, bruise or swelling. She has grazed her right elbow. When asked, she says she got up to go to the toilet and 'the next thing I was on the floor'; she cannot recall falling or how long she was there. Observations are unchanged from the evening. The nurse has completed the post-fall assessment tool and asks what the findings mean for her care.
lead_in: How should these findings be interpreted?

options.text: A normal GCS and absence of visible head injury mean intracranial bleeding is excluded and hourly neurological observations are sufficient
Amnesia for the fall in an anticoagulated patient means head injury cannot be excluded and a CT brain is indicated now
Amnesia for the event indicates delirium, and the priority is a 4AT screen and delirium workup rather than imaging
Apixaban must be reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate immediately, before any imaging is arranged

explanations.A: Anticoagulated older patients can have significant intracranial bleeding with a normal initial GCS and no external sign, and symptoms may be delayed; observations alone are not enough once head strike cannot be excluded.
explanations.B: She cannot say whether she struck her head or lost consciousness, so an unwitnessed fall with amnesia must be treated as a possible head injury. On apixaban, this meets criteria for urgent CT brain (with consideration of cervical spine imaging) rather than observation, and the registrar should be informed. Amnesia for the event also raises the possibility of syncope, which needs its own assessment.
explanations.C: Delirium should be screened for after any fall, but amnesia for a single event is more suggestive of transient loss of consciousness than delirium, and a delirium workup does not address the risk of intracranial haemorrhage.
explanations.D: Reversal agents are given for confirmed or strongly suspected life-threatening bleeding; reversing anticoagulation without a diagnosis exposes her to thrombotic risk. The next dose of apixaban should be withheld pending the scan, and reversal considered if bleeding is found.

learning_point: An unwitnessed fall with amnesia for the event in an anticoagulated patient is a possible head injury, and a normal GCS does not exclude intracranial bleeding; urgent CT brain is indicated.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without CT overnight, discuss with the on-call physician and the retrieval or telehealth service: an anticoagulated patient with possible head strike may need transfer for imaging, and close neurological observations are a bridge, not a substitute.

references.title: Preventing Falls and Harm From Falls in Older People: Best Practice Guidelines for Australian Hospitals (2009)
references.locator: Post-fall management: assessment for injury, anticoagulation and head injury

references.title: Clinical Excellence Commission (NSW): Post Fall Guide, management of patients who fall in hospital
references.locator: Unwitnessed fall, anticoagulation and head strike as indications for urgent CT brain and medical review

plan: Tests interpretation of a post-fall assessment where the only red flag is amnesia in an anticoagulated patient (1.4, 3.2, 1.5). A night fall on a general ward with a reassuring examination makes the decision subtle. Distractors are false reassurance from the normal GCS, relabelling amnesia as delirium, and premature reversal. Supported by the ACSQHC falls guidelines and the NSW CEC post-fall guide.
tutor_context: Key facts: after an inpatient fall, assess for head injury, fracture and the cause of the fall; anticoagulation plus possible head strike (including unwitnessed falls and amnesia) is an indication for urgent CT brain; intracranial haemorrhage on anticoagulants can present with a normal GCS and evolve over hours; withhold the next anticoagulant dose pending imaging; also assess for syncope (postural blood pressure, ECG). Misconceptions: no bump means no head injury; reversal before diagnosis. Out of scope: management of confirmed intracranial haemorrhage and choice of reversal agent.
uncertainty_note: Post-fall imaging criteria are set by local health service policy; all Australian post-fall guides treat anticoagulation with possible head strike or unexplained fall as an indication for urgent CT, but the exact wording and timeframe vary.

critic.blind_reasoning: An unwitnessed fall with amnesia in a patient on apixaban means head strike cannot be excluded; anticoagulation is an indication for urgent CT brain regardless of a normal GCS or absence of external injury, per post-fall guidance.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound, important safety teaching point.

soft_flags: cueing: absolute term in distractor D

stem: An 88-year-old man on the surgical ward of a metropolitan general hospital was admitted this afternoon with an intracapsular fractured neck of femur after a fall at home. Surgery is planned for tomorrow morning. He weighs 62 kg, has chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2) and mild cognitive impairment, and takes amlodipine and a statin. He received paracetamol in the emergency department and a fascia iliaca block four hours ago, but now rates his hip pain at 7 out of 10 at rest and cannot be repositioned. The nurse asks you, the intern, to chart analgesia for the night. The orthopaedic registrar is in theatre and the anaesthetic registrar is available by phone.
lead_in: Which analgesic is most appropriate to chart?

options.text: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times a day with food
Tramadol 100 mg orally every six hours as needed for pain
Morphine 10 mg intramuscularly every four hours as needed
Oxycodone immediate-release 2.5 mg orally four-hourly as needed

explanations.A: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided in older people with chronic kidney disease because of acute kidney injury, fluid retention, hypertension and gastrointestinal bleeding, particularly before anaesthesia and surgery.
explanations.B: Tramadol causes confusion and delirium in older people, lowers the seizure threshold, accumulates in renal impairment, and 100 mg is a full adult dose; it is a poor choice in a frail 88-year-old.
explanations.C: Intramuscular injections are painful and erratically absorbed, and 10 mg is an excessive starting dose for a frail older man with renal impairment; it risks respiratory depression and delirium.
explanations.D: The Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard requires regular pain assessment and multimodal analgesia. With regular paracetamol continuing and the block wearing off, a low-dose immediate-release oral opioid is the appropriate addition for an older patient with renal impairment: oxycodone 2.5 mg, titrated to effect with monitoring, and a laxative charted alongside. Ask the anaesthetic registrar whether the block can be repeated.

learning_point: For hip fracture pain in a frail older patient, give regular paracetamol with a low-dose oral immediate-release opioid such as oxycodone 2.5 mg and consider repeating the nerve block; avoid NSAIDs, tramadol and intramuscular opioids.

references.title: Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard (2023)
references.locator: Quality statement 2: Pain management, including nerve blocks and regular assessment

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pain and Analgesia

plan: Tests the intern's choice of breakthrough analgesic for hip fracture in a frail man with renal impairment (1.4, 3.2, 1.8). A surgical ward at night with the block wearing off is the typical call. Distractors are an NSAID, tramadol and intramuscular morphine, each wrong for a stated reason. Supported by the ACSQHC Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard and Therapeutic Guidelines Pain and Analgesia.
tutor_context: Key facts: multimodal analgesia with regular paracetamol, a fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block (repeatable), and low-dose oral immediate-release opioid titrated to effect; start oxycodone at 2.5 mg in frail or renally impaired older patients; chart a laxative and an antiemetic; monitor sedation score. Misconceptions: tramadol is safer than oxycodone in older people; intramuscular morphine is a reasonable breakthrough option. Out of scope: performing the block, and perioperative anticoagulation.

critic.blind_reasoning: An 88-year-old, 62 kg man with eGFR 38 and cognitive impairment needs low-dose, short-acting oral opioid titrated to effect; oxycodone IR 2.5 mg PRN is the standard choice. NSAIDs are contraindicated by CKD, tramadol is poorly tolerated in frail elderly with renal impairment, and IM morphine is an inappropriate route and accumulates in renal impairment.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Easy and safe.

stem: An 86-year-old woman on the medical ward of a large metropolitan teaching hospital, admitted with community-acquired pneumonia, slips while walking to the bathroom with a nurse. She lands on her left side and immediately complains of left groin pain. She is unable to weight-bear, and the left leg appears slightly shortened and externally rotated, with pain on any attempt at hip rotation. Distal pulses and sensation are normal. She has osteoporosis treated with denosumab. A pelvis and left hip X-ray performed within the hour is reported as: 'No fracture or dislocation identified. Osteopenic bones. Degenerative change in both hips.' The nurse asks whether the physiotherapist can mobilise her in the morning.
lead_in: How should the X-ray result be interpreted?

options.text: A fracture has been excluded and she can be mobilised with physiotherapy in the morning as her pain allows
Her symptoms reflect a soft tissue injury and she should be reviewed in a week if the pain persists
An occult hip fracture is not excluded given the clinical signs, and MRI or CT is required
The findings suggest septic arthritis of the hip and urgent joint aspiration should be arranged

explanations.A: Mobilising a patient with an undiagnosed hip fracture risks displacing it and converting an undisplaced fracture into one needing a more complex operation; a negative X-ray does not clear her to walk when she cannot weight-bear.
explanations.B: Groin pain, inability to weight-bear, shortening and external rotation after a fall in an osteoporotic woman are hip fracture signs, not soft tissue strain; delaying diagnosis by a week would delay surgery and increase complications.
explanations.C: Plain X-rays miss a proportion of hip fractures, especially undisplaced fractures in osteopenic bone. The Australian and New Zealand hip fracture guideline recommends that when a fracture is suspected clinically despite a negative X-ray, MRI should be performed, with CT if MRI is unavailable. She should remain non-weight-bearing with analgesia and the orthopaedic team informed.
explanations.D: There is a clear traumatic cause, the onset was immediate after a fall, and nothing suggests joint infection; septic arthritis does not fit.

learning_point: A normal hip X-ray does not exclude a fracture when the clinical picture is typical; keep the patient non-weight-bearing and arrange MRI, or CT if MRI is unavailable.

references.title: Australian and New Zealand Guideline for Hip Fracture Care (ANZHFR, 2014)
references.locator: Imaging: MRI if hip fracture is suspected despite negative X-rays; CT if MRI is not available

references.title: Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard (2023)
references.locator: Quality statement 1: Care at presentation, including timely diagnosis

plan: Tests interpretation of a negative X-ray against strong clinical signs of hip fracture (1.4, 3.2, 1.5). An inpatient fall in an osteoporotic woman with classic signs makes the mismatch clear. Distractors are mobilising on the strength of the report, a soft tissue label, and an irrelevant infective diagnosis. Supported by the ANZHFR guideline and the ACSQHC Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard.
tutor_context: Key facts: around 2 to 10% of hip fractures are occult on initial plain films; shortening and external rotation with inability to weight-bear is a hip fracture until proven otherwise; MRI is the most sensitive test, CT an acceptable alternative; keep non-weight-bearing and give analgesia while awaiting imaging; report the inpatient fall as an incident. Misconceptions: a radiology report of no fracture ends the question; pain alone can be managed and reviewed later. Out of scope: surgical options and timing of surgery.

critic.blind_reasoning: Shortening, external rotation, inability to weight-bear and pain on rotation after a fall in an osteoporotic woman are a hip fracture until proven otherwise; plain films miss occult fractures and MRI (or CT if MRI unavailable) is required before mobilising.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound easy item.

stem: A 78-year-old Aboriginal woman from a community on the Yorke Peninsula is admitted to the general ward of the local rural hospital after a fall at home. Her blood glucose on arrival was 3.1 mmol/L and she was sweaty and confused, improving after oral glucose. With her consent, the Aboriginal Health Practitioner helps you take a medication history with her daughter present: metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide modified-release 60 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily and pantoprazole 40 mg daily, started 'years ago for indigestion'. Her daughter says her appetite has been poor for a month and she sometimes skips meals. Her HbA1c last month was 6.1% (43 mmol/mol) and her eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg. You are the PGY2 preparing her medication review for the ward round.
lead_in: Which medication should be addressed first in the medication review?

options.text: Gliclazide, because it has caused hypoglycaemia and her HbA1c is already below target
Pantoprazole, because long-term use without a clear indication increases fracture and infection risk
Atorvastatin, because statins offer little benefit to people over 75 years without known vascular disease
Metformin, because it should be stopped once the eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2

explanations.A: A sulfonylurea in an older person with poor appetite and an HbA1c of 6.1% is over-treatment that has already caused a hypoglycaemic fall, the most immediate harm on this list. Reducing or ceasing gliclazide, with a glycaemic target relaxed to around 7 to 8% for a frail older person, is the priority and should be agreed with her and her daughter, with the Aboriginal Health Practitioner supporting follow-up.
explanations.B: Long-term proton pump inhibitors without a clear indication are a reasonable deprescribing target, but this is not causing immediate harm and can be addressed at a later review.
explanations.C: Statin benefit in older people depends on cardiovascular history and life expectancy, and she has vascular risk factors; this is a shared decision over time, not the priority today.
explanations.D: Metformin can continue, with dose review below an eGFR of 45 and cessation below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2; an eGFR of 52 does not require cessation, and metformin does not cause hypoglycaemia.

learning_point: In a frail older person, the first deprescribing priority is the drug causing active harm: a sulfonylurea producing hypoglycaemia when HbA1c is already below the relaxed target for frailty.
setting_note: In a rural hospital the Aboriginal Health Practitioner and the community clinic are key to safe follow-up: a clear written medication list, a phone call to her usual clinic and support for home glucose monitoring make the change stick after discharge.

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Sulfonylureas: hypoglycaemia and precautions in older people; Metformin: dose adjustment in renal impairment

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetes
references.locator: Glycaemic targets in older people and those with frailty; deprescribing glucose-lowering drugs

references.title: RACGP Management of type 2 diabetes: a handbook for general practice
references.locator: Individualising HbA1c targets; hypoglycaemia risk in older people

plan: Tests prioritisation within a medication review after a hypoglycaemic fall (1.4, 3.2, 1.3). An older Aboriginal woman in a rural ward with family and the Aboriginal Health Practitioner involved models culturally safe medication history-taking. Distractors are reasonable but non-urgent deprescribing targets and a common metformin misconception. Supported by the AMH, Therapeutic Guidelines Diabetes and the RACGP diabetes handbook.
tutor_context: Key facts: sulfonylureas are the commonest cause of drug-induced hypoglycaemia in older people, especially with poor intake and renal impairment; HbA1c targets are relaxed to about 7 to 8% in frailty; metformin continues to eGFR 30 with dose reduction below 45; proton pump inhibitors and statins are legitimate deprescribing targets but are not urgent. Culturally safe practice: involve the Aboriginal Health Practitioner and family, and plan follow-up through her community clinic. Misconceptions: tight HbA1c is always better; eGFR under 60 means stop metformin. Out of scope: choice of alternative glucose-lowering agents.

critic.blind_reasoning: She presented with a symptomatic sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia causing a fall, with HbA1c 6.1% (below any target for a frail 78-year-old) and poor oral intake; gliclazide is the medication causing current harm and must be addressed first. Metformin is fine at eGFR 52, the statin is reasonable in diabetes, and the PPI is a lower-priority deprescribing target.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good model of culturally safe framing. Explanation should name the 'Hb A1c too low in a frail older person' concept.

stem: A 79-year-old woman on the medical ward of a regional hospital has been bed-bound for six days with severe pneumonia and heart failure, requiring oxygen and with poor oral intake. She has type 2 diabetes with peripheral neuropathy and a body mass index of 19. During the evening skin check the nurse finds a 4 cm area over her left heel that is deep purple, feels boggy compared with the surrounding skin, and is painful to touch. The skin is intact with no blister. The foot is warm, pedal pulses are palpable and capillary refill is normal. She did not fall before admission. The nurse asks you what the finding means and whether an incident report is needed.
lead_in: How should this finding be interpreted?

options.text: A stage 1 pressure injury with non-blanchable redness that will resolve with regular repositioning and skin care
A suspected deep tissue pressure injury that needs offloading, wound team review and an incident report
A bruise from minor trauma that needs only documentation and review at the next routine skin check
Acute limb ischaemia from peripheral arterial disease that needs urgent vascular surgical referral tonight

explanations.A: Stage 1 injuries show non-blanchable erythema of intact skin; a purple or maroon colour with boggy texture indicates damage to deeper tissue and is classified separately because it carries a much worse prognosis.
explanations.B: Persistent purple or maroon discolouration of intact skin that is boggy, painful and differs in temperature from surrounding tissue over a bony prominence is a suspected deep tissue pressure injury. It frequently evolves over days into a full-thickness ulcer even with good care. Management is complete heel offloading, a pressure-redistributing surface, nutrition review, wound or nurse specialist input, documentation with photographs, and an incident report as a hospital-acquired complication.
explanations.C: There is no history of trauma, and the location over a bony prominence in a bed-bound patient with risk factors points to pressure; labelling it a bruise would miss the chance to prevent progression.
explanations.D: A warm foot with palpable pulses and normal capillary refill excludes acute ischaemia; the lesion is localised to the pressure point.

learning_point: Purple or maroon discolouration of intact, boggy, painful skin over a bony prominence is a suspected deep tissue pressure injury that needs immediate offloading, specialist wound review and incident reporting, because it often progresses despite intact skin.
setting_note: Regional hospitals may not have a dedicated wound nurse; use the SA Health pressure injury resources, photograph and document carefully, and seek telehealth advice from the wound service or the physician on call, since progression could require transfer for surgical debridement.

references.title: NSQHS Standards (2nd edition): Comprehensive Care Standard
references.locator: Preventing and managing pressure injuries; Hospital-Acquired Complications list

references.title: Pan Pacific Clinical Practice Guideline for the Prevention and Management of Pressure Injury (Australian Wound Management Association)
references.locator: Classification of pressure injuries, including suspected deep tissue injury; heel offloading

plan: Tests interpretation of a nurse's skin finding as a suspected deep tissue pressure injury (1.4, 3.2, 1.1). A bed-bound, malnourished diabetic woman in a regional ward is the classic setting. Distractors are under-staging, a bruise label, and an ischaemia label excluded by the examination. Supported by the NSQHS Comprehensive Care Standard and the Pan Pacific pressure injury guideline.
tutor_context: Key facts: pressure injury stages 1 to 4 plus unstageable and suspected deep tissue injury; deep tissue injury is purple or maroon intact skin or a blood-filled blister, often boggy or painful, and can progress rapidly; heels are high risk in immobile, malnourished, diabetic and neuropathic patients; management is offloading, support surfaces, nutrition and wound expertise; hospital-acquired pressure injuries are reportable complications. Misconceptions: intact skin means minor injury; a purple heel is a bruise. Out of scope: dressing selection and debridement.

critic.blind_reasoning: A localised purple, boggy, painful area of intact skin over the heel in an immobile, malnourished patient is the classic description of a suspected deep tissue pressure injury; it needs immediate offloading, wound/skin integrity review and an incident report as a hospital-acquired pressure injury.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound; the diabetic neuropathy adds a nice reason the injury went unnoticed.
