explanations.A: The abbreviation 'mcg' is on the ACSQHC list of error-prone abbreviations to avoid because it has been misread as 'mg', producing thousand-fold overdoses; 'micrograms' must be written in full.
explanations.B: This order uses the generic name, the dose with the unit written in full, the route and an accepted frequency, with no error-prone abbreviations, no trailing zero and no naked decimal. It should also carry the indication, the prescriber's signature, printed name and the date.
explanations.C: A decimal with no leading zero can be read as 625 mg. If a decimal is unavoidable a leading zero is mandatory, and expressing the dose in micrograms avoids the decimal altogether.
explanations.D: A trailing zero after a decimal point (62.50) can be read as 6250 micrograms, a hundred-fold overdose; trailing zeros must never be used.

learning_point: Write 'micrograms' and 'units' in full, never use trailing zeros, and always put a leading zero before a decimal point; these are the ACSQHC national rules for safe medication charting.
setting_note: Paper charts remain common in country hospitals, so legible, standardised writing matters more; electronic prescribing systems in tertiary hospitals enforce many of these rules automatically.

references.title: Recommendations for terminology, abbreviations and symbols used in medicines documentation (2016)
references.locator: Dose expression: micrograms and units in full; no trailing zeros; leading zero before decimal point; error-prone abbreviations

references.title: National Inpatient Medication Chart user guide
references.locator: Writing a regular medicine order

plan: Tests the basic management skill of writing a safe digoxin order on a paper chart, evidencing 1.8, 1.10 and 1.1. Elderly man admitted overnight in a country hospital with paper charts. Distractors are the three classic error-prone forms: mcg, naked decimal, trailing zero. Supported by the ACSQHC terminology recommendations and NIMC user guide.
tutor_context: Key facts: write micrograms, units, international units in full; no trailing zeros; leading zero before a decimal; avoid 'u', 'IU', 'mcg', 'ug', 'OD', 'qd'; generic names; include indication, route, frequency, date, signature and printed name. Misconceptions: 'mcg' is acceptable because it is common. Out of scope: digoxin dosing itself, electronic prescribing workflows.

critic.blind_reasoning: ACSQHC terminology recommendations: write 'micrograms' in full (no mcg or ug), no trailing zeros and no decimal without a leading zero. 'Mane' is an accepted abbreviation.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Easy but valid; 'mcg' remains in common use so A is a worthwhile distractor.

stem: On the medical ward of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide, a 70-year-old woman admitted with community-acquired pneumonia develops new central chest tightness. The nurse brings the ECG machine and asks you, the intern, to record a 12-lead ECG while she phones the registrar. You attach the limb electrodes, place V1 at the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal edge and V2 at the fourth intercostal space at the left sternal edge, and then need to locate V4 so that V3, V5 and V6 can be placed in relation to it. The patient had an ECG in the emergency department yesterday and the registrar will want to compare the two.
lead_in: Where should the V4 electrode be placed?

options.text: Fifth intercostal space at the left sternal edge
Fourth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line
Fifth intercostal space in the left anterior axillary line
Fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line

explanations.A: The left sternal edge in the fourth space is the V2 position; no standard chest electrode sits at the sternal edge in the fifth space.
explanations.B: V4 is one interspace lower than V1 and V2. Placing it in the fourth space shifts the anterior leads upward and can mimic or conceal anterior ST changes when serial ECGs are compared.
explanations.C: The fifth space in the anterior axillary line is the V5 position, placed horizontally level with V4.
explanations.D: V4 is placed in the fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line. V3 is then placed midway between V2 and V4, and V5 and V6 at the same horizontal level as V4 in the anterior axillary and midaxillary lines. In a woman with large breasts the electrodes are placed beneath the breast to reach the correct landmarks. Consistent placement is what makes serial ECGs comparable.

learning_point: V4 is at the fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line, and V5 and V6 are placed at the same horizontal level as V4 rather than following the rib space.
setting_note: Interns in small hospitals often record their own ECGs overnight without a technician, so correct placement is a core skill; the landmarks do not change with setting.

references.title: Society for Cardiological Science and Technology. Clinical guidelines by consensus: recording a standard 12-lead electrocardiogram (2017)
references.locator: Section on chest electrode positions (V1 to V6)

references.title: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: ECG lead positioning
references.locator: Precordial lead placement

plan: Tests recall of standard precordial electrode placement, evidencing 1.6 and 1.5. Older woman with chest tightness on a ward where the intern records the ECG. Distractors are neighbouring positions commonly confused (V2's level, the fourth space, V5's line). Supported by the SCST consensus guideline and LITFL lead positioning summary.
tutor_context: Key facts: V1 fourth ICS right sternal edge; V2 fourth ICS left sternal edge; V3 midway between V2 and V4; V4 fifth ICS left midclavicular line; V5 anterior axillary line level with V4; V6 midaxillary line level with V4; limb electrodes distal on limbs (or proximal if tremor, noting on the trace); electrodes under the breast; document any non-standard placement. Misconceptions: V5 and V6 follow the interspace rather than a horizontal line; V4 at the fourth space. Out of scope: ECG interpretation, posterior and right-sided leads.

critic.blind_reasoning: V4 is placed in the fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line; V3 is midway between V2 and V4, V5 and V6 at the same horizontal level in the anterior and mid-axillary lines.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Pure recall; stem could be shortened.

stem: A 36-year-old man with a severe asthma exacerbation is in the emergency department of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. Forty minutes ago you, the junior doctor, took an arterial blood gas from his right radial artery after two failed attempts; the nurse applied a firm pressure bandage. He now says his right hand is painful and 'numb'. It is pale and cool compared with the left, capillary refill is 5 seconds, and you cannot feel the radial pulse at the wrist, though the ulnar pulse is palpable. His breathing has improved on nebulised salbutamol and he is awaiting the physician's review. There is no vascular surgeon or CT angiography available in the hospital tonight.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Remove the pressure bandage, reassess now and get urgent vascular advice if it does not recover
Elevate the arm on pillows, apply a warm pack to the hand and review it again in 4 hours
Start a therapeutic heparin infusion immediately on the assumption of a radial artery thrombosis
Take a repeat arterial sample from the right ulnar artery to confirm that his gas has improved

explanations.A: A pale, cool, pulseless hand after arterial puncture is a time-critical limb threat. The first step is to remove any constricting dressing, which may be the whole cause, and reassess. If the signs persist, radial artery thrombosis, dissection or spasm with inadequate collateral flow must be assumed, and vascular surgical advice sought immediately, with retrieval if intervention is needed. The physician and senior nurse are told at the same time.
explanations.B: Waiting 4 hours with an ischaemic hand risks irreversible tissue loss; elevation and review suit a simple haematoma, not pulselessness with a capillary refill of 5 seconds.
explanations.C: Anticoagulation may be advised, but starting it before vascular assessment in a patient who may have a dissection or compressive haematoma is a specialist decision, not the junior doctor's first step.
explanations.D: Puncturing the ulnar artery of a hand that may be surviving on ulnar flow alone could complete the ischaemia; it is contraindicated.

learning_point: A pale, cool, painful or pulseless hand after radial arterial puncture is a vascular emergency: release any pressure dressing, reassess immediately and escalate to vascular surgery without delay.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without vascular surgery or CT angiography after hours, early phone contact with the Adelaide vascular service and MedSTAR retrieval is the only route to intervention, so the threshold to call is lower than in a tertiary centre where the vascular team can review at the bedside.

references.title: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) Critical Care Compendium: Arterial blood gas sampling
references.locator: Complications of arterial puncture and their management

references.title: Dougherty L, Lister S (eds). The Royal Marsden Manual of Clinical Nursing Procedures, 10th edition
references.locator: Arterial puncture: post-procedure care and complications (haematoma, thrombosis, ischaemia)

plan: Tests management of a rare but critical complication of arterial puncture, evidencing 1.6, 1.9 and 1.1. Young man in a regional ED without vascular services makes early escalation the hinge. Distractors: elevation and wait (under-reaction), empirical heparin (over-reach), ulnar puncture (dangerous). Supported by LITFL arterial sampling complications and a standard procedural manual.
tutor_context: Key facts: complications of radial puncture include haematoma, arterial spasm, thrombosis, dissection, infection and nerve injury; a modified Allen test or Doppler before puncture checks collateral ulnar flow; a pressure dressing that is too tight can itself occlude; signs of ischaemia (pain, pallor, coolness, slow refill, absent pulse) require immediate reassessment and vascular escalation, as warm ischaemia time for the hand is measured in hours. Misconceptions: a palpable ulnar pulse makes the hand safe; observation is reasonable overnight. Out of scope: surgical or endovascular techniques, anticoagulation regimens.
uncertainty_note: No single Australian guideline covers management of limb ischaemia after arterial puncture; the key reflects standard procedural and vascular surgical practice described in Australian procedural references.

critic.blind_reasoning: A pale, cool, pulseless hand with delayed refill under a firm pressure bandage after arterial puncture is limb-threatening; remove the bandage immediately and reassess, then escalate to vascular surgery and retrieval if perfusion does not recover. Observation for 4 hours or an unsupervised heparin infusion would be unsafe.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Target difficulty 5 seems high for this item; shorten A to reduce cueing.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): A is much longer than the other options and the only one with an escalation pathway.

stem: You are the PGY2 in the recovery area of the theatre suite of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward. An 81-year-old woman, 55 kg, has just arrived from theatre after a hip hemiarthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia with intravenous sedation; she received fentanyl 50 micrograms 20 minutes ago. The anaesthetist has gone back into theatre to start the next case. The recovery nurse calls you because the patient has become unrousable to voice, is snoring loudly with see-saw chest and abdominal movement, and her SpO2 has fallen from 96% to 86% on 6 L oxygen via a Hudson mask. Heart rate 92, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg. A bag-valve-mask, oropharyngeal airways and suction are on the trolley beside you.
lead_in: What should you do first?

options.text: Give naloxone 100 micrograms intravenously and repeat every 2 minutes until she wakes
Insert a size 3 laryngeal mask airway yourself and connect it to the oxygen circuit
Do a chin lift or jaw thrust, give 15 L/min oxygen and have the anaesthetist recalled
Sit her upright and apply continuous positive airway pressure through the ward CPAP machine

explanations.A: Opioid-related sedation is probably contributing and naloxone may well follow, but drawing up and giving a drug while the airway remains obstructed delays the manoeuvre that corrects hypoxia within seconds; airway opening comes first (ANZCOR Guideline 4).
explanations.B: A laryngeal mask requires a deeply unconscious patient and skills most PGY2s do not have; it is the anaesthetist's decision, after simple manoeuvres have been tried.
explanations.C: Snoring with see-saw movement and falling saturations means upper airway obstruction from loss of tone. A head-tilt, chin-lift or jaw thrust relieves it immediately, high-flow oxygen buys time, and the anaesthetist, who is seconds away, must be recalled at once. An oropharyngeal airway and bag-valve-mask ventilation follow if breathing remains inadequate.
explanations.D: CPAP needs a patent airway and a cooperative patient; it does not treat obstruction from reduced consciousness, and sitting a sedated patient upright risks losing the airway altogether.

learning_point: Noisy, obstructed breathing in a sedated patient is treated first with basic airway manoeuvres and high-flow oxygen while help is called; drugs and airway devices come after the airway is open.
setting_note: In a regional theatre suite the anaesthetist may be the only person able to manage an advanced airway, so the junior doctor must be able to maintain a basic airway alone for several minutes and should call early; in a tertiary hospital a second anaesthetist or ICU team is usually available.

references.title: ANZCOR Guideline 4: Airway
references.locator: Basic airway management: head tilt, chin lift and jaw thrust; airway adjuncts

references.title: ANZCOR Guideline 3: Recognition and first aid management of the unconscious person
references.locator: Airway and breathing assessment and calling for help

plan: Tests prioritisation of basic airway manoeuvres and calling help over drugs or devices, evidencing 1.6 and 1.9. Elderly woman in recovery at a regional hospital with the anaesthetist in theatre. Distractors: naloxone first (plausible cause but wrong order), LMA (beyond scope), CPAP (wrong tool). Supported by ANZCOR Guidelines 3 and 4.
tutor_context: Key facts: sequence for obstructed airway in a sedated patient is open the airway (head tilt/chin lift, jaw thrust), high-flow oxygen, call for help, then adjuncts (oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway), bag-valve-mask ventilation if breathing inadequate, then consider reversal agents; naloxone in titrated doses (for example 100 micrograms IV) is appropriate once the airway is supported. Misconceptions: reversal drugs are the first step; CPAP treats obstruction from reduced consciousness. Out of scope: supraglottic airway insertion technique, intubation.

critic.blind_reasoning: Snoring with see-saw movement indicates upper airway obstruction from sedation/opioid; the first step is a basic airway manoeuvre with high-flow oxygen and immediate recall of the anaesthetist. Naloxone is appropriate soon after but does not open the airway now; an LMA or CPAP is not the first action.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Sound; consider trimming C and noting in the explanation that naloxone follows once airway is supported.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): C is the longest option and bundles three actions, making it the comprehensive choice.

stem: In the pre-admission clinic and theatre suite of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide, a 55-year-old woman is about to have a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Four years ago she had a left mastectomy with axillary node clearance for breast cancer and has mild left arm lymphoedema controlled with a compression sleeve. Her right forearm has good visible veins and both antecubital fossae have large veins. She has no arteriovenous fistula. The anaesthetist asks you, the resident, to site an intravenous cannula suitable for induction and for a possible postoperative patient-controlled analgesia pump, and mentions that the surgeon wants the left arm tucked by her side during the operation.
lead_in: Which cannulation site is most appropriate?

options.text: Left antecubital fossa, 16 gauge, because it has the largest vein
Right forearm, 18 or 20 gauge, avoiding the antecubital crease
Left dorsum of the hand, 20 gauge, to keep the antecubital fossa for blood sampling
Right foot, 22 gauge, to keep both arms free

explanations.A: The arm on the side of axillary node clearance with established lymphoedema should be avoided for cannulation, venepuncture and blood pressure cuffs where a reasonable alternative exists, as the Australasian Lymphology Association advises; a tucked arm is also inaccessible to the anaesthetist during the case.
explanations.B: The right forearm has good veins, avoids the lymphoedema arm, avoids the flexion point at the elbow (which kinks, dislodges and is discouraged for routine use in the ACSQHC PIVC Clinical Care Standard), and an 18 or 20 gauge cannula is adequate for induction, fluids and a PCA.
explanations.C: This site is in the at-risk arm, and the hand is a less comfortable and less durable site; preserving the fossa for sampling does not override the lymphoedema precaution.
explanations.D: Lower-limb cannulation in an adult carries higher thrombosis and infection risk and is reserved for when no upper-limb site is usable.

learning_point: Avoid cannulating an arm with lymphoedema or prior axillary node clearance where another site exists, and prefer forearm veins over flexion points for a cannula that will stay in after surgery.
setting_note: No change between settings; in a regional hospital the junior doctor is more often the one inserting theatre cannulas and should ask the patient directly about previous breast or axillary surgery and fistulas before choosing a site.

references.title: Management of Peripheral Intravenous Catheters Clinical Care Standard (2021)
references.locator: Quality statement on insertion: site selection (avoid areas of flexion, limbs with lymphoedema, fistula or prior axillary surgery)

references.title: Australasian Lymphology Association. Position statement: Lymphoedema risk reduction (venepuncture, cannulation and blood pressure in the at-risk limb)
references.locator: Recommendations for the at-risk limb

plan: Tests the management decision of cannula site selection in a woman with prior axillary clearance and lymphoedema, evidencing 1.6 and 1.1. Tertiary theatre suite with anaesthetist delegating. Distractors: biggest vein in the wrong arm, hand of the wrong arm, foot vein. Supported by the ACSQHC PIVC standard and the Australasian Lymphology Association position statement.
tutor_context: Key facts: choose the non-dominant forearm where possible; avoid flexion points, the at-risk limb after axillary node clearance or with lymphoedema, fistula arms, limbs with cellulitis or planned surgery, and lower limbs in adults; 18 to 20 gauge suits most adult theatre cases; document site, date and gauge. Misconceptions: biggest vein is always best; a tucked arm with a cannula can be monitored. Out of scope: ultrasound-guided cannulation, central access.
uncertainty_note: Evidence that cannulation in the at-risk arm causes or worsens lymphoedema is limited, but Australian practice and the Australasian Lymphology Association still advise avoiding it where an alternative exists.

critic.blind_reasoning: Avoid the left arm after axillary node clearance with lymphoedema; a forearm 18 or 20 gauge in the right arm away from the antecubital crease is suitable for induction and PCA and will not kink with flexion. Foot cannulation is a last resort.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Distractors C and D are weak; a right antecubital 16 gauge option would make the item more discriminating.

stem: You are the intern covering the general ward and emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. A 32-year-old woman, 60 kg, admitted with pyelonephritis, slips in the bathroom and sustains a clean 6 cm laceration to her left forearm with no tendon or nerve involvement. The nurse has irrigated it and set up a suture tray with 1% lignocaine (lidocaine) without adrenaline. The woman has no allergies, no cardiac history and is not pregnant. The GP on call asks you by phone to close the wound and reminds you to stay within the maximum safe dose of local anaesthetic.
lead_in: What is the maximum volume of 1% lignocaine without adrenaline you may infiltrate for this woman?

options.text: 10 mL
30 mL
42 mL
18 mL

explanations.A: 10 mL (100 mg) is well within the safe limit but is not the maximum; underestimating the ceiling can lead to inadequate anaesthesia and a painful closure when more could safely be used.
explanations.B: 30 mL of 1% is 300 mg, which is 5 mg/kg, above the 3 mg/kg limit for plain lignocaine and risks systemic toxicity (perioral tingling, tinnitus, confusion, seizures, arrhythmia).
explanations.C: 42 mL (420 mg) corresponds to 7 mg/kg, the maximum for lignocaine with adrenaline, not for the plain solution on this tray.
explanations.D: Plain lignocaine has a maximum of 3 mg/kg up to 200 mg (Therapeutic Guidelines and the Australian Medicines Handbook). For 60 kg this is 180 mg; a 1% solution contains 10 mg/mL, so 18 mL. Aspirating before injecting and injecting slowly reduce the risk of intravascular injection, and a 6 cm laceration usually needs well under this volume.

learning_point: The maximum lignocaine dose is 3 mg/kg (up to 200 mg) without adrenaline and 7 mg/kg (up to 500 mg) with adrenaline; a 1% solution contains 10 mg/mL.
setting_note: In a country hospital the junior doctor closes wounds alone overnight and must know the dose limit, the early signs of local anaesthetic toxicity and where lipid emulsion is kept, because help is by phone; the arithmetic is unchanged in a metropolitan emergency department.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pain and Analgesia (Local anaesthetics)
references.locator: Maximum doses of local anaesthetics for infiltration: lidocaine with and without adrenaline

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Lidocaine (lignocaine): dosage for local infiltration, maximum dose

plan: Tests recall of the plain lignocaine maximum dose and the percentage-to-mg conversion, evidencing 1.6 and 1.8. Young woman on a country ward closed by the lone intern overnight. Distractors: a safe but sub-maximal volume, the 5 mg/kg error, the with-adrenaline limit. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines local anaesthetic doses and AMH lidocaine.
tutor_context: Key facts: 1% = 10 mg/mL, 2% = 20 mg/mL; plain lignocaine maximum 3 mg/kg (200 mg); with adrenaline 7 mg/kg (500 mg); bupivacaine 2 mg/kg; signs of toxicity progress from perioral tingling and tinnitus to seizures and cardiovascular collapse; treatment includes stopping injection, airway support, benzodiazepine for seizures and intravenous lipid emulsion. Misconceptions: percentage equals mg per mL; adrenaline limits apply to plain solution. Out of scope: digital blocks, wound closure technique.

critic.blind_reasoning: Maximum lignocaine without adrenaline is 3 mg/kg (AMH/TG): 60 kg x 3 = 180 mg, and 1% solution is 10 mg/mL, giving 18 mL. 42 mL corresponds to the 7 mg/kg with-adrenaline limit.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Clean calculation item.

stem: You are the only doctor overnight in the 4-bed emergency department of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, with the GP on call at home. A 19-year-old man with a previous appendicectomy presents with 12 hours of colicky abdominal pain, distension and repeated bilious vomiting; heart rate 108, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray taken before the radiographer went home shows dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels. You have inserted a cannula, started intravenous fluids and given analgesia, and the GP has agreed by phone that he needs a nasogastric tube and transfer to Adelaide in the morning. You pass a 16 Fr nasogastric tube to 60 cm without difficulty; he is talking comfortably and no fluid has yet drained.
lead_in: What should you do first before leaving the tube in place?

options.text: Aspirate and test with pH indicator paper, accepting pH 5 or less as gastric placement
Inject 20 mL of air down the tube while auscultating over the epigastrium for a 'whoosh'
Call the on-call radiographer back in for a chest X-ray before anything else is done
Connect the tube to free drainage, secure it and reassess its position at handover

explanations.A: Australian guidance (the NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation guideline, mirrored in SA Health local procedures) recommends confirming gastric placement with an aspirate pH of 5 or less using pH indicator paper as the first-line check. If no aspirate is obtained, the patient is repositioned or a little air insufflated and aspiration repeated; an X-ray is used when pH testing fails or is unreliable. Even a tube placed for drainage can coil in the oesophagus or enter the airway, so position is confirmed before it is secured.
explanations.B: The 'whoosh' test is unreliable and has been abandoned; a tube in a bronchus can produce an identical sound.
explanations.C: Radiography is the second-line confirmation when pH testing is unavailable or equivocal. Recalling the radiographer before attempting pH testing wastes a scarce overnight resource and time, though it becomes appropriate if pH cannot confirm placement.
explanations.D: Leaving an unconfirmed tube in place until handover risks aspiration or a wrongly sited tube going unnoticed for hours.

learning_point: Confirm nasogastric tube position with an aspirate pH of 5 or less before use or leaving it in place; the 'whoosh' test is obsolete and X-ray is the second-line method when pH testing fails.
setting_note: In a rural hospital an overnight X-ray means calling in a radiographer, so pH testing is the practical first check; a tertiary emergency department can obtain an X-ray quickly, but pH testing remains the first step there too.

references.title: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation. Guideline: Insertion and management of nasogastric and orogastric tubes in adults (2021)
references.locator: Confirming tube position: pH testing first line, X-ray second line

references.title: SA Health local health network procedure: Nasogastric tube insertion and confirmation of position in adults
references.locator: Position confirmation prior to use

plan: Tests prioritisation of position confirmation by pH before using or leaving a nasogastric tube, evidencing 1.6 and 1.1. Young man with small bowel obstruction in a rural ED overnight where X-ray means recalling a radiographer. Distractors: whoosh test (obsolete), X-ray first (wasteful), defer to handover (unsafe). Supported by the NSW ACI nasogastric guideline and SA Health procedure.
tutor_context: Key facts: confirm position by aspirate pH 5 or less (indicator paper, not litmus); if no aspirate, reposition, wait, insufflate a small volume of air and retry; X-ray if pH testing fails, pH is above 5, or the patient is on acid suppression; the whoosh test and bubbling in water are not acceptable; document the method, external length and date. Contraindications to the nasal route include base-of-skull fracture and severe facial trauma. Misconceptions: a drainage tube does not need confirming; talking comfortably proves the tube is not in the airway. Out of scope: feeding tube management, bridle fixation.
uncertainty_note: The pH threshold of 5 or less is used by NSW ACI and most Australian hospital procedures; some local procedures use 5.5. The principle of pH first, X-ray second is consistent.

critic.blind_reasoning: First-line confirmation of NG tube position is aspiration and pH testing, with gastric placement accepted at pH 5 or less (or 5.5 depending on local policy); X-ray is reserved for when aspirate cannot be obtained or pH is higher. The whoosh test is unreliable and leaving the tube unconfirmed is unsafe.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Explanation should mention that if no aspirate or pH above threshold, the radiographer is recalled for X-ray before use.

stem: A 52-year-old woman attends the emergency department of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide at 23:00 with a closed, minimally displaced distal radius fracture after a fall. A below-elbow plaster backslab was applied at 15:00 and she was discharged with paracetamol and ibuprofen and a fracture clinic appointment. She has returned because the pain has steadily worsened over 6 hours, is 9/10 and unrelieved by her analgesia, and she describes 'tightness'. On examination the fingers are swollen and she is reluctant to move them; gentle passive extension of the fingers causes severe forearm pain. Capillary refill is 2 seconds, the radial pulse is palpable and sensation to light touch is intact across all fingers. The orthopaedic registrar is in theatre and the ED consultant is on the floor.
lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for these findings?

options.text: Expected post-fracture pain that will settle with elevation and stronger analgesia
Median nerve neuropraxia caused directly by the distal radius fracture itself
Raised pressure from a constricting cast or an evolving forearm compartment syndrome
Arterial injury, which is excluded here because the pulse is present and refill is normal

explanations.A: Pain that escalates despite immobilisation and analgesia, with pain on passive stretch, is not expected post-fracture pain; it is the cardinal early sign of rising compartment pressure or a cast that has become too tight as swelling increases.
explanations.B: Median nerve neuropraxia causes numbness and weakness in the median distribution; her sensation is intact and the dominant feature is pain out of proportion with passive stretch pain.
explanations.C: Pain out of proportion, worsening over hours, with pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles is the earliest and most reliable sign; pulselessness, pallor and paraesthesia are late. The immediate response is to split the plaster and all padding to skin along its full length, keep the limb at heart level, and have the orthopaedic registrar see her now, with the ED consultant's help to insist, with a plan for compartment pressure measurement or fasciotomy if symptoms do not settle promptly.
explanations.D: A present pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome because tissue pressure exceeds capillary but not arterial pressure; arterial injury is also not suggested by the mechanism or the normal refill.

learning_point: Escalating pain out of proportion with pain on passive stretch under a cast is compartment syndrome or a tight cast until proven otherwise; pulses and capillary refill stay normal until late, so split the cast to skin and escalate immediately.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the junior doctor splits the cast and calls the on-call orthopaedic service in Adelaide and retrieval early, as fasciotomy cannot wait for a morning transfer; in a tertiary emergency department the registrar may be in theatre, so the ED consultant should be involved to ensure review within minutes.

references.title: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation, Emergency Care Institute: Plaster and cast care; Compartment syndrome
references.locator: Recognition of a tight cast and compartment syndrome; splitting the cast

references.title: British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma (BOAST): Diagnosis and management of compartment syndrome of the limbs (2016)
references.locator: Clinical diagnosis: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch; pulses unreliable

plan: Tests interpretation of pain out of proportion and passive stretch pain under a cast as compartment syndrome despite normal pulse and refill, evidencing 1.6, 1.4 and 1.9. Middle-aged woman re-presenting to a tertiary ED at night. Distractors: expected pain (anchoring on the simple fracture), median neuropraxia (plausible for distal radius), pulse-based reassurance (classic error). Supported by NSW ECI plaster guidance and BOAST compartment syndrome standard.
tutor_context: Key facts: early signs are pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling and increasing analgesic requirement; paraesthesia, pallor, paralysis and pulselessness are late; management is to split cast and padding to skin, limb at heart level (not elevated above it), analgesia, urgent orthopaedic review and compartment pressure measurement or fasciotomy. Misconceptions: a palpable pulse excludes compartment syndrome; elevation high above the heart helps (it reduces perfusion pressure). Out of scope: fasciotomy technique, pressure measurement thresholds.
uncertainty_note: No Australian national guideline on compartment syndrome; the key reflects the NSW Emergency Care Institute plaster guidance and the British Orthopaedic Association standard widely used in Australian orthopaedic practice.

critic.blind_reasoning: Pain out of proportion, tightness, swelling and pain on passive finger extension in a cast are the early signs of a constricting cast or compartment syndrome; pulses and capillary refill are preserved until late and do not exclude it. Immediate action is to split the cast and escalate.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Move the rationale out of option C into the explanation.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): C is the longest option and embeds the teaching point ('a palpable pulse ... do not exclude the diagnosis'), which reads as the examiner's voice.

stem: You are the resident on the general ward of a large metropolitan teaching hospital. At 10:30, while taking blood from a 32-year-old man admitted with cellulitis who has a history of injecting drug use and whose hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV status are not documented, the needle slips as you withdraw it and punctures your gloved thumb, drawing blood. You still have the rest of the ward round jobs to do and the registrar is at the bedside of another patient. The hospital's occupational exposure procedure directs staff to the staff health clinic during business hours or the emergency department after hours. You completed hepatitis B vaccination at university but do not know your antibody level.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wash the puncture with soap and running water, finish the ward round jobs, then report the injury at the end of the shift
Wash the puncture with soap and water, tell the registrar, go to staff health now, and seek his consent to test his blood
Squeeze the puncture to expel blood, apply an alcohol swab, take your own bloods on the ward and check the results tomorrow
Ask his nurse to add hepatitis and HIV serology to his morning bloods without telling him, to guide your treatment

explanations.A: Washing is correct but delay is not. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is most effective when started within hours (ideally within 2 and no later than 72), and the source patient's rapid testing, hepatitis B immunoglobulin decisions and incident documentation all depend on prompt reporting. Ward jobs can be handed over.
explanations.B: This follows SA Health and the ASHM national guidance: first aid, immediate reporting to the supervisor, prompt assessment by the designated service, baseline serology of the exposed worker, rapid testing of the source with consent, a risk assessment for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis and hepatitis B immunoglobulin or booster, and an incident report. The registrar covering the ward is the right person to tell.
explanations.C: Squeezing the wound is not recommended and does not reduce risk, alcohol is unnecessary, and self-ordered bloods bypass the risk assessment, counselling and the time-critical decision about prophylaxis.
explanations.D: Testing the source patient without his knowledge and consent breaches his rights. Source testing requires informed consent with a pre-test discussion; most patients agree to rapid testing when asked respectfully.

learning_point: After a needlestick, wash the wound, report immediately, attend the designated service for risk assessment and baseline bloods the same day, and arrange source testing only with the patient's informed consent.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the designated service is usually the emergency department, and HIV post-exposure prophylaxis starter packs and rapid source testing may need to be arranged through the ED or by phone with the SA infectious diseases service, which makes immediate reporting even more important.

references.title: ASHM. National guidelines for post-exposure prophylaxis after non-occupational and occupational exposure to HIV (2nd edition 2016, updated 2023)
references.locator: Occupational exposure: timing of PEP, source testing with consent, baseline testing of the exposed person

references.title: SA Health: Management of occupational exposure to blood and body fluids (Infection Control Service guideline)
references.locator: Immediate first aid, reporting and risk assessment

plan: Tests management of a needlestick from a high-risk source, evidencing 1.6, 1.1 and 2.2. Resident on a busy metropolitan ward with competing jobs. Distractors: delay until end of shift (common real behaviour), squeeze and self-test (folk practice), covert source testing (ethical breach). Supported by ASHM national PEP guidelines and SA Health occupational exposure guidance.
tutor_context: Key facts: first aid is washing with soap and water (do not squeeze, no caustic agents); report immediately; designated service performs risk assessment considering source status and exposure type; HIV PEP ideally within 2 hours and up to 72; hepatitis B management depends on vaccination and antibody status (booster or immunoglobulin); hepatitis C has no prophylaxis but needs follow-up testing; source testing requires informed consent; complete an incident report. Misconceptions: squeezing helps; the injured doctor can self-manage. Out of scope: PEP drug regimens.

critic.blind_reasoning: Occupational exposure: wash with soap and water, report immediately, attend staff health for risk assessment, baseline serology and timely PEP decision, and test the source with informed consent. Delaying to end of shift, squeezing, or covert source testing are all wrong.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Trim B; explanation should mention HIV PEP is time-critical (ideally within hours, no later than 72 h).

soft_flags: cueing (critic): B is far longer than the others and bundles all correct steps.

stem: You are the intern in the recovery and surgical ward area of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, with the GP anaesthetist still in the building. A 78-year-old man with known benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin had an inguinal hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia this afternoon. Eight hours later he has not passed urine, is uncomfortable, and a bladder scan shows 720 mL. The nurse has attempted a 14 Fr catheter without success. You attempt a 16 Fr catheter with lignocaine lubricant gel, using aseptic technique. The catheter passes to about 20 cm with mild resistance at one point, and about 30 mL of clear urine returns. As you begin to inflate the balloon with sterile water he cries out with sharp pain in the penis, and the water is hard to inject.
lead_in: What do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Normal transient discomfort of catheterisation that should settle once the balloon is fully inflated
Bladder spasm from rapid decompression of a distended bladder
A urethral stricture that will require a suprapubic catheter
The balloon is being inflated within the urethra because the catheter tip has not fully entered the bladder

explanations.A: Balloon inflation in the bladder is painless. Sharp pain with resistance to inflation is never normal, and continuing to inflate can rupture the urethra, causing bleeding, false passage and later stricture.
explanations.B: Bladder spasm produces suprapubic cramping after drainage, not sharp penile pain synchronous with balloon inflation, and 30 mL has barely begun decompression.
explanations.C: The mild resistance was passed and urine returned, so the lumen was negotiated; a stricture presents as inability to pass the catheter. Suprapubic catheterisation is a decision for the surgeon or GP anaesthetist after failed urethral attempts, not an inference from this picture.
explanations.D: Urine can return once the tip is just past the external sphincter in the prostatic urethra, especially in a man with an enlarged prostate and a long urethra. Pain and resistance on inflation indicate the balloon is in the urethra: stop inflating, withdraw the water, advance the catheter to the hub, confirm a free flow of urine, then inflate slowly. If pain recurs or there is bleeding, stop and seek senior help, as the ANZUNS catheterisation guideline advises.

learning_point: Pain or resistance while inflating a urinary catheter balloon means the balloon is in the urethra: stop, deflate, advance to the hub and confirm urine flow before inflating.
setting_note: In a rural hospital there is no urology registrar; if the catheter still cannot be sited safely the junior doctor calls the surgeon or GP anaesthetist and may need to arrange transfer for suprapubic drainage, so recognising the error early avoids a urethral injury that would itself require transfer.

references.title: Australian and New Zealand Urological Nurses Society (ANZUNS). Catheterisation Clinical Guidelines (2021)
references.locator: Male urethral catheterisation: insertion to the hub, confirming urine flow before balloon inflation, troubleshooting pain or resistance

plan: Tests interpretation of pain and resistance during balloon inflation as a urethrally placed balloon, evidencing 1.6 and 1.4. Elderly man with BPH in postoperative retention at a rural hospital, intern catheterising. Distractors: normal discomfort (dangerous reassurance), bladder spasm, stricture needing suprapubic (over-reach). Supported by the ANZUNS catheterisation guidelines.
tutor_context: Key facts: in men insert the catheter to the hub (bifurcation) and confirm urine flow before inflating; pain or resistance on inflation means stop and deflate; after prostatic resistance a larger (16 to 18 Fr) catheter or a coude tip may pass more easily; postoperative retention after spinal anaesthesia and alpha blocker use are common; document residual volume. Misconceptions: urine return proves the tip is in the bladder; smaller catheters are always easier in BPH. Out of scope: suprapubic insertion technique, trial of void planning.

critic.blind_reasoning: Sharp penile pain and resistance on balloon inflation after insertion to only 20 cm with scant urine return indicate the balloon is in the prostatic/urethra; stop inflating, deflate, advance to the hilt and only inflate once urine flows freely with the catheter fully inserted.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good; explanation should state the corrective action (deflate, advance to hilt, consider escalation if resistance persists).

stem: On the surgical ward of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward, a 79-year-old woman who had a bowel resection 4 days ago becomes febrile to 38.6 with rigors; heart rate 104, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20. She has a peripheral cannula in her left forearm inserted 3 days ago and no central line. The registrar, by phone, asks you, the intern, to take blood cultures before the first dose of antibiotics, which the nurse is already drawing up, and to send a full blood count and electrolytes at the same time. The nurse asks how you want the cultures collected.
lead_in: Which blood culture collection technique is correct?

options.text: Two sets from separate venepunctures after chlorhexidine-alcohol antisepsis, 8 to 10 mL per bottle, before antibiotics
One set drawn through the existing peripheral cannula after flushing it, to avoid a second needle in a frail patient
A single set of 2 to 3 mL in each bottle taken with the other bloods from one venepuncture, as volume matters less than speed
Two sets taken 30 minutes apart from the same venepuncture site, after the first antibiotic dose so that treatment is not delayed

explanations.A: Therapeutic Guidelines and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard recommend two sets (aerobic and anaerobic bottles) from separate venepunctures, with adequate skin antisepsis (2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol, allowed to dry) and 8 to 10 mL per bottle in adults, because yield rises with volume and two sites help distinguish contaminants from true bacteraemia. Cultures are taken before antibiotics but must not delay them by more than a few minutes; the other bloods are collected after the culture bottles from the same venepuncture.
explanations.B: Cultures drawn from an existing peripheral cannula have high contamination rates and are not recommended unless no other access is possible, and then only as one of two sets.
explanations.C: Low-volume cultures markedly reduce the chance of detecting bacteraemia; the volume inoculated is the single most important factor in yield.
explanations.D: Two sets can be taken at the same time from different sites; spacing them 30 minutes apart delays antibiotics unnecessarily, and taking cultures after antibiotics reduces yield.

learning_point: Adult blood cultures are two sets from two separate venepuncture sites, 8 to 10 mL per bottle, after chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antisepsis, before but without delaying antibiotics.
setting_note: The technique is the same in any hospital; in a regional hospital cultures may travel to a distant laboratory, so correct labelling with time and site and prompt transport matter, and the intern should ensure antibiotics are not held up waiting for a second site.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Sepsis and septic shock: investigations, blood culture collection (two sets, adequate volume, before antibiotics)

references.title: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard (2022)
references.locator: Quality statements on time-critical management: cultures before antimicrobials without delaying treatment

plan: Tests recall of correct adult blood culture technique, evidencing 1.6, 1.5 and 1.1. Elderly postoperative woman with rigors on a regional surgical ward, intern instructed by phone. Distractors: cannula draw (convenience), low volume (speed), spaced sets after antibiotics (misremembered rule). Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines sepsis investigations and the ACSQHC Sepsis standard.
tutor_context: Key facts: two sets from separate sites (or one peripheral plus one from a central line if line infection suspected), 8 to 10 mL per bottle (20 mL per set) in adults, chlorhexidine-alcohol antisepsis of skin and bottle tops, inoculate aerobic bottle first with a syringe, do not draw cultures from existing peripheral cannulas, label with time and site, collect before antibiotics but never delay antibiotics in sepsis by more than minutes. Misconceptions: a single set suffices; cultures must be spaced in time. Out of scope: antibiotic selection, interpretation of contaminants.

critic.blind_reasoning: Blood cultures: two sets from separate fresh venepuncture sites after chlorhexidine/alcohol antisepsis, 8-10 mL per bottle, before antibiotics. Drawing through an existing cannula increases contamination; low volume reduces yield; sampling after antibiotics reduces sensitivity.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Shorten A or add detail to B/C so length does not give it away.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): A is the longest and most detailed option; D contains an obvious error (after antibiotics).

stem: You are a PGY2 in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital. A 31-year-old man has right iliac fossa pain, fever and a CT report of acute appendicitis. When you phone the surgical registrar with an ISBAR referral, she interrupts, calls you 'useless' for not having a lactate, says 'don't waste my time, call me when you have actually done your job' and hangs up. This is the third time this week she has spoken to you or your intern colleagues this way; one intern was in tears yesterday. The patient needs surgical admission tonight. The ED consultant is on the floor and your term supervisor, a physician, is on call for the department. Your hospital has a Director of Clinical Training and a medical education unit.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Accept that this is surgical culture, obtain the lactate and call the registrar back without comment
Confront the registrar in front of the team when she next comes to the department, so others see it challenged
Have the ED consultant escalate the referral, then record the exchange and raise it with your term supervisor
Describe the interaction in the junior doctors' group chat so that colleagues are warned about her

explanations.A: Tolerating the behaviour harms you and your colleagues, normalises it and leaves a patient's care hostage to a registrar's mood. Good medical practice and the AMC framework expect doctors to contribute to a culture free of bullying, which includes not accepting it as normal.
explanations.B: A public confrontation escalates conflict, is unlikely to change behaviour and could itself be seen as unprofessional; the hospital has processes for exactly this situation.
explanations.C: Patient care comes first: the ED consultant can secure the admission at a senior level. Then a factual, dated note of what was said, and raising it with the term supervisor, Director of Clinical Training or medical education unit (or the hospital's complaint and support pathways), uses the graded, supported route the hospital provides. Checking on the affected intern is part of a safe workplace.
explanations.D: An informal group chat spreads the issue without resolving it, may breach confidentiality and professional standards, exposes you to allegations of defamation, and does nothing for the patient or the interns.

learning_point: When a senior colleague's behaviour is abusive, secure the patient's care through your own senior first, then document the facts and raise it through the hospital's supervision and support processes rather than retaliating or ignoring it.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the same registrar or surgeon may be the only surgical contact and the supervisor may be the director of medical services; the health network's prevocational education unit and the Rural Support Service can be contacted, and the principle of securing patient care first, then escalating formally, is unchanged.

references.title: Medical Board of Australia. Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia (2020)
references.locator: Section 4.2 Respect for medical colleagues and other healthcare professionals (bullying, harassment and discrimination)

references.title: AMC National Framework for Prevocational (PGY1 and PGY2) Medical Training: Outcome statements
references.locator: Outcome 2.6 Safe and supportive workplaces; Outcome 1.1 graded assertiveness and escalation

plan: Tests the management of registrar bullying during a referral while keeping patient care first, evidencing 2.6, 2.1 and 2.4. PGY2 in a metropolitan ED with a consultant and supervisor available. Distractors: tolerate (common), public confrontation, group chat. Supported by Good medical practice and the AMC framework outcome statements.
tutor_context: Key facts: bullying and harassment are breaches of Good medical practice and of SA Health workplace policy; the junior doctor's duties are to keep the patient safe (escalate the referral via their own senior), document contemporaneously, and use formal channels (term supervisor, DCT, medical education unit, Employee Assistance Program, AMA SA Doctors' Health); support colleagues who were affected. Misconceptions: it must be tolerated to get a reference; social media or group chats are a safe outlet. Out of scope: formal HR investigation processes, AHPRA notification thresholds.
uncertainty_note: Section numbering in Good medical practice (2020) for respect for colleagues and bullying is cited from memory and should be verified; the content of the obligation is not in doubt.

critic.blind_reasoning: Patient safety first: ensure the admission happens via consultant-to-consultant escalation, then document the behaviour factually and raise it through the appropriate supervisor/DCT process, consistent with Good medical practice and SA Health bullying policy. Public confrontation and group-chat exposure are unprofessional; acceptance perpetuates harm.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Distractors are too weak; consider a more tempting alternative (e.g., obtain the lactate and re-refer, then report later) and trim C.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): C is markedly longer and the only option with a process-based pathway; distractors are short and obviously wrong.

stem: You are the intern on the medical ward of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward and CT only in business hours. A 56-year-old woman was admitted yesterday after a witnessed first generalised tonic-clonic seizure; her CT head and bloods are normal and she has recovered fully. She drives the local school bus. When you explain that she must not drive for the present and will need neurology follow-up, she becomes distressed: in this town everyone knows everyone, her job is the family's only income, and she asks you to 'keep this between us'. She says she will keep driving the bus because 'nothing will happen'. She has decision-making capacity. Your consultant will do a phone ward round in an hour.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Respect her confidentiality completely, document the advice not to drive and leave the decision with her
Telephone her employer to tell them she has had a seizure and must not drive the school bus
Ask the ward nurse, who knows the family, to persuade her relatives to take away her car keys
Tell her not to drive and, with your consultant, notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, telling her so

explanations.A: Confidentiality is not absolute. In South Australia, section 148 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1959 places a legal duty on medical practitioners to notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles when they believe a patient is unfit to drive, and Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive sets a substantial non-driving period after a first seizure that is far longer for commercial drivers. A first seizure in a bus driver who intends to keep driving is the clearest case for this duty.
explanations.B: Disclosure to an employer is not authorised by the Act or by privacy principles; the legal pathway is notification to the Registrar, who acts on her licence. Telling the employer would be a breach of confidence.
explanations.C: Using a nurse's personal connections and involving family without the patient's consent breaches her privacy, is unprofessional and unreliable, and does not discharge the legal duty.
explanations.D: This is candid with the patient, documents the advice (which also protects the doctor), involves the senior for a decision an intern should not make alone, fulfils the statutory obligation, and limits disclosure to the minimum necessary to the authorised recipient. Austroads notes that a practitioner who notifies in good faith is protected from civil liability. Offering social work support and a clear neurology plan is part of good care.

learning_point: In South Australia doctors have a legal duty to notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles when a patient is unfit to drive; tell the patient, involve your senior, disclose only to the Registrar and document.
setting_note: In a small town the stakes for confidentiality are higher because any disclosure beyond the Registrar will spread quickly; the duty is the same in Adelaide, where the patient's anonymity is less fragile and social work and neurology are closer at hand.

references.title: Austroads and National Transport Commission. Assessing Fitness to Drive for commercial and private vehicle drivers (2022)
references.locator: Part A: Reporting responsibilities of health professionals (mandatory reporting in SA and NT); Part B: Seizures and epilepsy, first seizure, commercial standards

references.title: Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (South Australia)
references.locator: Section 148: duty of medical practitioners to notify the Registrar of a person unfit to drive

references.title: Medical Board of Australia. Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia (2020)
references.locator: Confidentiality and privacy; disclosure required by law

plan: Tests management of a confidentiality conflict with a statutory reporting duty in SA, evidencing 2.1, 1.2 and 2.4. Middle-aged bus driver on a regional ward after a first seizure, consultant by phone. Distractors: absolute confidentiality (misreads the law), telling the employer (over-disclosure), informal family pressure (unprofessional). Supported by Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, the SA Motor Vehicles Act and Good medical practice.
tutor_context: Key facts: SA and NT have mandatory reporting of drivers believed unfit; elsewhere reporting is discretionary; the doctor tells the patient, documents, and discloses only to the licensing authority; first seizure means no private driving for a defined period (commonly 6 months if investigations normal) and much longer non-driving for commercial licences, decided with neurology; good-faith notifiers are protected. Misconceptions: the employer can be told; capacity means the patient's wish is final. Out of scope: exact non-driving periods, seizure treatment.
uncertainty_note: South Australia and the Northern Territory are the jurisdictions with mandatory reporting of unfit drivers by health professionals; the exact section (s148 Motor Vehicles Act 1959) should be verified against the current Act.

critic.blind_reasoning: South Australia (Motor Vehicles Act 1959 s148) imposes a legal duty on doctors to notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles when they believe a patient is unfit to drive; a commercial bus driver after a first seizure who states she will keep driving clearly meets this. Disclosure is limited to the Registrar, the patient is informed, and the employer is not contacted.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Clinically and legally sound; condense D and consider making A more tempting (e.g., 'document and ask her GP to follow up') to test knowledge of SA's mandatory reporting.

soft_flags: cueing: absolute term in distractor B
cueing (critic): D is roughly three times longer than the other options and contains the legal rationale; strongly cued.

secondary_areas: Palliative care and goals of care
stem: You are a PGY1 on a rural placement in a general practice linked to a Yorke Peninsula hospital whose 4-bed emergency department is staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. At 07:30 the practice nurse tells you that a 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer, known to the practice and receiving community palliative care, was found dead in bed by his wife this morning. His GP last reviewed him 6 days ago and had discussed that death was expected within weeks. The wife mentions that yesterday he fell down the back steps and hit his head but "seemed alright". She asks you to complete the paperwork so the funeral director can collect him. The GP is on the road and will arrive in an hour.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Complete the medical certificate of cause of death, recording metastatic lung cancer as the cause.
Explain the death is reportable and notify police or the State Coroner's Office before certifying.
Ask the community palliative care nurse to confirm the death so the funeral director can proceed.
Leave the body undisturbed and ask the wife to wait until the GP arrives to complete the certificate.

explanations.A: Completing a cause-of-death certificate is wrong here even though death was anticipated. Under the Coroners Act 2003 (SA), a death that may have been caused or contributed to by injury, including a fall with head strike the day before, is reportable, and a doctor must not certify a reportable death.
explanations.B: Reporting the death is correct. A recent fall with head strike means the death cannot be assumed to be natural; it must be reported to the Coroner, usually by notifying police, who attend and liaise with the State Coroner's Office. The Coroner may still release the body quickly if the history is clear, but that decision is not the junior doctor's to make.
explanations.C: Confirming that death has occurred is different from certifying its cause. A nurse verifying death does not resolve the reporting duty, and the funeral director cannot remove the body of a reportable death without the Coroner's authority.
explanations.D: Waiting for the GP delays the legally required report and leaves the wife without an explanation. The duty to report applies to any doctor who becomes aware of a reportable death, and a PGY1 should recognise and act on it, while also informing the GP.

learning_point: An expected death becomes reportable to the Coroner if injury may have contributed, such as a recent fall, and a junior doctor must not certify cause of death until the Coroner declines jurisdiction.
setting_note: In a rural town the GP often knows the family well and police may be some distance away; the junior doctor should still initiate the report promptly, explain the process compassionately to the family, and inform the GP, who may speak with the Coroner's office about expediting release of the body.

references.title: Coroners Act 2003 (SA), s 3 (definition of reportable death) and s 28 (duty to report)
SA Health, Reporting of Deaths to the Coroner and Medical Certificate Cause of Death guidance
references.locator: Reportable deaths

plan: Tests the legal duty to report a death that may have an injury contribution even when a terminal illness makes death expected. The rural general practice makes the junior doctor the first clinician involved with the GP an hour away. Distractors: certify because death was expected, delegate verification to a nurse, or wait for the GP. Supported by the Coroners Act 2003 (SA).
tutor_context: Key facts: reportable deaths in SA include unexpected, unnatural, unusual or violent deaths, deaths from injury or accident (even if delayed), deaths in custody or care, within 24 hours of surgery or anaesthesia, and deaths where cause is unknown. A doctor who completes a cause-of-death certificate for a reportable death commits an offence. Common misconception: that a palliative diagnosis makes every death certifiable. Out of scope: the Coroner's decision about autopsy and release of the body.
uncertainty_note: The practical pathway (police attendance versus direct phone call to the State Coroner's Office) varies between SA towns; the reporting duty itself is not in doubt.

critic.blind_reasoning: A fall with head strike the day before death means the cause cannot be confidently recorded as natural; under the SA Coroners Act the death should be reported (via police/State Coroner's Office) and no medical certificate of cause of death issued until the Coroner decides. The PGY1 has also never attended this patient, so certifying is not appropriate anyway.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Key defensible but D will attract strong candidates for 'wait for the senior'; consider softening B's 'must' to 'should be discussed with/reported to' and making clear the PGY1 has not attended the patient.

stem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a 30-bed Mid North regional hospital, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, after a witnessed first generalised tonic-clonic seizure at a roadhouse. He drives a B-double truck for a living and also drives his family car. He has recovered fully, examination is normal, blood glucose and electrolytes are normal, and he had no alcohol, drug use, head injury or sleep deprivation. CT is available in the morning and the physician on call advises outpatient neurology referral and EEG. He asks whether he can drive the truck back to the depot tomorrow, and whether he can at least drive his car in the meantime.
lead_in: Which statement best describes his driving status under the Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive standards?

options.text: He may keep driving the truck until neurology review, because a single seizure does not establish epilepsy.
He may drive his car in the meantime, but not the truck until a neurologist clears him for commercial driving.
He must not drive either vehicle, for at least 6 months (car) or years (truck), and must notify the Registrar.
He must stop driving both vehicle classes for 12 months and may then resume driving without any specialist review.

explanations.A: Continuing commercial driving is unsafe and contrary to the standards. The risk of recurrence after a first unprovoked seizure is highest in the following months, and the commercial standard is far stricter than the private one.
explanations.B: Private driving is also prohibited immediately after a first seizure. The default private non-driving period is 6 months, which may be modified by a specialist, and the patient must be advised not to drive any vehicle until cleared.
explanations.C: This is the correct interpretation. After a first unprovoked seizure the private non-driving period is 6 months and the commercial period is measured in years, with specialist review required. The patient has a legal duty to notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, and in South Australia the doctor must also notify if they believe the person's driving is likely to endanger the public. The advice and the patient's response must be documented.
explanations.D: The periods differ between private and commercial licences, and return to driving depends on specialist assessment, not simply time elapsed.

learning_point: After a first seizure a patient must stop driving all vehicles immediately, with much longer restrictions for commercial licences, and the junior doctor must give and document clear non-driving advice and address notification to the Registrar.
setting_note: In a regional town where there is no public transport and the patient's livelihood depends on driving, the conversation is harder but the standard is unchanged; involve the physician on call, give written advice, and arrange follow-up with the GP and neurology by telehealth.

references.title: Austroads and NTC, Assessing Fitness to Drive for commercial and private vehicle drivers (2022)
references.locator: Part B, Seizures and epilepsy: first seizure; Part A, Legal and ethical responsibilities

references.title: Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (SA)
references.locator: s 148 (notification by medical practitioners)

plan: Tests interpretation of fitness-to-drive standards after a first seizure in a commercial driver, a common ED task. Distractors reflect common misconceptions: no epilepsy so no restriction, private driving allowed, or a fixed period without specialist review. Supported by AFTD 2022 and the SA Motor Vehicles Act.
tutor_context: Key facts: first unprovoked seizure means no driving for at least 6 months (private) and far longer for commercial licences, subject to specialist review; the patient must notify the Registrar; SA is one of the jurisdictions where doctors have a statutory duty to notify when they believe a driver would endanger the public, and are protected when doing so. Misconceptions: that a single seizure carries no restriction, or that a private car is exempt. Out of scope: antiepileptic drug choice and EEG interpretation.
uncertainty_note: Exact commercial non-driving period for a first seizure (5 years off treatment in current AFTD) is described as 'years' to avoid depending on an edition-specific figure; the SA statutory duty for doctors to notify under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959 s 148 should be confirmed by reviewers.

critic.blind_reasoning: Austroads AFTD: after a first unprovoked seizure the private non-driving period is at least 6 months and the commercial period is years (5 years default), with a legal duty in SA to notify the Registrar of Motor Vehicles. He cannot drive either vehicle now.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Trim C to a single statement (e.g. 'must not drive any vehicle; private 6 months, commercial several years; must notify the Registrar') or lengthen distractors to match.

soft_flags: cueing: absolute term in distractor D
cueing (critic): C is roughly twice the length of every other option and bundles three correct facts; the longest, most hedged option is the answer.

stem: You are the junior doctor covering the ward and the emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. Earlier in the week you treated a 34-year-old woman for anaphylaxis to a wasp sting; she recovered fully and was discharged with an adrenaline autoinjector and an action plan. At 21:00 she comes to the emergency department desk with her partner and hands you an envelope containing $300 in cash "to say thank you for saving my life", plus a large box of chocolates for the nurses. The triage nurse is watching and the department is otherwise quiet. She is clearly emotional and says she will be offended if you refuse.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Accept the cash so as not to offend her, and declare it to the Director of Medical Services in the morning.
Accept the cash on the condition that it is shared among the nursing staff who were on duty that night.
Decline both the cash and the chocolates and explain that staff are not permitted to accept anything from patients.
Decline the cash, suggest a card or hospital donation instead, and let the nurses keep the chocolates per policy.

explanations.A: Accepting cash from a patient is not acceptable under Good medical practice or SA Health policy, and declaring it afterwards does not cure the conflict of interest or the perception of one. Declining is the required action, not disclosure after the fact.
explanations.B: Redistributing the money does not change its character: a cash gift from a patient to clinicians creates a real or perceived conflict of interest and is not permitted under the SA Health gifts and benefits policy.
explanations.C: Refusing everything is unnecessarily rigid and risks humiliating a grateful patient. Token gifts of nominal value shared with a team are generally permitted, provided they are declared where required and not sought.
explanations.D: This response protects professional boundaries while respecting the patient's gratitude: cash is declined with a clear explanation, an acceptable alternative is offered, and a modest shared gift is handled according to local policy, including declaration if the policy requires it.

learning_point: Doctors must not accept money from patients; gratitude can be acknowledged by declining graciously, explaining the rule and redirecting to a card or hospital donation, while nominal shared gifts are managed under the local gifts and benefits policy.
setting_note: In a small country town the doctor and patient will meet again socially, which makes declining feel harder but makes clear boundaries more important; knowing the local hospital's gifts and benefits policy and register in advance helps.

references.title: Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia (2020)
references.locator: Section 10.12 Conflicts of interest; 10.13 Financial and commercial dealings

references.title: SA Health Gifts, Benefits and Hospitality Policy Directive
references.locator: Acceptance and declaration of gifts

plan: Tests the immediate handling of a cash gift from a grateful patient, a situation junior doctors commonly meet in small communities. Distractors: accept and declare, accept and share, refuse everything rigidly. Supported by Good medical practice section 10.12 and the SA Health gifts policy.
tutor_context: Key facts: cash or cash equivalents from patients must be declined; token gifts of nominal value shared with a team may be accepted and declared under the local policy; gifts must never influence care or be solicited. Misconceptions: that declaring a gift afterwards makes acceptance acceptable, or that all gifts must be refused. Out of scope: industry sponsorship rules, which are covered elsewhere.

critic.blind_reasoning: Cash can never be accepted under SA Health gifts and benefits policy and Good medical practice; a gracious decline with an alternative (card, hospital donation) and acceptance of a shared nominal gift if policy allows is the professional response.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Shorten D and remove the hedge, or give C and A equivalent nuance so length does not give it away.

soft_flags: cueing (critic): D is the longest option, is the only one with warmth ('thank her warmly') and includes a hedged 'if local policy allows' clause, all pointing to it.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the medical ward of a metropolitan general hospital at 01:30. The medical registrar on site overnight has just arrived from the residents' room to review a 58-year-old man with new central chest pain, a heart rate of 104 and an ECG showing 1 mm ST depression in the lateral leads. As the registrar leans over the chart you notice a strong smell of alcohol, slurred speech and an unsteady gait; the registrar fumbles the ECG and says "just give him some morphine, he's fine". The nurse looks at you with concern. The on-call consultant physician is available by phone and there is an after-hours hospital coordinator in the building.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action now?

options.text: Phone the on-call consultant immediately about both the patient and the registrar, and ensure the patient is managed by a doctor who is fit to practise.
Manage the patient yourself using the chest pain pathway and raise your concerns about the registrar with the Director of Clinical Training in the morning.
Ask the registrar to rest in the residents' room, cover the ward alone for the rest of the shift, and document what you observed.
Phone AHPRA now to make a mandatory notification, then continue the shift with the registrar once the call is made.

explanations.A: Patient safety comes first. A deteriorating patient with possible acute coronary syndrome needs a competent senior decision-maker now, and an apparently intoxicated registrar must not continue to practise tonight. Escalating immediately to the on-call consultant and the after-hours coordinator achieves both, and the hospital then manages the colleague, including any notification obligations.
explanations.B: Managing an unstable patient alone as an intern, without senior support, is outside safe scope, and delaying action on an intoxicated colleague leaves other patients exposed overnight.
explanations.C: Removing the registrar from the floor without telling anyone leaves the hospital's only medical registrar unavailable, you unsupported, and the colleague without help. Documentation is appropriate but is not a substitute for escalation.
explanations.D: Practising while intoxicated is a ground for mandatory notification, but the notification is not the urgent first action at 01:30 and AHPRA cannot make the ward safe tonight. Allowing the registrar to continue working after the call would be unsafe.

learning_point: When a colleague appears impaired at work, the junior doctor's first duty is to make the patient safe by escalating immediately to the on-call consultant and hospital management, not to manage alone or defer the concern to the morning.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the impaired colleague may be the only senior doctor on site, so escalation goes to the on-call GP or consultant by phone and the after-hours manager, and retrieval or telehealth advice may be needed for the patient.

references.title: Medical Board of Australia, Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia (2020)
references.locator: Section 11.2 Other doctors' health; 11.3 Mandatory reporting

references.title: AHPRA and National Boards, Guidelines: Mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners (2020)
references.locator: Intoxication at work

plan: Tests the immediate management when a supervising registrar appears intoxicated while an unstable patient needs review. The key is dual escalation to the on-call consultant for patient and colleague safety. Distractors: intern manages alone, hides the registrar, or treats AHPRA notification as the first step. Supported by Good medical practice sections 11.2-11.3 and the AHPRA mandatory notification guidelines.
tutor_context: Key facts: an intoxicated colleague must not continue clinical work; escalate to the senior on call and hospital management immediately; the hospital usually makes any mandatory notification, though the individual duty remains. Misconceptions: that reporting a colleague is disloyal, or that the intern should quietly cover. Out of scope: the details of the AHPRA notification process and employer disciplinary pathways.

critic.blind_reasoning: An apparently intoxicated registrar cannot be allowed to direct care of an unstable chest pain patient; the PGY1 must escalate immediately to the on-call consultant (and/or after-hours coordinator) so that the patient is managed by a fit doctor and the registrar is removed from duty. Mandatory notification to AHPRA follows later, not at 01:30.
critic.notes_for_reviewer: Good item; explanation should mention the after-hours coordinator as an alternative escalation route and that the AHPRA notification is still required subsequently.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the general ward of a regional hospital with a small medical ward and no ICU. You and the intern are looking after a 55-year-old woman admitted with cellulitis, whose care has been thorough and appropriate. Over coffee the intern confides that he was diagnosed with depression 4 months ago, sees his GP monthly and a psychologist fortnightly, takes sertraline 100 mg daily, is sleeping well and feels he is coping at work. He asks you not to tell anyone. The ward nurse manager, who overheard part of the conversation, later asks you whether you now have to "report him to AHPRA".
lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the nurse manager's question?

options.text: Yes; any mental illness diagnosed in a registered practitioner must be notified to AHPRA within 30 days.
Yes, but the notification should be made through the Director of Clinical Training rather than directly.
No; a treated condition not placing patients at substantial risk is below the notification threshold.
No notification is needed provided he stops clinical duties until a psychiatrist confirms he is fit to work.

explanations.A: A health condition alone is not a notifiable matter. Mandatory notification for impairment applies only when the practitioner is placing the public at substantial risk of harm, and the National Law explicitly aims not to deter practitioners from seeking treatment.
explanations.B: Routing a notification through a supervisor does not change the threshold; there is nothing to notify here. Sharing his confidential disclosure without consent would also breach his trust unless there was a safety concern.
